<a name="chapter-6"></a>
# Chapter 6: OSPFv2/v3 — Multi-Area, Summarization & Filtering

> **Blueprint:** ENCOR 3.2.b — Configure simple OSPFv2/v3 environments, including multiple normal areas, summarization, and filtering (neighbor adjacency, point-to-point and broadcast network types, and passive-interface).

The CCNA guide built single-area OSPF (16.3–16.10) and then lifted the lid in 16.11: adjacency states, LSA types, and stub areas. This chapter turns that preview into a working multi-area design — the shape almost every real OSPF network has — and adds the two tools that make areas worth having: **summarization** and **filtering**. It finishes with **OSPFv3**, which is OSPF for IPv6 (and, optionally, IPv4 too).

Chapter 27 goes further for ENARSI: NBMA network types, virtual links, the full area-type matrix and authentication.

**Terms used throughout** (all from CCNA, restated so nothing is assumed): an **LSA** (link-state advertisement) is one fact a router floods, such as "I have these links at these costs". The **LSDB** (link-state database) is the collection of every LSA a router holds, which is its map. **SPF** (shortest path first, Dijkstra's algorithm) is the calculation each router runs over that map. The **RID** (router ID) is the 32-bit dotted number that names each OSPF router. The **DR** and **BDR** (designated and backup designated router) are the routers that collect and redistribute updates on a shared LAN segment.

---

## 6.1 Why Multiple Areas — and the Router Roles They Create

Recall the reason areas exist (CCNA guide 16.5): in one big area, every router stores every link and reruns SPF whenever **any** link anywhere flaps. Areas **contain the detail**. Inside an area, routers know the full map; between areas, they exchange only **summaries** of what's reachable.

**Story Time 📖:** Think of a large company. Inside the Finance department, everyone knows exactly who sits at which desk. Reception on the ground floor doesn't need that detail. It only needs to know "Finance: 3rd floor". When someone in Finance moves desks, only Finance has to update its seating plan. Reception's directory doesn't change. OSPF areas work the same way: routers inside an area hold the full detailed map, and everyone else holds a short "this range of addresses is over there" line. The **ABR** is the receptionist who knows both sides.

**Worked example: what a flap costs with and without areas.** A user-facing link in area 1 goes up and down every few seconds.

1. **One big area of 200 routers:** the router with the flapping link floods a new Type 1 LSA to all 200 routers. All 200 rerun SPF every time it flaps.
2. **Area 1 with 20 routers, plus area 0 and other areas:** the new Type 1 floods only to the 20 routers in area 1, and only they rerun full SPF. ABR1 updates the one Type 3 LSA for that prefix in the other areas. Routers there recalculate just that route, which is cheap.
3. **And with a summary at ABR1 (6.5):** the /22 summary is still valid while any of its component networks is up, so routers outside area 1 see **no change at all**.

That creates four router roles — one router can hold several at once:

| Role | Definition | Example below |
|------|------------|---------------|
| **Internal router** | All interfaces in one area | R1 |
| **Backbone router** | At least one interface in area 0 | R3, ABR1, ABR2 |
| **ABR** (Area Border Router) | Interfaces in area 0 **and** at least one other area | ABR1, ABR2 |
| **ASBR** (Autonomous System Boundary Router) | Redistributes routes from outside OSPF | R5 |

![Multi-area OSPF with an ABR between each area and an ASBR in an NSSA](images/c06_multiarea.png)

**The golden rule:** every non-backbone area must touch **area 0**, and traffic between two non-backbone areas always crosses area 0. **Why?** Because inter-area routing in OSPF is really **distance vector**. An ABR doesn't pass area 1's map into area 0 — it passes "network X, cost Y", the same kind of rumour RIP trades. Rumours can loop. Forcing every inter-area exchange through a single backbone gives the rumours a strict hub-and-spoke shape with no path back around, so they can't loop. *Inside an area OSPF is link state; between areas it's a distance-vector star centred on area 0.* (An area that can't physically reach area 0 needs a **virtual link** — Chapter 27.)

**📝 Exam-style questions — 6.1**

**Q1.** R7 has interfaces in area 0 and area 2, and it also redistributes static routes into OSPF. Which two roles does R7 hold? (Choose two.)

- **A.** Internal router
- **B.** ABR
- **C.** DR
- **D.** Stub router
- **E.** ASBR

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B, E.** Interfaces in area 0 *and* another area make R7 an ABR. Redistributing routes from outside OSPF makes it an ASBR. One router can hold both roles. **Why not the others:** A is wrong because an internal router has all its interfaces in one area. C is a role on one broadcast segment, decided by election, not by where the router sits in the design. D isn't an OSPF router role (stub is a type of *area*).
</details>

**Q2.** Why must traffic between two non-backbone OSPF areas always cross area 0?

- **A.** Because only area 0 routers are allowed to hold Type 5 LSAs.
- **B.** Because the DR for every area is elected in area 0.
- **C.** Because routing between areas works like distance vector: ABRs pass "network X, cost Y", and forcing every exchange through one backbone gives those advertisements a loop-free hub-and-spoke shape.
- **D.** Because an ABR can only be connected to two areas.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Inside an area OSPF is link state, but between areas an ABR only passes on summaries, much like RIP. Summaries could loop, so OSPF forces them through a single backbone with no path back around. **Why not the others:** A is wrong because Type 5s flood into every normal area. B is wrong because a DR is elected per broadcast segment. D is wrong because an ABR can connect several areas.
</details>

**Q3.** In area 1, the link for 10.1.2.0/24 starts flapping. ABR1 advertises `area 1 range 10.1.0.0 255.255.252.0`, and 10.1.0.0/24, 10.1.1.0/24 and 10.1.3.0/24 stay up. What do routers in area 0 see while the link flaps?

- **A.** No change, because the /22 summary stays valid while any of its components is up
- **B.** A new Type 1 LSA from the router with the flapping link, each time it flaps
- **C.** The Type 3 for 10.1.2.0/24 withdrawn and re-advertised each time
- **D.** A full SPF run on every router in every area

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Area 0 knows only the /22. ABR1 keeps advertising it as long as at least one component route exists, so the flap is hidden from area 0 entirely. **Why not the others:** B is wrong because Type 1 LSAs stay inside area 1. C would happen without the summary. D is wrong because only area 1's routers rerun full SPF.
</details>

---

## 6.2 LSA Types — What Each Router Says, and How Far It Travels

The CCNA guide listed the LSA types (16.11). Here's what each one is **for** in a multi-area network, and the command that shows it:

| Type | Name | Generated by | Floods within | Becomes route code | `show ip ospf database …` |
|------|------|--------------|---------------|--------------------|---------------------------|
| **1** | Router | Every router | Its own area | `O` | `router` |
| **2** | Network | The **DR** on a broadcast segment | Its own area | `O` | `network` |
| **3** | Summary | **ABR** — one per prefix (or per range) | Into the next area | `O IA` | `summary` |
| **4** | ASBR summary | **ABR** — "the ASBR is reachable via me" | Into the next area | — (none) | `asbr-summary` |
| **5** | External | **ASBR** | Whole OSPF domain (not stub areas) | `O E1` / `O E2` | `external` |
| **7** | NSSA external | **ASBR inside an NSSA** | That NSSA only | `O N1` / `O N2` | `nssa-external` |

Following the diagram from left to right:

1. **R1** describes its links in a **Type 1**; a DR on any area 1 LAN adds a **Type 2**. Both stay inside area 1.
2. **ABR1** reads area 1's Type 1/2 database, works out each prefix and its cost, and advertises each prefix into area 0 as a **Type 3**. Area 0 routers see `O IA` routes — "inter-area, reached via ABR1."
3. **R5** redistributes EIGRP routes. Because area 2 is an NSSA (6.3), they enter as **Type 7**.
4. **ABR2** translates each Type 7 into a **Type 5** and floods it to the rest of the domain. In the translated LSA, **ABR2 itself** is the advertising router, not R5. Area 0 routers already know how to reach ABR2 from its Type 1 LSA, so nothing more is needed there. Routers in **area 1** don't have ABR2's Type 1, so **ABR1** advertises a **Type 4** into area 1 saying "ABR2, the router advertising these externals, is reachable through me."

**Why is a Type 4 needed at all?** A Type 5 says "network X is reachable via ASBR R5" — but routers in area 1 have never seen R5's Type 1 LSA (it's in another area), so they have no idea how to reach R5. The ABR fills the gap with a Type 4: "R5 is reachable through me, at this cost." *Type 5 says what's out there; Type 4 says how to get to the router that said it.* (When an NSSA ABR translates Type 7 to Type 5, **the ABR itself** becomes the advertising router, so other areas just need a path to the ABR.)

### E1 versus E2

External routes come in two metric styles, chosen at redistribution time (`metric-type 1` or `2`):

| Type | Metric used | Default? | Use when |
|------|-------------|----------|----------|
| **E2 / N2** | The external **seed metric only** — internal cost to the ASBR is ignored | **Yes** (seed 20; 1 for routes from BGP) | One exit point, or you don't care which ASBR is used |
| **E1 / N1** | Seed metric **plus** the internal cost to reach the ASBR | No | Several ASBRs advertise the same prefix and you want the *closest* one used |

With E2, if two E2 routes have the same seed metric, OSPF does break the tie on the cost to the ASBR (the "forward metric") — but it never adds it into the displayed metric.

For the **same prefix**, OSPF also prefers an E1 route over an E2 route whatever their metrics, following the route-type order in 5.7 (intra-area, inter-area, E1, E2).

**Worked example: why E1 exists.** Two ASBRs both redistribute 172.16.0.0/16. From R1, the internal OSPF cost to ASBR-A is **10** and to ASBR-B is **50**.

| Case | Via ASBR-A | Via ASBR-B | R1 picks | Why |
|------|-----------|-----------|----------|-----|
| E2, both seed 20 | 20 | 20 | **A** | Tie on the metric, broken by the forward metric (10 < 50). Shown as `[110/20]` |
| E2, A seed 30, B seed 20 | 30 | 20 | **B** | E2 compares seeds only. R1 crosses 50 internal cost to save 10 |
| E1, A seed 30, B seed 20 | 30 + 10 = **40** | 20 + 50 = **70** | **A** | E1 counts the trip to the ASBR, so the genuinely closer exit wins |

The middle row is the trap: with E2, a router can pick a far-away exit because the seed metric is all it compares. When several exits advertise the same prefixes, use E1 so every router uses the exit nearest to it.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 6.2**

**Q1.** Which router originates a Type 3 LSA, and which route code does it produce in the receiving area?

- **A.** The ASBR; `O E2`
- **B.** The DR; `O`
- **C.** Every router; `O`
- **D.** The ABR; `O IA`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** An ABR reads one area's Type 1 and Type 2 LSAs, works out each prefix and cost, and advertises it into the next area as a Type 3. There it shows as `O IA` (inter-area). **Why not the others:** A describes a Type 5. B describes a Type 2 network LSA. C describes a Type 1 router LSA.
</details>

**Q2.** Why do ABRs generate Type 4 LSAs?

- **A.** To summarize several Type 5 LSAs into one advertisement
- **B.** Because routers in other areas can't see the ASBR's Type 1 LSA, so the ABR tells them how to reach the router that advertised the externals
- **C.** To carry NSSA external routes into the backbone
- **D.** To advertise the default route into a stub area

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** A Type 5 says "network X is reachable via this ASBR", but the ASBR's Type 1 LSA stays in its own area. The Type 4 fills the gap: "the ASBR is reachable through me, at this cost." **Why not the others:** A is wrong because Type 5s are summarized with `summary-address` on the ASBR. C is wrong because NSSA externals are Type 7s, which the NSSA ABR translates into Type 5s. D is wrong because a stub area's default arrives as a Type 3.
</details>

**Q3.** Two ASBRs redistribute 172.20.0.0/16 as E2 routes. ASBR-A uses seed metric 50 and ASBR-B uses seed metric 40. R1's internal cost is 5 to ASBR-A and 60 to ASBR-B. Which route does R1 install, and what metric does it show?

- **A.** Via ASBR-A, `[110/55]`
- **B.** Via ASBR-A, `[110/50]`
- **C.** Via ASBR-B, `[110/100]`
- **D.** Via ASBR-B, `[110/40]`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** E2 routes compare the seed metric only, so 40 beats 50, and the displayed metric is just the seed. R1 crosses an internal cost of 60 to save 10, which is the classic E2 trap. **Why not the others:** A and C add the internal cost, which is how *E1* routes work. B picks the higher seed.
</details>

**Q4.** R1 learns 172.30.0.0/16 twice: as `O E1` with metric 70 and as `O E2` with metric 20. Which does it install?

- **A.** The E2 route, because 20 is lower than 70
- **B.** The E1 route, because OSPF prefers E1 over E2 for the same prefix, whatever the metrics
- **C.** Both, as unequal-cost paths
- **D.** Whichever ASBR has the higher router ID

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** OSPF's route-type order is intra-area, inter-area, E1, then E2. Metrics are compared only between routes of the same type. **Why not the others:** A compares metrics across types. C is wrong because OSPF has no unequal-cost load balancing. D is invented.
</details>

---

## 6.3 Area Types at ENCOR Depth

**The problem:** some areas have only one way out, typically a branch site behind one ABR. Holding hundreds of external routes there costs memory and CPU and adds nothing, because every one of them points at the same ABR anyway. Special area types replace that detail with a default route.

ENCOR 3.2.b asks for **multiple normal areas**; Chapter 5.7 summarised the special types. Configuration is short:

| Area type | Config (in `router ospf`) | Where |
|-----------|---------------------------|-------|
| Stub | `area 1 stub` | **Every** router in area 1 |
| Totally stubby | `area 1 stub no-summary` | ABR only (other routers just need `area 1 stub`) |
| NSSA | `area 2 nssa` | Every router in area 2 |
| Totally NSSA | `area 2 nssa no-summary` | ABR only (others need `area 2 nssa`) |

**Why must every router in a stub area agree?** Because the stub setting is carried as a **flag in the Hello** (the E-bit). Two routers that disagree about whether external LSAs may exist in their area would build different databases — so OSPF refuses the adjacency. *A mismatched stub flag is one of the quieter reasons neighbours never form.*

**Default routes:** stub and totally stubby areas get a Type 3 default from the ABR automatically, and so does a totally NSSA. A plain **NSSA does not** — add `area 2 nssa default-information-originate` on the ABR if area 2 needs one.

**Worked example: the same router, three area types.** R1 is an internal router in area 1. The network has 50 prefixes in area 1, 400 in other areas and 2,000 externals (redistributed from elsewhere).

| Area 1 configured as | What R1's routing table holds | Roughly how many OSPF routes |
|----------------------|-------------------------------|------------------------------|
| Normal | `O` for area 1, `O IA` for other areas, `O E2` for externals | 50 + 400 + 2,000 = 2,450 |
| Stub (`area 1 stub` everywhere) | `O`, `O IA`, plus `O*IA 0.0.0.0/0` from the ABR | 50 + 400 + 1 = 451 |
| Totally stubby (`no-summary` added on the ABR) | `O` plus `O*IA 0.0.0.0/0` | 50 + 1 = 51 |

R1 can still reach every one of those destinations in all three cases. Anything it no longer knows about matches the default and goes to the ABR, which is exactly where it would have gone anyway.

### Originating a Default Into Normal Areas

In normal areas, a default route is just another external route, and it's created on the router that owns the exit (typically the internet edge) with **`default-information originate`**:

```
EDGE(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1          ! the real exit
EDGE(config)# router ospf 1
EDGE(config-router)# default-information originate          ! only while a default is in RIB
EDGE(config-router)# default-information originate always   ! ...or: advertise it regardless
EDGE(config-router)# default-information originate metric 10 metric-type 1  ! optional
```

The command makes EDGE an **ASBR** and floods `0.0.0.0/0` as a **Type 5** LSA, seen elsewhere as `O*E2 0.0.0.0/0` (metric 1, type E2 by default).

**Without `always`**, nothing is originated unless EDGE has a default route in its routing table from **some other source**, such as a static route, DHCP or BGP. If that default disappears, the Type 5 is withdrawn. **Why is that the safer default behaviour?** Because the default route is a promise: "send me anything you can't route and I'll deliver it." If EDGE has lost its own exit, it can't keep that promise, and withdrawing the advertisement lets the rest of the network fail over to another exit. **`always`** keeps advertising even with no default in EDGE's RIB. Use it when the default should point at EDGE no matter what, for example when EDGE forwards to a firewall reached by a route that isn't a default. Used carelessly, it **black-holes** traffic at a router that has nowhere to send it.

With two internet exits, advertise the default from both and use `metric-type 1` (E1) so each router picks the **closest** exit, or give one exit a lower `metric` to make it primary.

For example, EDGE-A and EDGE-B both use `default-information originate metric 10 metric-type 1`. R7 is cost 5 from EDGE-A and cost 20 from EDGE-B, so it sees `O*E1 0.0.0.0/0 [110/15]` via EDGE-A (10 + 5, against 10 + 20 = 30 via EDGE-B). A router on the other side of the network, close to EDGE-B, picks EDGE-B. If EDGE-A loses its own default route, it withdraws the Type 5, and R7 moves to EDGE-B at metric 30.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 6.3**

**Q1.** Area 1 must become totally stubby. What is the minimum correct configuration?

- **A.** `area 1 stub` on the ABR only
- **B.** `area 1 nssa no-summary` on the ABR, and `area 1 nssa` on the other routers
- **C.** `area 1 stub no-summary` on the ABR, and `area 1 stub` on every other router in area 1
- **D.** `area 1 stub no-summary` on the internal routers only

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Every router in the area needs the stub flag or adjacencies fail. Only the ABR needs `no-summary`, because only the ABR generates the Type 3s that it then suppresses. **Why not the others:** A sets the flag on one side only, so the ABR's adjacencies into area 1 drop, and it creates a plain stub area anyway. B creates a totally NSSA, which is a different area type. D leaves the ABR without the stub flag.
</details>

**Q2.** A new router is added to stub area 1. The engineer forgets `area 1 stub` on it. What happens?

- **A.** It forms adjacencies and receives Type 5 LSAs that the other routers drop.
- **B.** It cannot form adjacencies with its neighbours, because the stub flag is carried in the Hello and must match.
- **C.** It becomes the area's ABR and converts the area back to normal.
- **D.** It forms adjacencies but never runs SPF.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** The stub setting is the E-bit in every Hello. Two routers that disagree would build different databases, so OSPF refuses the adjacency. `debug ip ospf hello` shows a mismatched stub/transit option bit. **Why not the others:** A is wrong because the adjacency never forms. C is invented. D is wrong because a router either forms adjacencies and runs SPF, or doesn't form them at all.
</details>

**Q3.** EDGE is configured with `default-information originate` (without `always`). Its only default route is a static route to the ISP. The static route is removed. What happens?

- **A.** EDGE keeps advertising 0.0.0.0/0, because the command makes it an ASBR permanently.
- **B.** EDGE advertises 0.0.0.0/0 with metric 16 to mark it unreachable.
- **C.** EDGE converts the default into a Type 3 LSA.
- **D.** EDGE withdraws its Type 5 default, so the rest of the network can fail over to another exit.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** Without `always`, the default is advertised only while EDGE has a default route in its own routing table from some other source. That's the safe behaviour: a router that has lost its own exit shouldn't attract traffic it can't deliver. **Why not the others:** A describes `always`. B is a RIP idea; OSPF has no "infinite metric" like that. C is wrong because a default from `default-information originate` is always a Type 5.
</details>

**Q4.** Area 2 is a plain NSSA. Its internal routers have no default route. What must you add, and where?

- **A.** `area 2 nssa default-information-originate` on the ABR
- **B.** `default-information originate always` on every router in area 2
- **C.** `area 2 stub` on the ABR
- **D.** Nothing; an NSSA always receives a default automatically

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Stub, totally stubby and totally NSSA areas get a default automatically, but a plain NSSA does not. You add it on the ABR. **Why not the others:** B would make every router an ASBR advertising a default, which is wrong for internal routers with no exit. C changes the area type and breaks adjacencies. D is the trap the question tests.
</details>

---

## 6.4 Configuring Multi-Area OSPFv2

**The problem:** each interface has to be placed in exactly the right area. An interface in the wrong area won't form an adjacency (the area ID must match), or it will advertise its subnet into the wrong part of the design.

Two ways to put an interface in an area. Both are valid IOS XE, and you'll see both on the exam:

```
! Method 1 - network statements (wildcard match, as in CCNA)
ABR1(config)# router ospf 1
ABR1(config-router)# router-id 2.2.2.2
ABR1(config-router)# network 10.1.12.0 0.0.0.255 area 1
ABR1(config-router)# network 10.0.23.0 0.0.0.255 area 0

! Method 2 - directly on the interface (clearer, and wins over network statements)
ABR1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
ABR1(config-if)# ip ospf 1 area 1
ABR1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/2
ABR1(config-if)# ip ospf 1 area 0
```

**Why prefer interface mode?** Because it's explicit. A `network` statement is a pattern; if someone later adds an interface whose address happens to match, it silently joins OSPF, in whatever area the pattern says. Interface-level `ip ospf 1 area 1` puts exactly one interface in exactly one area, and reading the interface config tells you everything. *Patterns surprise you; statements don't.*

An ABR needs nothing special — it **becomes** an ABR the moment it has interfaces in area 0 and another area. Verify with:

```
ABR1# show ip ospf | include border|Number of areas in
 It is an area border router
 Number of areas in this router is 2. 2 normal 0 stub 0 nssa
```

The full `show ip ospf` output then lists each area (`Area BACKBONE(0)`, `Area 1`) with its interface count, authentication and configured ranges.

To check which area each interface landed in, use one line per interface:

```
ABR1# show ip ospf interface brief
Interface    PID   Area            IP Address/Mask    Cost  State Nbrs F/C
Gi0/2        1     0               10.0.23.2/24       1     BDR   1/1
Gi0/1        1     1               10.1.12.2/24       1     DR    1/1
```

**Reading it:** Gi0/2 is in area 0 and Gi0/1 in area 1, which is what makes ABR1 an ABR. **State** is this router's role on that segment (DR, BDR, DROTHER, or P2P on point-to-point links). **Nbrs F/C** is "neighbours FULL / total neighbours". On a link with only two routers, a value like `0/1` means a neighbour has been seen but the adjacency hasn't completed. On a busy LAN, a DROTHER legitimately shows F lower than C, because it stays in 2WAY with the other DROTHERs.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 6.4**

**Q1.** ABR1 has `network 10.1.12.0 0.0.0.255 area 1` under `router ospf 1`. Its GigabitEthernet0/1 is 10.1.12.2/24 and is also configured with `ip ospf 1 area 0`. Which area is Gi0/1 in?

- **A.** Area 1, because `network` statements are processed first
- **B.** Area 0, because interface-level configuration wins over `network` statements
- **C.** Both areas, so ABR1 becomes an ABR on that one interface
- **D.** Neither; IOS rejects the conflicting configuration

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** `ip ospf 1 area 0` on the interface takes priority over a matching `network` statement. **Why not the others:** A has the priority the wrong way round. C is wrong because one interface belongs to exactly one area. D is wrong because both commands are accepted.
</details>

**Q2.** Refer to the exhibit. GigabitEthernet0/1 connects ABR1 to exactly one other router. What does the output tell you about that link?

```
ABR1# show ip ospf interface brief
Interface    PID   Area            IP Address/Mask    Cost  State Nbrs F/C
Gi0/2        1     0               10.0.23.2/24       1     DR    1/1
Gi0/1        1     1               10.1.12.2/30       1     P2P   0/1
```

- **A.** The link is healthy; P2P links never show FULL neighbours.
- **B.** No neighbour has been heard on Gi0/1.
- **C.** A neighbour has been seen on Gi0/1, but the adjacency has not reached FULL.
- **D.** Gi0/1 is passive.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** `Nbrs F/C` is neighbours FULL over neighbours total. `0/1` means one neighbour is known but none is FULL. On a two-router link that's a stuck adjacency to investigate (MTU, network type and so on). **Why not the others:** A is wrong because P2P neighbours do reach FULL. B would show `0/0`. D would show no neighbours at all, because a passive interface ignores Hellos.
</details>

**Q3.** Why is `ip ospf <process> area <area>` on each interface usually preferred over `network` statements?

- **A.** `network` statements cannot place interfaces in area 0.
- **B.** Interface mode allows OSPF to run without a router ID.
- **C.** Interface mode is the only way to create an ABR.
- **D.** A `network` statement is a pattern, so an interface added later whose address happens to match joins OSPF silently; interface mode is explicit.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** Interface mode puts exactly one interface in exactly one area, and reading the interface config tells you everything. **Why not the others:** A is false. B is false, since every OSPF router needs a router ID. C is false, because a router becomes an ABR the moment it has interfaces in area 0 and another area, however they were configured.
</details>

## 6.5 Summarization

**The problem:** without summaries, every prefix in every area is advertised separately everywhere, and every change to any of them ripples through the whole network.

Without summarization, ABR1 sends one Type 3 LSA into area 0 for **every** prefix in area 1. A flap of any one of them ripples into every other area as a changed Type 3. Summarization replaces the list with one advertisement — and a single summary only changes if **every** component route disappears.

OSPF can summarize in exactly **two** places, each with its own command:

| Where | Summarizes | Command (under `router ospf`) |
|-------|-----------|-------------------------------|
| **ABR** | Internal routes (Type 1/2) of an area, into Type 3s | `area <area-id> range <net> <mask>` |
| **ASBR** | Redistributed externals (Type 5 or 7) | `summary-address <net> <mask>` |

### Inter-Area Summary at the ABR

Area 1 contains 10.1.0.0/24, 10.1.1.0/24, 10.1.2.0/24 and 10.1.3.0/24:

```
ABR1(config)# router ospf 1
ABR1(config-router)# area 1 range 10.1.0.0 255.255.252.0    ! one /22 instead of four /24s
```

**How to work out the summary.** Write the third octet (the one that changes) in binary:

| Network | Third octet | Binary |
|---------|-------------|--------|
| 10.1.0.0 | 0 | 000000**00** |
| 10.1.1.0 | 1 | 000000**01** |
| 10.1.2.0 | 2 | 000000**10** |
| 10.1.3.0 | 3 | 000000**11** |

The first 6 bits are identical in all four, and the last 2 bits take every combination. So the common part is 8 + 8 + 6 = **22** bits: **10.1.0.0/22**, mask 255.255.252.0. The summary covers exactly these four /24s and nothing else. If area 1 had only 10.1.0.0–10.1.2.0, the /22 would also claim 10.1.3.0/24, which doesn't exist. That's legal, and the Null0 route below is what makes it safe.

**Story Time 📖:** A summary is like a postcode. A sorting office in another city doesn't need every street name in your town. "All of 10.1.x up to 10.1.3.x → ABR1" is enough to get the packet to the right town, and ABR1 knows the streets.

The `area` number is the area **the routes live in** (area 1), not the area the summary is sent to. Now area 0 sees a single `O IA 10.1.0.0/22`. On ABR1 itself a new route appears:

```
ABR1# show ip route ospf | include Null0
O        10.1.0.0/22 is a summary, 00:01:12, Null0
```

**Why does the ABR install a summary route pointing at Null0?** To prevent a loop. Suppose 10.1.3.0/24 goes down. Other areas still route 10.1.3.x toward ABR1 (the /22 summary is still advertised). ABR1 has no /24 anymore, so without the discard route it would follow its **default route** — possibly straight back into area 0, which sends it back to ABR1, and so on until the TTL dies. The Null0 summary catches anything inside the /22 that has no more specific route and **drops it** on the spot. *A summary is a promise; the Null0 route makes sure the router can't keep that promise by bouncing traffic in circles.*

### External Summary at the ASBR

```
R5(config)# router ospf 1
R5(config-router)# summary-address 172.16.0.0 255.255.0.0   ! summarize redistributed routes
```

> **Exam trap — right command, right router.** `area range` on an ASBR does **nothing** to external routes, and `summary-address` on an ABR does **nothing** to inter-area routes. Inter-area: `area range` on the ABR. External: `summary-address` on the ASBR (or on the NSSA ABR doing the Type 7→5 translation).

**The design price of summarizing:** you lose detail. Routers outside the area can no longer see that 10.1.3.0/24 is down — they'll keep sending traffic to ABR1, which drops it. And with two ABRs advertising the same summary, a failure *behind* one of them is invisible to the other areas. Summaries trade precision for stability.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 6.5**

**Q1.** Area 3 contains 172.16.8.0/24 through 172.16.15.0/24, and nothing else in that range. Which single summary covers exactly these networks?

- **A.** 172.16.0.0/20
- **B.** 172.16.8.0/22
- **C.** 172.16.8.0/21
- **D.** 172.16.0.0/21

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** In binary, 8 is 00001000 and 15 is 00001111. The first 5 bits of the third octet match and the last 3 take every value, so the prefix is 16 + 5 = /21, starting at 172.16.8.0. **Why not the others:** A also claims 172.16.0.0–7.0, which aren't in area 3. B covers only 8–11. D covers 0–7, not 8–15.
</details>

**Q2.** R5 is an ASBR that redistributes 50 EIGRP routes from 172.16.0.0/16 into OSPF. On which router, and with which command, do you summarize them?

- **A.** On R5, with `summary-address 172.16.0.0 255.255.0.0`
- **B.** On R5, with `area 0 range 172.16.0.0 255.255.0.0`
- **C.** On the ABR, with `area 2 range 172.16.0.0 255.255.0.0`
- **D.** On the ABR, with `summary-address 172.16.0.0 255.255.0.0`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** External routes are summarized where they're created, on the ASBR, with `summary-address`. **Why not the others:** B and C use `area range`, which only summarizes internal routes into Type 3s. D puts `summary-address` on an ABR, where it has no externals to act on (unless it's an NSSA ABR translating Type 7s, which this isn't).
</details>

**Q3.** After `area 1 range 10.1.0.0 255.255.252.0` is configured on ABR1, the route `O 10.1.0.0/22 is a summary, Null0` appears on ABR1. Why?

- **A.** It marks the summary as unreachable until all four components are up.
- **B.** It drops packets inside the /22 that have no more specific route, so they can't loop back out via a default route.
- **C.** It advertises the summary to neighbours inside area 1.
- **D.** It is a temporary route that disappears after SPF completes.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** If 10.1.3.0/24 goes down, other areas still send 10.1.3.x to ABR1 because of the summary. Without the discard route, ABR1 could follow its default route back toward area 0 and loop the packet until its TTL runs out. **Why not the others:** A is wrong because the summary stays up while *any* component exists. C is wrong because the summary goes to the other areas, not into area 1. D is wrong because the route stays as long as the summary is configured.
</details>

**Q4.** Refer to the exhibit. ABR1 connects area 0 and area 1. The 10.1.x.0/24 networks are in area 1, but area 0 still receives the individual /24s instead of a summary. What is wrong?

```
ABR1# show running-config | section router ospf
router ospf 1
 router-id 2.2.2.2
 area 0 range 10.1.0.0 255.255.252.0
 network 10.0.23.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
 network 10.1.0.0 0.0.3.255 area 1
```

- **A.** The mask should be a wildcard mask, 0.0.3.255.
- **B.** `area range` must be configured on every router in area 1.
- **C.** The summary should use `summary-address` because it's on an ABR.
- **D.** The area in `area range` must be the area where the routes live, area 1, not the area the summary is sent to.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** `area 0 range` tries to summarize area 0's own routes. The command that summarizes area 1's prefixes into area 0 is `area 1 range 10.1.0.0 255.255.252.0`. **Why not the others:** A is wrong because `area range` takes a subnet mask. B is wrong because summarization happens only at the ABR. C is wrong because `summary-address` is for externals on an ASBR.
</details>

## 6.6 Filtering

**The problem:** sometimes part of the network shouldn't be reachable from elsewhere. Examples are a lab network, or a test prefix that mustn't leak into production. You need to stop those routes from spreading without breaking OSPF's database rules.

Filtering in OSPF is unusual, because of the link-state rule that **every router in an area must hold an identical LSDB**. You can't simply stop an LSA from reaching one router in the middle of an area. What you *can* do depends on where you are:

| Tool | Where | What it actually filters | Effect on LSDB |
|------|-------|--------------------------|----------------|
| `area X filter-list prefix NAME in|out` | ABR | **Type 3** LSAs entering (`in`) or leaving (`out`) area X | Changes other areas' LSDBs — consistently |
| `area X range … not-advertise` | ABR | Suppresses the summary (and its components) | Same — no Type 3 is created |
| `distribute-list … in` | Any router | Routes going from the LSDB **into the routing table** | **None** — LSAs still arrive and flood on |
| `distribute-list … out` | ASBR | Redistributed routes before they become Type 5/7 | Externals never created |

### Type 3 Filtering at the ABR

Stop area 0 (and everything beyond it) from learning area 1's lab network 10.1.3.0/24:

```
ABR1(config)# ip prefix-list NO-LAB seq 5 deny 10.1.3.0/24
ABR1(config)# ip prefix-list NO-LAB seq 10 permit 0.0.0.0/0 le 32   ! allow everything else
ABR1(config)# router ospf 1
ABR1(config-router)# area 1 filter-list prefix NO-LAB out           ! out OF area 1
```

How ABR1 checks each area 1 prefix against NO-LAB before creating a Type 3 for area 0 (assuming no `area 1 range` is configured):

1. **10.1.3.0/24:** seq 5 matches exactly and says deny, so no Type 3 is created. Area 0 never hears of it.
2. **10.1.2.0/24:** seq 5 doesn't match. Seq 10 (`0.0.0.0/0 le 32`, meaning any prefix of any length) matches and says permit, so the Type 3 is created.
3. Every other area 1 prefix takes the same path as step 2.

On a router in area 0, `show ip ospf database summary 10.1.3.0` now returns nothing, and `show ip route 10.1.3.0` says `% Network not in table`.

`out` means "Type 3s generated **from** area 1's routes"; `in` means "Type 3s being sent **into** area 1." Don't forget the final `permit … le 32`: like an ACL, a prefix list ends in an **implicit deny**, and without that line you'd filter every inter-area route. (Prefix-list syntax in full: Chapter 23.)

### The distribute-list "in" Trap

```
R3(config)# router ospf 1
R3(config-router)# distribute-list prefix NO-LAB in
```

This removes 10.1.3.0/24 from **R3's routing table only**. R3 still holds the LSA, still floods it to its neighbours, and they still install the route — and may forward traffic for it **to R3**, which now has no route and drops it (or follows a default). *A distribute-list in OSPF is a local blindfold, not a wall.* Use it deliberately, for example to stop one router installing a path it shouldn't use; use ABR filtering when you mean "this area should not know."

**📝 Exam-style questions — 6.6**

**Q1.** Routers in area 0 and beyond must not learn area 1's lab network 10.1.3.0/24. All other area 1 prefixes must still be advertised. Which configuration on ABR1 achieves this?

- **A.** `ip prefix-list NO-LAB seq 5 deny 10.1.3.0/24` and `area 1 filter-list prefix NO-LAB out`
- **B.** `ip prefix-list NO-LAB seq 5 deny 10.1.3.0/24`, `ip prefix-list NO-LAB seq 10 permit 0.0.0.0/0 le 32` and `area 1 filter-list prefix NO-LAB out`
- **C.** The same two prefix-list lines as B, and `area 1 filter-list prefix NO-LAB in`
- **D.** The same two prefix-list lines as B, and `distribute-list prefix NO-LAB in` under `router ospf 1`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** `area 1 filter-list … out` filters Type 3s created *from* area 1's routes. The final `permit 0.0.0.0/0 le 32` lets every other prefix through. **Why not the others:** A has no permit line, so the implicit deny blocks every area 1 prefix. C filters Type 3s going *into* area 1, the wrong direction. D only hides the route from ABR1's own routing table; the Type 3 is still advertised.
</details>

**Q2.** R3 is in area 0 and has `distribute-list prefix NO-LAB in` under `router ospf 1`, where NO-LAB denies 10.1.3.0/24. R3's neighbours still have the route, and some of them now send traffic for 10.1.3.0/24 to R3, which drops it. Why?

- **A.** The distribute-list blocks the LSA from reaching R3's neighbours, so they use a stale copy.
- **B.** The distribute-list only affects routes R3 redistributes.
- **C.** A distribute-list in OSPF only stops R3 installing the route in its routing table; R3 still holds and floods the LSA, so its neighbours still install the route.
- **D.** The prefix list is missing a `permit` line.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Every router in an area must hold the same LSDB, so an OSPF distribute-list can't stop LSAs. It only filters what goes from the LSDB into that router's own routing table: a local blindfold, not a wall. **Why not the others:** A has it backwards; the LSA still floods normally. B describes `distribute-list out` on an ASBR. D is wrong because a missing permit would hide more routes on R3, but it wouldn't explain the neighbours' behaviour.
</details>

**Q3.** An engineer configures `area 1 filter-list prefix NO-LAB out` with a prefix list that has only `seq 5 deny 10.1.3.0/24`. What is the result?

- **A.** Only 10.1.3.0/24 is filtered.
- **B.** No inter-area routes from area 1 reach area 0, because the prefix list ends with an implicit deny.
- **C.** The command is rejected because the prefix list has no permit entry.
- **D.** Area 1's Type 1 LSAs are filtered inside area 1.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** Like an ACL, a prefix list ends with an implicit deny, so every prefix that isn't 10.1.3.0/24 also matches "deny". All Type 3s from area 1 are suppressed. **Why not the others:** A is what the engineer intended, but not what the config does. C is wrong because IOS accepts it. D is wrong because filter-lists act only on Type 3s at the ABR.
</details>

## 6.7 Neighbor Adjacency — Network Types & Passive Interfaces

**The problem:** routes can only be exchanged once neighbours have formed, and how neighbours form depends on the type of link. On top of that, some interfaces should never form neighbours at all. This section covers getting adjacencies right and keeping them where they belong.

### Point-to-Point vs Broadcast

You know both from CCNA (16.10). The ENCOR-level detail is what happens when they **mismatch**:

| Network type | DR/BDR | Hello / Dead | Default on |
|--------------|--------|--------------|------------|
| **Broadcast** | Yes | 10 / 40 s | Ethernet |
| **Point-to-point** | No | 10 / 40 s | Serial (HDLC/PPP), GRE tunnels |
| Non-broadcast, point-to-multipoint | (Chapter 27) | 30 / 120 s | Frame Relay–style NBMA |

On an Ethernet link between exactly two routers, it's common to change the type so no DR election is held:

```
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point     ! configure on BOTH ends
```

### DR/BDR on Broadcast Links — a Recap

On a **broadcast** segment, OSPF elects a **DR** and **BDR** (CCNA guide 16.10). Every other router (DROTHER) forms a full adjacency only with those two. The rules that ENCOR still tests:

- **Highest interface priority wins** (`ip ospf priority 0–255`, default 1), then **highest router ID**.
- **Priority 0** = never DR or BDR.
- The election is **not preemptive**. A better router arriving later doesn't take over until the DR fails or OSPF is reset (`clear ip ospf process`).

```
R4(config-if)# ip ospf priority 0            ! R4 may never be DR/BDR on this segment
R4# show ip ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
1.1.1.1         100   FULL/DR         00:00:36    10.1.1.1        GigabitEthernet0/0
2.2.2.2          50   FULL/BDR        00:00:33    10.1.1.2        GigabitEthernet0/0
3.3.3.3           1   2WAY/DROTHER    00:00:38    10.1.1.3        GigabitEthernet0/0
```

**Read the last line carefully:** two DROTHERs stop at **2WAY** with each other by design, so `2WAY/DROTHER` is healthy, not stuck. FULL with the DR and BDR, 2WAY with other DROTHERs, is a correct broadcast segment. A neighbor stuck in 2WAY on a **point-to-point** link is the problem case.

**Why have a DR at all?** Without one, every router on a LAN would form a full adjacency with every other router and swap databases with each of them. With *n* routers that's *n*(*n* − 1)/2 adjacencies. With a DR and BDR, each other router (a **DROTHER**) needs only two.

| Routers on the LAN | Full adjacencies without a DR | With DR + BDR |
|--------------------|-------------------------------|---------------|
| 5 | 10 | 7 |
| 10 | 45 | 17 |

**Story Time 📖:** A team meeting where everyone has news. If all ten people tell each of the other nine individually, that's a lot of conversations. Instead one person takes the notes (the DR) and a second keeps a copy in case the first leaves (the BDR). Everyone gives their news to the note-taker, and the note-taker sends the summary to everyone. On OSPF terms: DROTHERs send updates to 224.0.0.6 (DR and BDR), and the DR re-floods them to 224.0.0.5 (all OSPF routers).

**Worked example: the election, and why it doesn't preempt.** Four routers boot on 10.1.1.0/24 at the same time:

| Router | Priority | RID |
|--------|----------|-----|
| R1 | 100 | 1.1.1.1 |
| R2 | 50 | 2.2.2.2 |
| R3 | 1 | 3.3.3.3 |
| R4 | 0 | 4.4.4.4 |

1. R4 has priority 0, so it's out of the running.
2. Highest priority wins: **R1 (100) becomes DR**, and **R2 (50) becomes BDR**. RID would only matter if priorities tied.
3. R3 is a DROTHER. This is the `show ip ospf neighbor` output above, seen from R4.
4. Later, R5 joins with priority 200. It does **not** take over. R1 stays DR and R5 becomes a DROTHER.
5. R1 fails. **R2 (the BDR) is promoted to DR** straight away, because it already has full adjacencies with everyone. A new BDR election follows, and R5 (200) wins it.

**Why no preemption?** Every change of DR forces the DROTHERs to build new adjacencies and resynchronise their databases. Keeping a working DR is better than chasing the "best" one. If you want a particular router to be DR, give it the highest priority *and* make sure it's up first, or reset the process during a maintenance window.

### The Sneaky Mismatch

One end set to `ip ospf network point-to-point`, the other left as broadcast. The timers are identical (10/40), so the hellos are accepted and the adjacency may even reach **FULL**. But the broadcast side expects a DR and describes the link through a Type 2 LSA, while the point-to-point side doesn't. The two routers describe the same link differently, SPF can't match them up, and **routes across that link never appear**. *FULL neighbours with missing routes should make you check `show ip ospf interface` on both ends.*

Neighbour requirements you must be able to recite (and the command that proves each):

| Must match | Proven by |
|------------|-----------|
| Area ID | `show ip ospf interface` |
| Subnet and mask (on broadcast links) | `show ip interface brief`, `show run interface` |
| Hello / dead intervals | `show ip ospf interface` |
| Authentication type and key | `debug ip ospf adj` ("Mismatched authentication") |
| Stub/NSSA flags | `debug ip ospf hello` ("mismatched Stub/Transit area option bit") |
| MTU (or the adjacency stalls in ExStart/Exchange) | `show interface | include MTU` |
| **Unique** router IDs | `show ip ospf` — duplicates log `%OSPF-4-DUP_RTRID` |

### Passive Interfaces

```
R1(config)# router ospf 1
R1(config-router)# passive-interface default                ! no hellos anywhere...
R1(config-router)# no passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/1  ! ...except to real neighbours
```

A passive interface **stops sending and processing hellos** — so no neighbour can form on it — but its subnet is **still advertised**. That's exactly right for user LANs: the users' subnet must be reachable, but no device there should be able to become an OSPF neighbour and inject routes.

**What goes wrong without it:** a user on 192.168.1.0/24 runs a lab router (or malware) that speaks OSPF. Gi0/3 isn't passive, so R1 forms an adjacency with it. The rogue device advertises 0.0.0.0/0 with a low cost, and part of the network starts sending internet traffic to a laptop. A passive interface ignores its Hellos, so the adjacency can never form, and adding OSPF authentication (Chapter 27) closes the gap on interfaces that must stay active.

**Why "passive-interface default" rather than listing the user ports?** Safety by default. A new interface added next year is passive unless someone consciously makes it a routing link. *Fail closed: an interface has to be invited into the routing protocol, not remembered and excluded.*

**📝 Exam-style questions — 6.7**

**Q1.** Four routers start at the same time on one Ethernet segment. Which routers become DR and BDR?

```
Router   Priority   Router ID
R1       1          5.5.5.5
R2       1          9.9.9.9
R3       10         1.1.1.1
R4       0          10.10.10.10
```

- **A.** DR R4, BDR R2
- **B.** DR R2, BDR R1
- **C.** DR R3, BDR R1
- **D.** DR R3, BDR R2

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** Highest priority wins first, so R3 (10) is DR. R1 and R2 tie at priority 1, so the higher router ID, R2 (9.9.9.9), is BDR. R4 has priority 0 and can never be DR or BDR, even with the highest RID. **Why not the others:** A ignores priority 0. B ignores priority and uses RID only. C picks the lower RID for BDR.
</details>

**Q2.** Refer to the exhibit. R4 is on a broadcast segment with three other OSPF routers. What is the state of this segment?

```
R4# show ip ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
1.1.1.1         100   FULL/DR         00:00:36    10.1.1.1        GigabitEthernet0/0
2.2.2.2          50   FULL/BDR        00:00:33    10.1.1.2        GigabitEthernet0/0
3.3.3.3           1   2WAY/DROTHER    00:00:38    10.1.1.3        GigabitEthernet0/0
```

- **A.** Healthy: DROTHERs form full adjacencies only with the DR and BDR, and stay in 2WAY with each other.
- **B.** Broken: R3 is stuck in 2WAY because of an MTU mismatch.
- **C.** Broken: R4 should be FULL with every neighbour.
- **D.** Broken: R3 has a lower priority, so it can't exchange routes.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** On a broadcast segment DROTHERs stop at 2WAY with each other by design, and the DR re-floods everyone's updates. FULL to the DR and BDR plus 2WAY to the other DROTHER is correct. **Why not the others:** B is wrong because an MTU problem shows up as EXSTART/EXCHANGE, not 2WAY. C describes a segment with no DR. D is wrong because R3 still gets every route through the DR.
</details>

**Q3.** R1's GigabitEthernet0/1 has `ip ospf network point-to-point`. R2's end of the same link was left at the default broadcast type. Both routers show each other as FULL, but no routes learned across the link appear. What is the cause?

- **A.** The hello timers don't match.
- **B.** The two routers describe the link differently (one expects a DR and a Type 2 LSA, the other doesn't), so SPF can't connect them.
- **C.** R2 needs a priority of 0 for point-to-point to work.
- **D.** Point-to-point network type isn't supported on Ethernet.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** Both types use 10/40 timers, so the hellos are accepted and the adjacency can reach FULL. But SPF needs both ends to describe the link the same way, so the routes never appear. Check `show ip ospf interface` on both ends. **Why not the others:** A is wrong because both types default to 10/40. C is invented. D is wrong because point-to-point on a two-router Ethernet link is common practice.
</details>

**Q4.** Which two statements describe an OSPF passive interface? (Choose two.)

- **A.** The interface's subnet is no longer advertised.
- **B.** The interface stops sending and processing Hellos, so no neighbour can form on it.
- **C.** The interface forms neighbours but doesn't send LSAs.
- **D.** The interface's subnet is still advertised to OSPF neighbours on other interfaces.
- **E.** The interface is administratively shut down.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B, D.** That's exactly what a user LAN needs: the users' subnet stays reachable, but no device there can become a neighbour and inject routes. **Why not the others:** A is the common misconception. C is wrong because no neighbours form at all. E is wrong because the interface stays up and forwards traffic.
</details>

---

## 6.8 OSPFv3 — OSPF for IPv6 (and IPv4)

**The problem:** IPv6 networks need a routing protocol too. OSPFv2 can only carry IPv4, so IPv6 needs OSPFv3. Modern OSPFv3 can carry IPv4 as well, which lets one protocol do both jobs.

OSPFv3 (RFC 5340) is the same protocol — same areas, LSA flooding, SPF, DR/BDR, network types — rebuilt for IPv6. What changed:

| Topic | OSPFv2 | OSPFv3 |
|-------|--------|--------|
| Runs over | IPv4 subnets | IPv6 **links** — an interface can have many prefixes |
| Multicast | 224.0.0.5 / 224.0.0.6 | **FF02::5 / FF02::6** |
| Neighbour addresses / next hops | Interface IPv4 address | **Link-local** addresses |
| Router ID | 32-bit | **Still 32-bit, dotted** — set it manually if the router has no IPv4 address |
| Addressing in Type 1/2 | Yes | **No** — topology only; prefixes moved to new LSAs |
| New LSAs | — | **Type 8** link LSA (link-local + prefixes on a link), **Type 9** intra-area-prefix LSA |
| Authentication | In OSPF itself | IPsec (or the OSPFv3 authentication trailer) |

**Why separate topology from addressing?** In OSPFv2 a prefix change on a router changes its Type 1 LSA, and a changed Type 1 means a full SPF run for the area. OSPFv3 keeps topology (Type 1/2) and prefixes (Type 8/9) in separate LSAs, so adding or removing a prefix triggers only a cheap partial recalculation. *The map of the roads and the list of addresses on each road change at different speeds, so OSPFv3 keeps them on different pages.*

### Traditional OSPFv3 Configuration

```
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing                     ! IPv6 routing is OFF by default
R1(config)# ipv6 router ospf 1
R1(config-rtr)# router-id 1.1.1.1                    ! required if no IPv4 address exists
R1(config-rtr)# passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/3
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:12::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 1 area 0                    ! no network statements in OSPFv3
```

### Address-Family OSPFv3 — One Process, Both Protocols

Modern IOS XE uses `router ospfv3` with **address families**, which can carry **IPv4 routes too** — over the same IPv6-style protocol machinery:

```
R1(config)# router ospfv3 1
R1(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-router)# address-family ipv6 unicast
R1(config-router-af)# passive-interface default
R1(config-router-af)# no passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-router-af)# area 1 range 2001:db8:1::/48    ! IPv6 inter-area summary
R1(config-router-af)# exit-address-family
R1(config-router)# address-family ipv4 unicast
R1(config-router-af)# exit-address-family
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ospfv3 1 ipv6 area 0
R1(config-if)# ospfv3 1 ipv4 area 0                  ! same link, IPv4 AF (needs IPv6 enabled)
```

Each address family runs as a **separate instance** with its own neighbours and database, so `show ospfv3 neighbor` lists them per AF. The IPv4 address family still needs IPv6 enabled on the interface, because OSPFv3 packets themselves always travel over IPv6 link-local addresses.

### Verifying OSPFv3

```
R1# show ospfv3 neighbor
          OSPFv3 1 address-family ipv6 (router-id 1.1.1.1)

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Interface ID    Interface
2.2.2.2           1   FULL/BDR        00:00:36    4               GigabitEthernet0/1

R1# show ipv6 route ospf
OI  2001:DB8:1::/48 [110/2]
     via FE80::2, GigabitEthernet0/1
```

How the OSPFv3 adjacency above came up, step by step:

1. Both routers source Hellos from their **link-local** address (FE80::1 and FE80::2 here, set with `ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local` for readability; without that, a link-local address is created automatically when IPv6 is enabled) and send them to **FF02::5**.
2. Each Hello carries the sender's 32-bit RID (1.1.1.1, 2.2.2.2). If a router has no IPv4 address and no `router-id` configured, it has no RID and the process can't start. That's why the config sets one explicitly.
3. The usual OSPF rules apply: matching area, timers and stub flags, then the DR/BDR election (on Ethernet, R2 became BDR), then the database exchange.
4. The routes are installed with the neighbour's **link-local** address as the next hop, because that's the address R1 heard the neighbour speaking from.

Note the **link-local next hop** (`FE80::2`) — that's normal and correct for OSPFv3. The traditional-mode commands (`show ipv6 ospf neighbor`, `show ipv6 ospf interface`) still work for processes configured with `ipv6 router ospf`.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 6.8**

**Q1.** R1 runs only IPv6 and has no IPv4 addresses. After `ipv6 router ospf 1` is configured, the OSPFv3 process won't start. What is missing?

- **A.** `ipv6 enable` on the loopback
- **B.** A `network` statement for each IPv6 prefix
- **C.** A 32-bit router ID set with `router-id`
- **D.** An IPv6 global address on every interface

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** OSPFv3 still uses a 32-bit dotted router ID. Normally it's taken from an IPv4 address; with none, you must set it manually. **Why not the others:** A doesn't create a router ID. B is wrong because OSPFv3 has no `network` statements (you use `ipv6 ospf 1 area 0` on the interface). D isn't needed, since OSPFv3 neighbours talk over link-local addresses.
</details>

**Q2.** Refer to the exhibit. An engineer worries that the next hop is not the neighbour's global address. What is the correct interpretation?

```
R1# show ipv6 route ospf
OI  2001:DB8:1::/48 [110/2]
     via FE80::2, GigabitEthernet0/1
```

- **A.** The neighbour is misconfigured; it should advertise its global address as the next hop.
- **B.** The route is an inter-area route that hasn't been summarized yet.
- **C.** The neighbour has no global address, so the route is unusable.
- **D.** This is normal: OSPFv3 neighbours talk over link-local addresses, so link-local next hops are expected.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** OSPFv3 Hellos come from the interface's link-local address, so routes are installed with the neighbour's link-local address plus the outgoing interface. **Why not the others:** A and C treat correct behaviour as a fault. B misreads `OI` (inter-area) and `/48` (which is already a summary).
</details>

**Q3.** Why does the IPv4 address family of OSPFv3 still need IPv6 enabled on the interface?

- **A.** Because OSPFv3 packets always travel over IPv6 link-local addresses, whichever address family's routes they carry.
- **B.** Because the IPv4 routes are converted into IPv6 prefixes.
- **C.** Because the router ID must be an IPv6 address.
- **D.** Because IPv4 routes are carried inside Type 5 LSAs that only exist in IPv6.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** The IPv4 AF is a separate instance with its own neighbours and database, but it uses the same IPv6 transport. Even `ipv6 enable` (a link-local address only) is enough. **Why not the others:** B is wrong because the routes stay IPv4. C is wrong because the RID is a 32-bit dotted number. D is invented.
</details>

**Q4.** OSPFv3 removed prefix information from router (Type 1) and network (Type 2) LSAs. Which two LSA types carry that information instead? (Choose two.)

- **A.** Type 3
- **B.** Type 5
- **C.** Type 8 link LSA
- **D.** Type 7
- **E.** Type 9 intra-area-prefix LSA

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C, E.** Type 8 carries a router's link-local address and the prefixes on one link. Type 9 carries the area's prefixes. Keeping topology (Types 1/2) and prefixes apart means adding a prefix doesn't trigger a full SPF run. **Why not the others:** A carries *inter-area* prefixes from an ABR, not the intra-area ones moved out of Types 1/2. B and D carry external routes.
</details>

---

## 6.9 Verification and Troubleshooting Toolkit

| Command | Answers |
|---------|---------|
| `show ip ospf interface brief` | Which interfaces run OSPF, in which area, cost, state (DR/BDR/P2P) |
| `show ip ospf interface Gi0/1` | Network type, timers, DR/BDR, passive status |
| `show ip ospf neighbor` | Neighbours and adjacency state |
| `show ip ospf database` | LSDB summary per area and LSA type |
| `show ip ospf border-routers` | How this router reaches each ABR and ASBR |
| `show ip route ospf` | What made it into the RIB (`O`, `O IA`, `O E1/E2`, `O N1/N2`) |
| `show ip protocols` | Router ID, areas, networks, passive interfaces, distribute-lists |

| Symptom | Likely cause | Prove it with |
|---------|--------------|---------------|
| No neighbour at all | Passive interface, wrong area, ACL blocking 224.0.0.5, subnet mismatch | `show ip ospf interface`, `show ip protocols` |
| Neighbour stuck in **Init** | One-way hellos — ACL or multicast problem on one side | `debug ip ospf hello` |
| Stuck in **ExStart/Exchange** | MTU mismatch | `show interface | include MTU` |
| FULL, but routes missing across the link | Network-type mismatch (p2p vs broadcast) | `show ip ospf interface` on both ends |
| Route present in LSDB but not in RIB | `distribute-list in`, or a better-AD route from another protocol | `show ip protocols`, `show ip route <prefix>` |
| Inter-area route missing everywhere | `area filter-list` or `range … not-advertise` on the ABR; area not connected to area 0 | `show run | section router ospf` on ABRs |
| External route missing in one area | Area is stub/totally stubby (by design) | `show ip ospf` — area type |
| Summary not appearing | `area range` used for externals, or `summary-address` used on an ABR | Check which router type you're on |

### Worked Example: A Stuck Adjacency

R1 and R2 are connected on Gi0/1. Users report that nothing beyond R2 is reachable.

1. `show ip ospf neighbor` on R1 shows R2 in **EXSTART**, and it never moves on. The table points to **MTU**.
2. `show interface Gi0/1 | include MTU` shows **MTU 1500 bytes** on R1 and **MTU 1400 bytes** on R2 (someone set it for a tunnel).
3. **Why it sticks:** in EXSTART/EXCHANGE the routers send Database Description packets that list their LSAs. R1 offers packets up to 1500 bytes. R2 sees that the MTU advertised in R1's packets exceeds its own and rejects them, so the exchange never finishes.
4. **Fix:** make the MTU match on both ends (`mtu 1500` on R2's Gi0/1). The neighbour moves through EXCHANGE and LOADING to **FULL** within seconds, and the routes appear. `ip ospf mtu-ignore` would also bring it up, but it hides the real problem: large packets would still be dropped on that link.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 6.9**

**Q1.** R1 shows R2 stuck in EXSTART and the state never progresses. Which command most directly proves the likely cause?

- **A.** `show ip ospf border-routers`
- **B.** `show interface GigabitEthernet0/1 | include MTU` on both routers
- **C.** `show ip protocols`
- **D.** `debug ip ospf hello`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** EXSTART/EXCHANGE stalls almost always mean an MTU mismatch: the router with the smaller MTU rejects the other's Database Description packets. **Why not the others:** A shows how ABRs and ASBRs are reached. C shows process settings. D is for Hello problems, which happen before EXSTART (stuck in INIT, or no neighbour at all).
</details>

**Q2.** R1 lists R2 as a neighbour in the INIT state, and it never moves on. What does this mean?

- **A.** The two routers have an MTU mismatch.
- **B.** R1 is a DROTHER and is waiting for the DR.
- **C.** R1 hears R2's Hellos, but R2 isn't hearing R1's, so R1's router ID never appears in R2's Hellos.
- **D.** The routers have duplicate router IDs.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** INIT means "I can hear you, but you haven't listed me yet", a one-way problem. It's often an ACL or a multicast problem on one side. Prove it with `debug ip ospf hello`. **Why not the others:** A shows as EXSTART/EXCHANGE. B is wrong because a DROTHER stops at 2WAY, after INIT. D logs `%OSPF-4-DUP_RTRID` instead.
</details>

**Q3.** An OSPF route is in R3's LSDB but not in its routing table. Which two causes are possible? (Choose two.)

- **A.** A `distribute-list in` under R3's OSPF process
- **B.** An MTU mismatch on R3's uplink
- **C.** The same prefix learned from another protocol with a lower administrative distance
- **D.** A passive interface on R3
- **E.** An `area filter-list` on R3's own ABR

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A, C.** The LSA has arrived, so the adjacency works. Something is stopping the route between the LSDB and the routing table: a local distribute-list, or a better-AD source winning for that prefix. **Why not the others:** B and D would prevent the adjacency, and then the LSA wouldn't be there at all. E would stop the Type 3 from being created, so it wouldn't be in the LSDB either.
</details>

**Q4.** The EXSTART problem can be fixed either by matching the MTU on both ends or by configuring `ip ospf mtu-ignore`. Why is matching the MTU the better fix?

- **A.** `ip ospf mtu-ignore` disables OSPF authentication.
- **B.** `ip ospf mtu-ignore` must be configured on every router in the area.
- **C.** Matching the MTU also resets the DR election.
- **D.** `ip ospf mtu-ignore` brings the adjacency up but hides the real problem: large packets are still dropped on that link.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** The mismatch is a real fault. Ignoring it lets OSPF finish the exchange, but full-size data packets will still be dropped by the side with the smaller MTU. **Why not the others:** A and C are invented. B is wrong because the command is per interface.
</details>
