## 11.3 MQC — the Three-Part Structure Every Config Uses

**Why a structure at all?** Older IOS had a different command for every QoS tool, each with its own syntax. **MQC (Modular QoS CLI)** replaced them with one pattern that separates *which* traffic, *what* to do and *where* to do it, so the same class can be reused in several policies and the same policy on many interfaces.

Every modern Cisco QoS configuration uses the **Modular QoS CLI**. Learn its three parts and you can read any of them:

| Part | Command | Answers |
|------|---------|---------|
| 1. **Class map** | `class-map [match-any|match-all] NAME` + `match …` | **Which** traffic? |
| 2. **Policy map** | `policy-map NAME` + `class NAME` + actions | **What** happens to it? |
| 3. **Service policy** | `service-policy {input|output} NAME` on an interface | **Where** and in which direction? |

- **`match-all`** (the default!) requires **every** `match` line to be true (logical AND). **`match-any`** needs just one (OR). **Exam trap:** a `match-all` class with `match dscp ef` and `match dscp cs3` matches nothing, because one packet can't carry two DSCP values.
- Classes in a policy are checked **top to bottom; first match wins**.
- Anything unmatched falls into **`class-default`**, which always exists, even if you don't configure it.

### Marking on Ingress — Reading a Classification Policy

Queuing policies (11.5, 11.7) *act on* markings, but someone has to *set* them first, at the trust boundary, **inbound** on the access port. ENCOR shows you policies like this one and asks what happens to a given packet:

```
class-map match-any VOICE-IN
 match protocol rtp audio                    ! NBAR: identify by application
class-map match-any WEBEX-IN
 match protocol webex-meeting
class-map match-all BULK-IN
 match access-group name BACKUP-SERVERS      ! ACL: identify by address/port
!
policy-map MARK-ACCESS-IN
 class VOICE-IN
  set dscp ef                                ! Layer 3 marking, survives routing
 class WEBEX-IN
  set dscp af41
 class BULK-IN
  set dscp af11
  set qos-group 10                           ! internal label, never leaves this box
 class class-default
  set dscp default                           ! untrusted: wipe whatever the PC sent
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
 description user port
 service-policy input MARK-ACCESS-IN
```

| `set` action | What it changes | Lifetime |
|--------------|-----------------|----------|
| `set dscp X` | The 6-bit DSCP in the IP header | End to end, until someone re-marks it |
| `set cos X` | The 3-bit PCP in the 802.1Q tag | Only while the frame stays tagged. Gone at the first router or access port |
| `set qos-group N` | An **internal** label inside this device | Never leaves the box. Lets an output policy match on a decision made at input (`match qos-group 10`) without changing the packet |
| `set precedence X` | The top 3 bits of the ToS byte (legacy) | End to end |

**Worked example — four packets arrive on Gi1/0/10.** The policy checks the classes top to bottom and stops at the first match:

| Packet | VOICE-IN? | WEBEX-IN? | BULK-IN? | Result |
|--------|-----------|-----------|----------|--------|
| RTP audio from a softphone, PC marked 0 | **yes** | (not checked) | (not checked) | Marked **EF** |
| Webex meeting traffic, PC marked EF | no | **yes** | (not checked) | Re-marked **AF41** |
| Backup to a server in BACKUP-SERVERS, marked 0 | no | no | **yes** | Marked **AF11**, internal qos-group 10 |
| Web browsing that the PC marked EF | no | no | no | class-default: reset to **0** |

**Reading it:** a Webex packet the PC marked EF is re-marked to AF41, because the policy classifies by **application** and ignores what the PC claimed. An unknown packet marked EF is reset to 0 by `class-default`. *An ingress marking policy is how an untrusted port is "re-colored" to match your design.*

**📝 Exam-style questions — 11.3**

**Q1.** Refer to the exhibit. Which traffic does class VOICE-AND-SIGNALING match?

```
class-map VOICE-AND-SIGNALING
 match dscp ef
 match dscp cs3
```

- **A.** None, because one packet can't be marked both EF and CS3
- **B.** Only packets marked EF, the first match line
- **C.** Packets marked either EF or CS3
- **D.** Only packets marked CS3, the last match line

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Class-maps default to `match-all`: a class-map typed with no keyword behaves as `match-all`, which requires every `match` line to be true for the same packet. A packet carries one DSCP value, so nothing matches. `class-map match-any` would match either. **Why not the others:** B and D, class-maps don't use only the first or last line. C is the `match-any` behavior, which this class-map doesn't have.
</details>

**Q2.** Refer to the exhibit. A PC on Gi1/0/10 sends Webex meeting screen-sharing traffic (not RTP audio) that it has marked EF itself. What DSCP does the traffic carry after the policy?

```
class-map match-any VOICE-IN
 match protocol rtp audio
class-map match-any WEBEX-IN
 match protocol webex-meeting
!
policy-map MARK-ACCESS-IN
 class VOICE-IN
  set dscp ef
 class WEBEX-IN
  set dscp af41
 class class-default
  set dscp default
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
 service-policy input MARK-ACCESS-IN
```

- **A.** EF, because the PC's marking is kept
- **B.** 0, because untrusted traffic falls into class-default
- **C.** AF11
- **D.** AF41

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** The policy classifies by application with NBAR. Screen sharing doesn't match VOICE-IN (it isn't RTP audio), it does match WEBEX-IN, and that class sets AF41, overwriting whatever the PC claimed. **Why not the others:** A, the policy ignores the PC's own marking. B, the packet matched WEBEX-IN first, so it never reaches class-default. C, there is no AF11 action in this policy.
</details>

**Q3.** An ingress policy contains `set qos-group 10` in one class. What does that do?

- **A.** It rewrites the DSCP of matching packets to 10 (AF11)
- **B.** It sets the 802.1Q CoS of matching frames to 10
- **C.** It attaches an internal label inside this device that an output policy can match, without changing the packet
- **D.** It places matching packets in hardware queue 10

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** A QoS group is an internal tag that never leaves the box. An egress policy can then use `match qos-group 10` to act on a decision made at ingress. **Why not the others:** A, that would be `set dscp af11` (DSCP 10). B, CoS is 3 bits, so 0–7; `set cos` is a different command. D, queue selection is done by the output policy, not by the group number.
</details>

**Q4.** An engineer applies a marking policy to a user access port with `service-policy output MARK-ACCESS-IN` instead of `input`. What is the effect?

- **A.** The policy is rejected, because marking is allowed only inbound
- **B.** It marks traffic the switch sends toward the PC, so traffic arriving from the PC keeps whatever marking the PC set
- **C.** It marks traffic in both directions
- **D.** It has the same effect as `input`, because MQC applies policies to both directions

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** A service policy acts only in the direction it's applied. To re-mark what a user's PC sends, the policy must be applied **inbound** at the trust boundary. Outbound, it marks frames on their way to the PC, which is the wrong traffic. **Why not the others:** A, marking actions are valid outbound too. C and D, one service policy covers one direction only.
</details>

---

## 11.4 Policing vs Shaping at CCNP Depth

**The problem:** sometimes the issue isn't *who goes first* but *how much* is allowed through. An ISP sells you 50 Mbps on a 1 Gbps port, or you want guests limited to 10 Mbps. You need a tool that measures a traffic rate and acts on whatever goes over it.

The CCNA guide gave the core difference: **policing drops (or remarks) the excess; shaping buffers it.** CCNP adds the mechanics.

**Story Time 📖:** A nightclub allows 100 people in per hour. A **policer** is a bouncer: once the hour's quota is used, anyone else arriving is turned away (dropped), or let in with a stamp saying "first out if it gets crowded" (re-marked). A **shaper** is a velvet rope with a queue: extra people wait outside and are let in steadily as space frees up. Nobody is turned away unless the queue outside gets too long, but everybody in the queue waits. That's why shaping adds **delay** and policing adds **loss**.

### The Token Bucket

Both tools use a **token bucket**. Tokens drip in at the **CIR** (committed information rate), sending traffic spends tokens, and the bucket's size is the **Bc** (committed burst). With tokens available, traffic **conforms**. Without them, it **exceeds**.

**Units trap:** IOS counts the buckets differently for the two tools. On **`shape`**, Bc and Be are in **bits**. On **`police`**, `bc` and `be` are in **bytes**. The CIR is in bits per second for both. So `shape average 50000000 200000` means a 200,000-*bit* burst, while `police cir 10000000 bc 312500` means a 312,500-*byte* (2.5 Mbit) burst. Read the command before you do the arithmetic.

| Term | Means |
|------|-------|
| **CIR** | The average rate being enforced (bps) |
| **Bc** | Committed burst: the amount allowed in one interval (**bits** on `shape`, **bytes** on `police`) |
| **Be** | Excess burst: extra allowed if previous intervals were under-used (same units as Bc) |
| **Tc** | Time interval = **Bc (bits) ÷ CIR (bps)**. A shaper releases Bc bits every Tc |

**Worked example — a shaper's rhythm.** `shape average 50000000` with Bc = 200,000 bits:

1. Tc = 200,000 ÷ 50,000,000 = **0.004 s = 4 ms**.
2. Every 4 ms, the shaper may send 200,000 bits = 25,000 bytes, which is about **16 full-size (1,500-byte) packets**.
3. The physical port runs at 1 Gbps, so those 16 packets leave in about 0.2 ms. The shaper then stays quiet for the rest of the 4 ms.
4. Over one second that's 250 intervals × 200,000 bits = **50,000,000 bits**, exactly the CIR. Anything more waits in the shaping queue for the next interval.

**Worked example — a three-color policer handling a burst.** `police cir 10000000 bc 312500 be 312500` (bytes). Both buckets start full, and refill is ignored for this instantaneous burst:

1. A burst of **700,000 bytes** arrives at once.
2. The first **312,500 bytes** take tokens from the Bc bucket → **conform** → transmitted.
3. The Bc bucket is empty, so the next **312,500 bytes** take tokens from the Be bucket → **exceed** → sent, re-marked AF13.
4. Both buckets are empty, so the last **75,000 bytes** → **violate** → dropped.
5. Tokens drip back into Bc at 10 Mbps (1,250,000 bytes per second). Tokens that overflow a full Bc bucket fill Be, so the policer allows a burst again only after a quiet spell.

Why Bc = 312,500 bytes? It equals 2.5 Mbit, which is **250 ms** worth of traffic at 10 Mbps (2.5 ÷ 10). That's the comment on the config line.

### Policer Flavors

| Policer | Rates / buckets | Results |
|---------|-----------------|---------|
| Single-rate, two-color | CIR, Bc | conform / exceed |
| Single-rate, three-color (RFC 2697) | CIR, Bc, Be | conform / exceed / **violate** |
| Two-rate, three-color (RFC 2698) | CIR **and PIR** | conform / exceed / violate |

```
policy-map POLICE-GUEST
 class class-default
  police cir 10000000 bc 312500 be 312500   ! 10 Mbps; bc/be in BYTES (250 ms)
   conform-action transmit
   exceed-action set-dscp-transmit af13      ! remark, don't drop: drop first later
   violate-action drop
```

### Choosing Between Them

| Situation | Tool | Why |
|-----------|------|-----|
| ISP enforcing your contract **inbound** at their edge | Policing | They don't want to buffer your excess |
| Your router sending into a 50 Mbps circuit delivered on a 1 Gbps port | **Shaping** (outbound) | Smooth to the contract rate yourself, or the ISP's policer drops it (and drops it blindly) |
| Limiting a guest VLAN or a scavenger class | Policing | Cheap, no buffering, no added delay |
| Voice/video | Neither on the voice itself, beyond the LLQ's built-in policer | Shaping adds delay. Voice is protected by the priority queue instead |

**Why does shaping only work outbound?** Because buffering means *holding packets you haven't sent yet*, and you can only hold what's waiting to leave. Traffic arriving inbound has already crossed the wire. You can drop or remark it, but you can't make it arrive later.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 11.4**

**Q1.** A router is configured with `shape average 20000000 40000`. How long is the shaper's time interval, Tc?

- **A.** 2 ms
- **B.** 20 ms
- **C.** 0.5 ms
- **D.** 4 ms

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** On `shape`, Bc is in bits. Tc = Bc ÷ CIR = 40,000 bits ÷ 20,000,000 bps = 0.002 s = 2 ms. Every 2 ms the shaper may release 40,000 bits. **Why not the others:** B is off by a factor of ten. C inverts the division. D is the chapter's 50 Mbps / 200,000-bit example, not this config.
</details>

**Q2.** A policer is configured with `police cir 8000000 bc 250000`. What does `bc 250000` represent?

- **A.** A burst of 250,000 bits, about 31 ms of traffic at the CIR
- **B.** A burst of 250,000 packets
- **C.** A burst of 250,000 bytes (2 Mbit), which is 250 ms of traffic at the CIR
- **D.** A measurement interval of 250 ms written in microseconds

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** On `police`, `bc` and `be` are in **bytes**. 250,000 bytes × 8 = 2,000,000 bits, and 2 Mbit ÷ 8 Mbps = 0.25 s. **Why not the others:** A uses the `shape` unit (bits), the classic trap. B, buckets hold bytes, not packets. D, `bc` is a size, not a time.
</details>

**Q3.** A branch router connects to a 50 Mbps WAN service through a 1 Gbps Ethernet port. The provider polices at 50 Mbps. Why should the branch router shape its outbound traffic to 50 Mbps?

- **A.** Because shaping is the only way to mark traffic for the provider
- **B.** Because policing can't be applied outbound
- **C.** Because shaping removes the need for a priority queue
- **D.** Because otherwise the router bursts at 1 Gbps and the provider's policer drops the excess blindly, voice included; shaping makes the router hold the excess where its own QoS policy decides who waits

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** If you don't smooth your traffic to the contract rate, someone else drops it, without knowing what's important. Shaping creates the congestion on your own router, where your queuing policy can protect voice. **Why not the others:** A, marking is done with `set`, not shaping. B, policing works in both directions. C, shaping adds delay and makes a priority queue *more* important, not less.
</details>

**Q4.** Refer to the exhibit. Both buckets are full when a 400,000-byte burst arrives all at once. Ignoring token refill during the burst, what happens to it?

```
policy-map POLICE-GUEST
 class class-default
  police cir 10000000 bc 312500 be 312500
   conform-action transmit
   exceed-action set-dscp-transmit af13
   violate-action drop
```

- **A.** All 400,000 bytes conform and are transmitted unchanged
- **B.** 312,500 bytes conform and are sent unchanged; 87,500 bytes exceed and are sent re-marked AF13; nothing is dropped
- **C.** 312,500 bytes conform; the remaining 87,500 bytes are dropped
- **D.** 312,500 bytes are re-marked AF13 and 87,500 bytes are dropped

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** The first 312,500 bytes use the Bc bucket and conform. The next 87,500 bytes find Bc empty but Be still holding 312,500 bytes, so they exceed: transmitted but re-marked AF13. Nothing reaches the violate stage. **Why not the others:** A ignores the 312,500-byte Bc limit. C forgets the Be bucket; this is a single-rate three-color policer. D starts the re-marking too early and drops traffic that Be can still cover.
</details>

---

## 11.5 Queuing — Who Leaves First

**The problem:** when packets pile up, the order they leave in decides the experience. A voice packet stuck behind 50 big file-transfer packets arrives late, and late voice is as bad as lost voice. Queuing sorts waiting packets into separate lines and decides which line is served next.

Queuing only matters during **congestion**, when the interface's hardware transmit ring is full and packets wait in software queues. With no congestion, every QoS queuing policy is idle.

**Story Time 📖:** A supermarket with several checkout lanes and one cashier who moves between them. **CBWFQ** is a rule like "serve the business lane 30% of the time, the regular lane 25%…": every lane is guaranteed its share of the cashier. **LLQ** adds an express lane with a special rule: *whenever anyone is in it, they're served next*. But the express lane is only allowed a limited number of customers per minute, so it can never take the cashier away from everyone else for good.

**Walk-through — how LLQ serves packets on a congested link:**

1. Packets are sorted into their class queues as they arrive (voice → priority queue; video, data and default → their own CBWFQ queues).
2. Each time the interface is ready to send, the scheduler **checks the priority queue first**. If a voice packet is waiting and the voice class is within its cap, it goes next.
3. If the priority queue is empty, the scheduler serves the other queues in proportion to their `bandwidth` guarantees.
4. If voice exceeds its cap while the link is congested, the extra voice packets are **dropped**, not queued.
5. A voice packet therefore waits only for the packet already being transmitted (and any voice packets ahead of it), never for the backlog in the other queues. That's why LLQ voice delay stays tiny.

| Mechanism | How it works | Problem it solves / leaves |
|-----------|--------------|----------------------------|
| **FIFO** | One queue | No differentiation |
| **WFQ** | Automatic per-flow fairness | Fair, but can't prioritize voice |
| **CBWFQ** | You define classes; each gets a **guaranteed minimum bandwidth** (`bandwidth`) | Guarantees bandwidth, but voice can still wait behind a full-size packet in another queue: **jitter** |
| **LLQ** | CBWFQ **plus one strict-priority queue** (`priority`) served before all others | Voice gets near-zero queueing delay |

**Why does the LLQ have a built-in policer?** A strict-priority queue is always served first. If it could take unlimited bandwidth, a misbehaving "voice" class could starve every other class completely. So `priority 10000` (or `priority percent 10`) is both a promise and a **cap**: up to that rate during congestion, and any excess in the priority class is **dropped**. *The fast lane is fast because it's small.* Cisco's guidance is to keep the total priority (real-time) traffic at or below about **33%** of the link.

**`bandwidth` vs `bandwidth remaining`:** `bandwidth percent 30` guarantees 30% of the **interface (or shaped) rate**. `bandwidth remaining percent 30` divides what's **left after the priority queue** is served. A single policy can't mix the two styles across its classes.

**Worked example.** A 100 Mbps link has `priority percent 20` for voice, leaving 80 Mbps. Then:

- `bandwidth percent 30` for data guarantees 30% of **100** = **30 Mbps**.
- `bandwidth remaining percent 30` for data instead guarantees 30% of the **80** left = **24 Mbps**.

Same number, different answer. Read which keyword is used before doing the arithmetic.

### Queuing on Catalyst 9000 Switches

Routers queue in software; Catalyst switches queue in **hardware** (the UADP ASIC), so the model is fixed. A Catalyst 9000 port supports up to **2P6Q3T**: **8 egress queues**, of which up to **2 are strict priority**, each with **3 drop thresholds** (WTD, weighted tail drop). An egress policy maps classes onto those queues:

```
policy-map C9K-EGRESS
 class VOICE
  priority level 1                           ! first strict-priority queue
  police rate percent 10                     ! cap it, as with router LLQ
 class VIDEO
  priority level 2                           ! second priority queue, served after level 1
  police rate percent 20
 class SIGNALING
  bandwidth remaining ratio 5                ! share of what the PQs leave
 class CRITICAL-DATA
  bandwidth remaining ratio 25
  queue-buffers ratio 20                     ! give this queue a bigger buffer slice
 class class-default
  bandwidth remaining ratio 25
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/49
 service-policy output C9K-EGRESS
```

| Command | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| `priority level 1` / `level 2` | Two strict-priority queues; level 1 is always served before level 2. Voice in 1, video in 2 |
| `police rate percent N` | Caps a priority queue so it can't starve the others (Catalyst doesn't add an implicit LLQ policer the way routers do, so configure it) |
| `bandwidth remaining ratio N` | Weights for sharing the bandwidth left after the priority queues. Ratios are relative to each other, not percentages of the link |
| `queue-buffers ratio N` | Share of the port's buffer memory given to this queue. Deeper buffers absorb bursts (good for data), at the cost of delay |

**Worked example — turning ratios into bandwidth** on a 1 Gbps port, assuming voice and video are both using their full caps (10% + 20% = 300 Mbps). That leaves 700 Mbps for the other classes. The ratios are 5 + 25 + 25 = **55** shares:

| Class | Ratio | Share of the 700 Mbps |
|-------|-------|-----------------------|
| SIGNALING | 5 | 5 ÷ 55 ≈ 9% ≈ **64 Mbps** |
| CRITICAL-DATA | 25 | 25 ÷ 55 ≈ 45% ≈ **318 Mbps** |
| class-default | 25 | 25 ÷ 55 ≈ 45% ≈ **318 Mbps** |

If voice and video are quiet, the same ratios divide the whole 1 Gbps instead. A ratio is a share of whatever is left, never a fixed rate.

**Why two priority queues?** Because voice and interactive video are both real-time, but video is bursty and far bigger. In one shared priority queue, a video burst would sit in front of voice packets. Level 1 for voice and level 2 for video keeps voice ahead of everything, including video.

### AutoQoS — Reading What It Generates

**Why it exists:** a full campus QoS design is dozens of lines per port, and typing it by hand on hundreds of access ports invites mistakes. **AutoQoS** is a macro: one interface command expands into Cisco's recommended trust, classification, marking and queuing config. Exam questions show the command (or the config it produced) and ask what it does:

| Command (interface) | Use it on | What it does |
|---------------------|-----------|--------------|
| `auto qos voip cisco-phone` | Access port with a Cisco IP phone | **Conditional trust**: trusts markings only while CDP detects a Cisco phone (it adds `trust device cisco-phone`), plus ingress and egress policies for voice |
| `auto qos trust dscp` | Uplinks between your own switches | Trusts incoming DSCP; adds the egress queuing policy |
| `auto qos voip cisco-softphone` | PCs running softphones | Classifies and polices voice/signalling from an untrusted PC |
| `auto qos classify [police]` | Untrusted user ports | Classifies by ACL/NBAR and marks; optionally polices |

`trust device cisco-phone` is the key line to recognize. If the phone is unplugged and a PC is connected directly, CDP no longer sees a phone, so the switch stops trusting and the PC's self-marked EF is ignored. The generated class-maps and policy-maps have names beginning `AutoQos-4.0-` (for example an input policy for Cisco phones and a shared output queuing policy). `show auto qos interface Gi1/0/10` lists what was applied, and `show running-config` shows the full expansion. *AutoQoS doesn't do anything you couldn't type yourself: it's the Cisco-validated design typed for you, and you still need to read it.*

**📝 Exam-style questions — 11.5**

**Q1.** A 200 Mbps link has a policy with `priority percent 25` for voice and `bandwidth remaining percent 40` for business data. During congestion, how much bandwidth is business data guaranteed?

- **A.** 80 Mbps
- **B.** 50 Mbps
- **C.** 60 Mbps
- **D.** 40 Mbps

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** The priority class takes 25% of 200 = 50 Mbps, leaving 150 Mbps. `bandwidth remaining percent 40` means 40% of what's left: 0.4 × 150 = 60 Mbps. **Why not the others:** A is 40% of the whole 200 Mbps, the `bandwidth percent 40` answer. B is the voice class's share. D treats the percentage as Mbps.
</details>

**Q2.** A voice class has `priority 5000` (5 Mbps). During congestion, the voice class receives 7 Mbps of traffic. What happens to it?

- **A.** All 7 Mbps is sent, because the priority queue is always served first
- **B.** The extra 2 Mbps waits in the priority queue until the congestion clears
- **C.** The extra 2 Mbps is moved into class-default
- **D.** 5 Mbps is sent with strict priority and the extra 2 Mbps is dropped by the LLQ's built-in policer

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** The priority command is both a guarantee and a cap. During congestion, priority traffic above the configured rate is dropped, so the priority queue can never starve the other classes. **Why not the others:** A ignores the implicit policer. B, excess priority traffic is dropped, not queued. C, MQC never moves packets between classes.
</details>

**Q3.** On a Catalyst 9000 1 Gbps port, the two priority queues are using their full caps of 400 Mbps in total. The other classes have `bandwidth remaining ratio` values of 10, 30 and 60. How much bandwidth does the class with ratio 30 get?

- **A.** 180 Mbps
- **B.** 300 Mbps
- **C.** 120 Mbps
- **D.** 30 Mbps

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** 1,000 − 400 = 600 Mbps is left after the priority queues. The ratios add up to 100 shares, so 30 shares = 30% of 600 = 180 Mbps. **Why not the others:** B is 30% of the whole 1 Gbps. C is 30% of the 400 Mbps the priority queues use. D treats the ratio as Mbps; ratios are relative weights, not rates.
</details>

**Q4.** An engineer runs `auto qos voip cisco-phone` on an access port. Which line in the generated configuration makes the port trust markings only while a Cisco phone is attached?

- **A.** `auto qos trust dscp`
- **B.** `trust device cisco-phone`
- **C.** `priority level 1`
- **D.** `mls qos trust cos`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** `trust device cisco-phone` is the conditional-trust line: the switch trusts markings only while CDP detects a Cisco phone. Unplug the phone and plug in a PC, and the PC's self-marked EF is no longer believed. **Why not the others:** A is a different AutoQoS command, used on uplinks and unconditional. C defines a priority queue in an egress policy. D is the legacy command that trusts CoS unconditionally, whatever device is attached.
</details>

## 11.6 Congestion Avoidance — Dropping Smartly

**The problem:** queuing decides who waits, but a queue still has a fixed size. Once it's full, something must be dropped, and *how* you drop matters a lot for TCP.

When a queue fills, new packets are **tail-dropped**. Tail drop hits every TCP flow in the queue at once, all of them back off together, the link goes idle, then all of them ramp up together again. That's **TCP global synchronization**, a sawtooth that wastes capacity. The CCNA guide covered this.

**WRED (Weighted Random Early Detection)** starts dropping *some* packets **before** the queue is full, randomly, so individual TCP flows slow down at different times:

| WRED parameter | Meaning |
|----------------|---------|
| **Minimum threshold** | Queue depth where random drops start |
| **Maximum threshold** | Depth where drop probability reaches its maximum; beyond it, everything is dropped (tail drop) |
| **Mark probability denominator** | Drop probability at the max threshold: 10 → 1 in 10 |

"Weighted" means each **DSCP** gets its own thresholds. With `random-detect dscp-based`, AF13 starts being dropped at a *shallower* queue depth than AF11. That's drop precedence (11.2) put into action.

**Story Time 📖:** A classroom is getting loud. One approach is to wait until it's deafening and then shout at everyone at once. They all go silent, then all start talking again together, and the cycle repeats. That's tail drop and global synchronization. A smarter teacher starts tapping a *few random* students on the shoulder as the noise rises, so the volume eases off gradually and never hits the ceiling. That's WRED. "Weighted" means the students already on a warning (AF13) get tapped sooner than the well-behaved ones (AF11).

**Worked example — WRED drop probability**, using the thresholds from the 11.7 output (both maximum 40 packets, mark probability 1/10 = 10%):

| Average queue depth | AF21 (min 32) | AF23 (min 24) |
|---------------------|---------------|---------------|
| 20 packets | 0% (below min) | 0% (below min) |
| 32 packets | 0% (just at min) | (32 − 24) ÷ (40 − 24) × 10% = **5%** |
| 36 packets | (36 − 32) ÷ (40 − 32) × 10% = **5%** | (36 − 24) ÷ 16 × 10% = **7.5%** |
| above 40 | 100%: tail drop | 100%: tail drop |

Between the two thresholds the drop chance climbs in a straight line from 0 to the mark probability. WRED uses the **average** queue depth, not the instantaneous one (the `Exp-weight-constant` in the output sets how fast that average moves), so a short burst doesn't trigger drops on its own.

**ECN** lets WRED **mark** packets (set the ECN bits to "congestion experienced") instead of dropping them, *if* both endpoints support ECN. The receiver echoes the signal and the sender slows down. The result is the same signal with no lost packet (`random-detect ecn`).

**Why not use WRED on the voice class?** Voice is UDP and has no congestion response, so dropping voice packets early just degrades the call for no benefit. WRED belongs on **TCP-heavy** classes.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 11.6**

**Q1.** WRED is configured for AF21 with a minimum threshold of 20 packets, a maximum threshold of 40 packets and a mark probability denominator of 10. The average queue depth is 30 packets. What is the drop probability for an arriving AF21 packet?

- **A.** 0%
- **B.** 10%
- **C.** 50%
- **D.** 5%

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** Between the thresholds, the drop chance rises in a straight line from 0 to the mark probability (1/10 = 10%). 30 is halfway between 20 and 40, so the chance is half of 10% = 5%. **Why not the others:** A would apply below 20 packets. B is the probability at the maximum threshold. C confuses "halfway" with the probability itself.
</details>

**Q2.** Why is WRED normally left off the voice class?

- **A.** Voice is UDP and has no congestion response, so dropping voice packets early only damages the call without slowing the sender
- **B.** WRED can only be applied to class-default
- **C.** WRED requires ECN, which phones don't support
- **D.** Voice packets have no DSCP value for WRED to read

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** WRED works by making TCP senders slow down before the queue overflows. Voice runs over UDP/RTP, which doesn't back off, so early drops just lose audio. Voice is protected by the priority queue instead. **Why not the others:** B, WRED can be used in any CBWFQ class. C, ECN is optional. D, voice is marked EF (46).
</details>

**Q3.** Which two statements about WRED and ECN are true? (Choose two.)

- **A.** With ECN enabled, WRED can mark packets as having experienced congestion instead of dropping them, if both endpoints support ECN
- **B.** WRED decides drops using the instantaneous queue depth, so any short burst causes drops
- **C.** With `random-detect dscp-based`, AF13 typically has a lower minimum threshold than AF11, so it starts being dropped sooner
- **D.** WRED prevents TCP global synchronization by dropping all flows at the same moment
- **E.** Above the maximum threshold, the drop probability equals the mark probability

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A, C.** ECN gives the same "slow down" signal without losing a packet, and dscp-based WRED is how drop precedence is put into action: higher drop precedence, shallower threshold. **Why not the others:** B, WRED uses the *average* depth, so short bursts don't trigger drops on their own. D, it does the opposite: random early drops hit different flows at different times. E, above the maximum threshold every packet is dropped (tail drop).
</details>

## 11.7 Interpreting a Real Policy — Line by Line

This is the skill ENCOR tests: given a policy, say what happens to a specific packet and why. Here's a typical **WAN edge**: a 1 Gbps interface handing off to a **50 Mbps** circuit.

![Hierarchical policy: parent shaper at 50 Mbps containing the child queuing policy](images/c11_hqos.png)

```
class-map match-any VOICE
 match dscp ef
class-map match-any VIDEO
 match dscp af41 af42 af43
class-map match-any SIGNALING
 match dscp cs3
class-map match-any CRITICAL-DATA
 match dscp af21 af22 af23
class-map match-all SCAVENGER
 match dscp cs1
!
policy-map WAN-QUEUING                     ! child: the queuing decisions
 class VOICE
  priority percent 10                      ! LLQ: strict priority, capped at 5 Mbps
 class VIDEO
  bandwidth percent 30                     ! guaranteed 15 Mbps during congestion
 class SIGNALING
  bandwidth percent 5
 class CRITICAL-DATA
  bandwidth percent 25
  random-detect dscp-based                 ! WRED: AF23 dropped before AF21
 class SCAVENGER
  bandwidth percent 1                      ! "less than best effort"
 class class-default
  bandwidth percent 25
  fair-queue                               ! flow fairness inside the default class
  random-detect dscp-based
!
policy-map WAN-SHAPER                      ! parent: create congestion at 50 Mbps
 class class-default
  shape average 50000000
  service-policy WAN-QUEUING               ! nest the child inside the shaper
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 description 50M MPLS handoff on a 1G port
 service-policy output WAN-SHAPER
```

**Reading it like an exam question:**

1. **Where and which way?** Outbound on Gi0/0/1, the only direction where queuing and shaping can work.
2. **Why the parent shaper?** This is the crucial insight. The interface is 1 Gbps, so it never congests at 50 Mbps of traffic, and the queuing policy *alone* would **never activate**. The ISP's policer at 50 Mbps would then drop the excess blindly, voice included. The parent **shapes to 50 Mbps**, which creates congestion *locally*, where your child policy decides who waits. This parent/child arrangement is **Hierarchical QoS (HQoS)**. *You can only prioritize traffic in a queue you control, so you make the queue happen on your own router.*
3. **What does each percentage mean?** They're percentages of the **parent's shaped rate** (50 Mbps), not of 1 Gbps. Voice gets strict priority up to 5 Mbps, video 15 Mbps guaranteed, and so on.
4. **What happens to a packet marked AF22?** `match-any` on CRITICAL-DATA matches it, so it goes into a queue guaranteed 12.5 Mbps, with WRED dropping it ahead of AF21 if the queue builds.
5. **And a packet marked AF31?** No class matches it, so it lands in **class-default**.
6. **What happens to a voice burst at 7 Mbps during congestion?** 5 Mbps goes via the priority queue. The other 2 Mbps is **dropped** by the LLQ's implicit policer, not queued.
7. **When there's no congestion?** Every class may use any spare bandwidth. Guarantees are minimums, enforced only when traffic is contending.

### Reading `show policy-map interface`

```
R1# show policy-map interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1 output
 GigabitEthernet0/0/1
  Service-policy output: WAN-SHAPER
    Class-map: class-default (match-any)
      18723401 packets, 9811625540 bytes
      30 second offered rate 48211000 bps, drop rate 212000 bps
      Match: any
      Queueing
      queue limit 208 packets
      (queue depth/total drops/no-buffer drops) 64/30211/0
      shape (average) cir 50000000, bc 200000, be 200000
      target shape rate 50000000

      Service-policy : WAN-QUEUING
        Class-map: VOICE (match-any)
          4011201 packets, 802240200 bytes
          30 second offered rate 3980000 bps, drop rate 0000 bps
          Match: dscp ef (46)
          Priority: 10% (5000 kbps), burst bytes 125000, b/w exceed drops: 0

        Class-map: CRITICAL-DATA (match-any)
          2210334 packets, 1489102776 bytes
          30 second offered rate 14870000 bps, drop rate 96000 bps
          Match: dscp af21 (18) af22 (20) af23 (22)
          Queueing
          (queue depth/total drops/no-buffer drops) 22/8120/0
          bandwidth 25% (12500 kbps)
            Exp-weight-constant: 9 (1/512)
            class  Transmitted  Random drop  Tail drop  Minimum  Maximum  Mark
                                                        thresh   thresh   prob
            af21   1.9M         120          0          32       40       1/10
            af23   0.2M         7990         10         24       40       1/10
```

| Line | What it tells you |
|------|-------------------|
| Parent `offered rate 48211000 bps` | About 48 Mbps offered against a 50 Mbps shaper. The circuit is nearly full |
| `queue depth 64`, `total drops 30211` | Congestion is real right now. The policy is earning its keep |
| `shape (average) cir 50000000`, `bc 200000` | Tc = 200,000 bits ÷ 50 Mbps = **4 ms** intervals |
| VOICE `Priority: 10% (5000 kbps)` | Percent resolved against the **shaped** rate: 5 Mbps, not 100 Mbps |
| VOICE `b/w exceed drops: 0` | The LLQ policer has never fired. Voice fits its cap |
| CRITICAL-DATA `offered 14.87 Mbps` vs `bandwidth 25% (12500 kbps)` | Offered above its guarantee, so drops in this class are expected when the link is full |
| WRED table: `af23` minimum threshold 24 vs `af21` 32 | AF23 starts random drops at a shallower depth. Its drop count (7,990) dwarfs AF21's (120): **drop precedence working as designed** |

### Reading a Policer's Counters

The guest policer from 11.4, applied inbound, under load:

```
R1# show policy-map interface GigabitEthernet0/0/2 input
 GigabitEthernet0/0/2
  Service-policy input: POLICE-GUEST
    Class-map: class-default (match-any)
      812334 packets, 498221010 bytes
      30 second offered rate 13200000 bps, drop rate 1100000 bps
      Match: any
      police:
          cir 10000000 bps, bc 312500 bytes, be 312500 bytes
        conformed 702113 packets, 421268000 bytes; actions:
          transmit
        exceeded 98112 packets, 66710000 bytes; actions:
          set-dscp-transmit af13
        violated 12109 packets, 10243010 bytes; actions:
          drop
        conformed 9980000 bps, exceeded 2100000 bps, violated 1100000 bps
```

| Line | What it tells you |
|------|-------------------|
| `offered rate 13200000 bps` | Guests are trying to send 13.2 Mbps into a 10 Mbps policy |
| `cir 10000000 bps, bc 312500 bytes` | The contract: 10 Mbps, with bursts measured in **bytes** (it's a policer) |
| `conformed … 9980000 bps` | Just under 10 Mbps passes untouched: the CIR is being used fully |
| `exceeded … set-dscp-transmit af13` | 2.1 Mbps of burst above CIR is **sent but re-marked** AF13, so it will be dropped first if a queue downstream fills |
| `violated … drop` | 1.1 Mbps (matching the class `drop rate`) is discarded outright |

*Conformed + exceeded + violated = offered. If the drop rate equals the violated rate, the policer is the only thing dropping in this class.*

**Exam-style reasoning:** "Users complain voice is choppy. Which counter do you check?" Check VOICE `b/w exceed drops`. If it's climbing, the priority queue is too small, or something non-voice is marked EF. "Video is fine but bulk transfers are slow during business hours." Bulk drops in class-default are expected behavior under contention, not a fault.

### QoS Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Command that proves it |
|---------|--------------|------------------------|
| All counters stay at 0 | Policy applied in the wrong direction or on the wrong interface | `show policy-map interface` / `show running-config interface` |
| Everything lands in class-default | Markings not arriving (untrusted port reset them) or `match-all` misuse | Class-map `Match:` counters, `show class-map` |
| Queuing configured but never activates on a fast port | No parent shaper; the interface never congests | Offered rate far below interface speed, queue depth 0 |
| Voice choppy despite LLQ | Priority policer drops; or jitter introduced elsewhere (no QoS on another hop) | `b/w exceed drops`, then check each hop's policy |
| Policy rejected when applied | Mixing `bandwidth` and `bandwidth remaining`, or total over 100% | The CLI error on `service-policy` |

**📝 Exam-style questions — 11.7**

**Q1.** Refer to the exhibit. These are the class-maps used by the WAN-QUEUING policy, whose classes are VOICE, VIDEO, SIGNALING, CRITICAL-DATA, SCAVENGER and class-default. Which class handles a packet marked AF31?

```
class-map match-any VOICE
 match dscp ef
class-map match-any VIDEO
 match dscp af41 af42 af43
class-map match-any SIGNALING
 match dscp cs3
class-map match-any CRITICAL-DATA
 match dscp af21 af22 af23
class-map match-all SCAVENGER
 match dscp cs1
```

- **A.** VIDEO
- **B.** CRITICAL-DATA
- **C.** class-default
- **D.** None; the packet is dropped because no class matches it

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** No class-map matches AF31: VIDEO matches AF41–AF43, CRITICAL-DATA matches AF21–AF23. Anything unmatched falls into class-default, which always exists. **Why not the others:** A and B match different AF classes. D, unmatched packets are never dropped for lack of a class; they go to class-default.
</details>

**Q2.** Refer to the exhibit. Why is the queuing policy nested inside a parent shaper instead of being applied directly to the interface?

```
policy-map WAN-SHAPER
 class class-default
  shape average 50000000
  service-policy WAN-QUEUING
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 description 50M MPLS handoff on a 1G port
 service-policy output WAN-SHAPER
```

- **A.** The 1 Gbps interface would never congest at 50 Mbps of traffic, so the queuing policy alone would never activate; the shaper creates congestion at 50 Mbps where the child policy can act
- **B.** IOS XE doesn't allow `priority` outside a hierarchical policy
- **C.** The parent shaper polices voice to 50 Mbps
- **D.** The shaper converts the percentages in WAN-QUEUING into absolute values in bytes

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Queuing only acts when packets are waiting. Without the shaper, the router sends at up to 1 Gbps, its own queues never fill, and the provider's 50 Mbps policer drops the excess blindly. This parent/child arrangement is Hierarchical QoS. **Why not the others:** B, `priority` works in a flat policy on an interface that congests. C, the shaper buffers the aggregate; it doesn't police voice. D, the percentages are resolved against the shaped rate, but in bps, and that isn't why the hierarchy exists.
</details>

**Q3.** Refer to the exhibit. Users report choppy voice on this 50 Mbps WAN link. What explains it?

```
        Class-map: VOICE (match-any)
          30 second offered rate 6100000 bps, drop rate 1100000 bps
          Match: dscp ef (46)
          Priority: 10% (5000 kbps), burst bytes 125000, b/w exceed drops: 18322
```

- **A.** WRED in the VOICE class is dropping packets early
- **B.** More EF traffic is arriving than the 5 Mbps priority cap, so the LLQ's policer drops the excess
- **C.** The parent shaper is set higher than the circuit rate
- **D.** class-default is starving the priority queue

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** 6.1 Mbps is offered into a 5 Mbps priority class, and `b/w exceed drops` is climbing, with a 1.1 Mbps drop rate. Either there are more calls than the design allowed for, or something that isn't voice is marked EF. Raise the priority rate or fix the marking. **Why not the others:** A, there's no `random-detect` in the VOICE class. C, nothing in this output points to the shaper. D, the priority queue is always served first, so no other class can starve it.
</details>

**Q4.** In the WAN-QUEUING policy nested under the 50 Mbps WAN-SHAPER, VIDEO has `bandwidth percent 30`. How much bandwidth is VIDEO guaranteed during congestion?

- **A.** 300 Mbps
- **B.** 30 Mbps
- **C.** 50 Mbps
- **D.** 15 Mbps

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** In a child policy, percentages are of the parent's shaped rate: 30% of 50 Mbps = 15 Mbps. **Why not the others:** A is 30% of the 1 Gbps interface, which the child policy never sees. B treats the percent as Mbps. C is the whole shaped rate.
</details>

---

## 11.8 Chapter Summary

| Concept | Remember |
|---------|----------|
| DiffServ | Mark at the edge, PHB per hop, no per-flow state |
| DSCP | 6 bits; EF = 46; AFxy = 8x + 2y; CSn = 8n |
| AF drop precedence | Same queue, **higher y dropped first** |
| CoS | 3 bits in the 802.1Q tag; lost at the first router |
| MQC | class-map (which) → policy-map (what) → service-policy (where) |
| `match-all` | Default; AND logic |
| LLQ | Strict priority **with an implicit policer** |
| Shaping | Outbound only, buffers, adds delay; Tc = Bc ÷ CIR |
| HQoS | Parent shaper creates the congestion the child queues manage |
| WRED | Early random drops per DSCP; prevents global sync; not for voice |
