<a name="chapter-13"></a>
# Chapter 13: Network Virtualization: LISP & VXLAN

> **Blueprint:** ENCOR 2.3 — Describe network virtualization concepts (2.3.a LISP, 2.3.b VXLAN)

Chapter 12 virtualized *devices* and *paths*. This chapter virtualizes the **network itself**: a logical network (an *overlay*) built on top of a plain routed IP network (the *underlay*). Two protocols do the heavy lifting, and they're worth learning together because **SD-Access uses both** (Chapter 14): **LISP** answers *where is this endpoint?* and **VXLAN** carries the traffic once you know.

ENCOR asks you to *describe* them, so you won't configure these. You do need to know every role, message and number precisely.

---

## 13.1 The Problem Overlays Solve

Traditional IP addressing does two jobs with one number. `10.2.3.4` says **who** the device is (its identity) *and* **where** it is (its location, because the prefix ties it to one subnet in one place).

**Why is that a problem?** Because the two jobs conflict as soon as something **moves**:

- A VM live-migrates to a host in another building (12.3). Its identity must stay the same, so applications and sessions survive, but its location just changed.
- A laptop roams from floor 1 to floor 4, onto a different switch and different subnet.
- A branch with two ISPs (multihoming) wants one stable set of addresses while choosing between providers.

If the address *is* the location, moving means renumbering, which breaks sessions. The old workaround was **stretching Layer 2** (the same VLAN everywhere), which brings back huge broadcast domains and spanning tree across the campus or data center.

*The overlay idea: give each endpoint a stable identity, and keep a separate, changeable record of where it currently is.*

**📝 Exam-style questions — 13.1**

**Q1.** Overlay technologies such as LISP separate two jobs that a traditional IP address does at the same time. Which two jobs?

- **A.** Unicast delivery and multicast delivery
- **B.** Network address and broadcast address
- **C.** Identity (who the device is) and location (where it is attached)
- **D.** Layer 2 forwarding and Layer 3 forwarding

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Because the prefix ties an address to one subnet in one place, a device that moves must change its identity too. Overlays keep a stable identity and a separate, changeable record of location. **Why not the others:** A, B and D are real distinctions, but none of them is the conflict that appears when an endpoint moves.
</details>

**Q2.** Before overlays, the usual way to let a VM keep its IP address after moving to another building was to stretch its VLAN everywhere. What was the main drawback?

- **A.** Every move required renumbering the host.
- **B.** It required a LISP mapping system in every building.
- **C.** It stopped VMs from keeping their MAC addresses.
- **D.** It created huge broadcast domains with spanning tree running across the whole campus or data center.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** A stretched VLAN works, but one Layer 2 domain everywhere means flooding, blocked links and a large failure domain. **Why not the others:** A is the problem stretching *avoided*. B is wrong because LISP is the overlay alternative, not part of the old workaround. C is false; MACs don't change when VLANs are stretched.
</details>

## 13.2 Underlay vs Overlay

| Term | What it is | Example |
|------|------------|---------|
| **Underlay** | The physical, routed IP network. Only needs to get packets between tunnel endpoints | OSPF or IS-IS between switches, all links routed |
| **Overlay** | The logical network built from tunnels on top of the underlay | VXLAN segments, LISP-routed endpoint prefixes |
| **Encapsulation** | How overlay packets ride the underlay | VXLAN (UDP 4789), LISP data plane (UDP 4341) |
| **Control plane** | How tunnel endpoints learn *who is behind which endpoint* | LISP mapping system, BGP EVPN, or flood-and-learn |

**Story Time 📖:** the underlay is the motorway network. It only knows how to get a lorry from one depot to another, and it doesn't care what's inside. The overlay is the parcel company's own delivery network that runs on top of it: parcels are addressed to people, sorted at the depot, loaded into lorries addressed depot-to-depot, and unpacked at the other end. You can reorganise parcel routes (move a customer, add a new delivery zone) without building a single new road. *Where it breaks:* real roads can jam, but a well-built routed underlay mostly doesn't, because ECMP spreads the load over every link.

**Why is a simple routed underlay so attractive?** Because routed links have **no spanning tree**, use **every link at once with ECMP**, and converge in milliseconds. The overlay provides the flexibility endpoints need (mobility, segmentation, stretched subnets) *without* turning the physical network back into one giant Layer 2 domain.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 13.2**

**Q1.** Which statement correctly describes the underlay and the overlay?

- **A.** The underlay is the set of tunnels; the overlay is the physical routed network the tunnels cross.
- **B.** The underlay is the physical routed network that only needs to connect the tunnel endpoints; the overlay is the logical network built from tunnels on top of it.
- **C.** The underlay carries endpoint MAC addresses; the overlay carries only routing protocol traffic.
- **D.** The underlay and the overlay are two names for the same network, used by different vendors.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** The underlay only has to move packets between tunnel endpoints (for example OSPF or IS-IS between loopbacks); the overlay provides what endpoints need. **Why not the others:** A swaps the two. C is wrong because the underlay never learns endpoint MACs; it only routes between tunnel endpoints. D is wrong; they are separate layers.
</details>

**Q2.** Which two are advantages of a fully routed underlay? (Choose two.)

- **A.** It learns every endpoint's MAC address, so no overlay control plane is needed.
- **B.** It has no spanning tree, so no links sit blocked.
- **C.** It extends VLANs between every pair of switches.
- **D.** It uses all links at the same time with ECMP and converges quickly.
- **E.** It removes the need for any encapsulation.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B, D.** Routed links don't run STP between switches, so ECMP uses every path and convergence is fast. **Why not the others:** A is wrong because a routed underlay knows only tunnel endpoints, not endpoints' MACs. C describes a Layer 2 design, the opposite of a routed underlay. E is wrong; the overlay depends on encapsulation to cross the underlay.
</details>

---

## 13.3 LISP — Locator/ID Separation Protocol

**LISP** (RFC 9300/9301, originally RFC 6830) splits the address into two namespaces:

| Name | Stands for | Answers | Example |
|------|-----------|---------|---------|
| **EID** | Endpoint Identifier | **Who** — the address of the host or prefix | `10.2.3.4`, `10.2.0.0/16` |
| **RLOC** | Routing Locator | **Where** — the address of the LISP router that the EID currently sits behind | `198.51.100.2` |

The underlay only routes **RLOCs**. It never needs to know any EID. EID-to-RLOC mappings live in a **mapping system**, which works rather like DNS for locations.

**Story Time 📖:** an EID is your name and an RLOC is the address of the hotel you're staying at tonight. When you change hotels you update one directory entry ("Alex is now at the Riverside"). Your friends still look you up by name, and the postal service only ever needs to know how to reach hotels.

### The LISP Roles

| Role | Job |
|------|-----|
| **ITR** (Ingress Tunnel Router) | Receives packets from local hosts, looks up the destination EID's RLOC, **encapsulates** and sends it |
| **ETR** (Egress Tunnel Router) | Receives LISP-encapsulated packets, **decapsulates** and delivers them to local EIDs. Also **registers** its EIDs with the mapping system |
| **xTR** | A router doing both ITR and ETR — the normal case at a site edge |
| **MS** (Map Server) | Accepts **Map-Registers** from ETRs; holds the authoritative EID-to-RLOC database |
| **MR** (Map Resolver) | Accepts **Map-Requests** from ITRs and passes them into the mapping system |
| **MS/MR** | Both functions on one box — the usual deployment (and SD-Access's *control plane node*) |
| **PITR** (Proxy ITR) | Attracts traffic **from non-LISP sites** to LISP EIDs, and encapsulates it on their behalf |
| **PETR** (Proxy ETR) | Receives traffic **from LISP sites to non-LISP destinations** (e.g. the internet) and decapsulates it |
| **PxTR** | A router doing both proxy roles — the bridge between the LISP and non-LISP worlds |

**Why have proxy roles at all?** Because most of the world doesn't speak LISP. The internet has no idea that `10.2.0.0/16` sits behind RLOC `198.51.100.2`. The PxTR stands at the border and translates: traffic coming in from the non-LISP world is encapsulated toward the right RLOC (PITR), and traffic going out is decapsulated and routed normally (PETR).

### The Conversation, Step by Step

![LISP map-register, map-request and map-reply flow](images/c13_lisp_flow.png)

0. **Map-Register.** Each ETR tells the Map Server which EID prefixes are behind it ("10.2.0.0/16 is reachable at RLOC 198.51.100.2"). This repeats periodically (about every 60 seconds), authenticated with a shared key. If the ETR asks for it, the Map Server acknowledges each registration with a **Map-Notify**, so the ETR knows it was accepted.
1. **Map-Request.** A host at site A sends a packet to `10.2.3.4`. The ITR has no mapping in its cache, so it sends a Map-Request to the **Map Resolver**.
2. **Forwarding.** The MR/MS finds which ETR registered that prefix and **forwards the request to that ETR**. (Alternatively, the MS can be configured to answer on the ETR's behalf — *proxy reply*.)
3. **Map-Reply.** The ETR replies **directly to the ITR** with the mapping: EID prefix, RLOC(s), plus a **priority and weight** for each RLOC (used for multihoming and load sharing) and a TTL.
4. **Data.** The ITR caches the mapping in its **map-cache** and encapsulates packets to the RLOC. Every later packet to that prefix uses the cache with no further lookups until the TTL expires. The default map-cache TTL in a Map-Reply is **24 hours** (1,440 minutes); mobility events refresh entries long before that (see below).

**Worked example.** Site A's xTR (RLOC `198.51.100.1`) has just sent its first packet to `10.2.3.4` and received a Map-Reply from Site B's xTR. Its map-cache (output trimmed) now shows:

```
xTR-A# show ip lisp map-cache
LISP IPv4 Mapping Cache for EID-table default (IID 0), 2 entries

0.0.0.0/0, uptime: 00:05:12, expires: never, via static-send-map-request
  Negative cache entry, action: send-map-request
10.2.0.0/16, uptime: 00:00:05, expires: 23:59:54, via map-reply, complete
  Locator         Uptime    State      Pri/Wgt
  198.51.100.2    00:00:05  up           1/100
```

**Reading it:** the first line is the catch-all: "for anything I don't know, send a Map-Request". The second entry was learned from a Map-Reply 5 seconds ago and expires in just under 24 hours. Its single locator is up with priority 1, weight 100. Every packet to anything in `10.2.0.0/16` now gets an outer IP header `198.51.100.1 → 198.51.100.2`, UDP destination port 4341, and an 8-byte LISP header carrying IID 0. If Site B had two RLOCs with priority 1/weight 50 each, the ITR would share flows between them equally; an RLOC with a higher priority number is used only as a backup.

If the mapping system answers with a **negative Map-Reply** (the destination isn't a LISP EID), the ITR forwards natively or sends traffic to a **PETR**.

**Why does the ETR, not the Map Server, send the reply?** Because the ETR is the **authority on its own site**. It knows which of its RLOCs are currently up and what priorities and weights to advertise. Answering itself guarantees the ITR gets the freshest possible locator information. *The mapping system is a directory that routes questions to the right person; it isn't the person.*

**Why is this "pull" model scalable?** An ITR only learns mappings for destinations it actually talks to, on demand. A branch xTR talking to five sites holds five cache entries, not a full table of every EID in the company. Compare BGP or OSPF, which **push** every route to every router whether it's needed or not.

### Instance IDs — VRFs Inside LISP

A LISP EID is really a pair: **(Instance ID, EID prefix)**. The **Instance ID (IID)** is a 24-bit number carried in the LISP header and in every register, request and reply, and each IID maps to one VRF on the xTR. Two customers (or two SD-Access virtual networks) can therefore both use 10.1.0.0/16 without colliding in the mapping system, because the Map Server stores them under different IIDs. *The IID does for LISP exactly what the VNI does for VXLAN and the route distinguisher does for MPLS VPNs: it keeps overlapping address spaces apart.* In SD-Access, every virtual network (VN) gets its own IID.

### LISP on the Wire

| Plane | Transport | Notes |
|-------|-----------|-------|
| Control (Map-Register/Request/Reply) | **UDP 4342** | |
| Data (encapsulated packets) | **UDP 4341** | Outer IP (20) + UDP (8) + LISP header (8) = **36 bytes** for IPv4 |

**Mobility, the payoff.** When an endpoint moves to a new xTR, that xTR registers the EID from its own RLOC. The Map Server updates the mapping and sends a **Map-Notify** to the old xTR, which tells any ITR still sending to the old location (a *Solicit-Map-Request*) to refresh its cache. The host keeps its IP address and the underlay never changes. *This is the mechanism SD-Access uses for wired and wireless roaming.*

**The same move, step by step.** Laptop `10.50.1.25` (a /32 host EID) roams from Edge 1 (RLOC `192.168.255.1`) to Edge 2 (RLOC `192.168.255.2`). Edge 3 (RLOC `192.168.255.3`) has a printer that is talking to the laptop:

1. Edge 2 sees traffic from `10.50.1.25` on a local port and sends a **Map-Register**: `10.50.1.25/32 → 192.168.255.2`.
2. The Map Server overwrites the old entry (which pointed at Edge 1) and sends a **Map-Notify** to Edge 1: "this EID has left you".
3. Edge 3 doesn't know yet. It still encapsulates the printer's packets to Edge 1, using its cached mapping.
4. Edge 1 receives them, sees the EID is no longer local, and sends Edge 3 a **Solicit-Map-Request (SMR)**: "your cache is stale, ask again".
5. Edge 3 sends a fresh Map-Request, gets `→ 192.168.255.2`, updates its cache and sends to Edge 2 from then on.

The laptop kept `10.50.1.25`, its TCP sessions survived, and no underlay route changed. Only one directory entry and one cache entry did.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 13.3**

**Q1.** Which LISP role registers the EID prefixes behind it with the Map Server?

- **A.** ITR
- **B.** ETR
- **C.** Map Resolver
- **D.** PITR

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** The ETR sends periodic Map-Registers (about every 60 seconds) for its EIDs, and is also what answers Map-Requests for them. **Why not the others:** A, the ITR, *asks* for mappings and encapsulates. C, the Map Resolver, receives Map-Requests from ITRs. D, the PITR, attracts traffic from non-LISP sites.
</details>

**Q2.** A host behind ITR-A sends the first packet to an EID behind ETR-B. ETR-B registered its prefix earlier. Which sequence correctly orders what happens next?

- **A.** ITR-A sends a Map-Request to the Map Resolver → the Map Server forwards it to ETR-B → ETR-B sends a Map-Reply directly to ITR-A → ITR-A caches the mapping and encapsulates to ETR-B's RLOC
- **B.** ITR-A sends a Map-Register → the Map Server sends a Map-Reply → ITR-A floods the packet to every RLOC
- **C.** ITR-A sends a Map-Request to ETR-B → ETR-B forwards it to the Map Server → the Map Server sends the Map-Reply to ITR-A
- **D.** ITR-A forwards the packet natively → ETR-B sends a Solicit-Map-Request → ITR-A sends a Map-Register

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** The ITR doesn't know where ETR-B is, so it asks the mapping system; the mapping system passes the question to the authority (ETR-B), which answers directly. **Why not the others:** B uses Map-Register, which only ETRs send, and LISP never floods to find an EID. C has the ITR contacting the ETR before it knows the ETR's RLOC. D misuses the Solicit-Map-Request, which is for stale caches after a move.
</details>

**Q3.** Refer to the exhibit. How does the ITR send traffic to 10.2.0.0/16?

```
xTR-A# show ip lisp map-cache
LISP IPv4 Mapping Cache for EID-table default (IID 0), 2 entries

0.0.0.0/0, uptime: 00:05:12, expires: never, via static-send-map-request
  Negative cache entry, action: send-map-request
10.2.0.0/16, uptime: 00:00:05, expires: 23:59:54, via map-reply, complete
  Locator         Uptime    State      Pri/Wgt
  198.51.100.2    00:00:05  up           1/100
  198.51.100.3    00:00:05  up           2/100
```

- **A.** It shares flows 50/50 between the two locators, because their weights are equal.
- **B.** It sends everything to 198.51.100.3, because a higher priority value is preferred.
- **C.** It sends everything to 198.51.100.2 and uses 198.51.100.3 only if .2 becomes unavailable.
- **D.** It alternates packet by packet between the two locators.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Priority is compared first and the *lower* number wins; weight only shares traffic among locators with the same priority. So .3, with priority 2, is a backup. **Why not the others:** A would be true only if both had priority 1. B gets the priority rule backwards. D is wrong because LISP shares by flow, not per packet.
</details>

**Q4.** A laptop with EID 10.50.1.25/32 roams from Edge 1 to Edge 2. Edge 3 keeps sending the laptop's traffic to Edge 1 using its cached mapping. What makes Edge 3 refresh its cache?

- **A.** The Map Server sends a Map-Notify directly to Edge 3.
- **B.** Edge 3 sends a Map-Register for the laptop's EID.
- **C.** Nothing; Edge 3 waits for the 24-hour map-cache TTL to expire.
- **D.** Edge 1, which no longer has the EID, sends Edge 3 a Solicit-Map-Request, and Edge 3 sends a fresh Map-Request.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** The old edge receives traffic for an EID that has left, so it tells the sender its cache is stale. The new Map-Reply points at Edge 2. **Why not the others:** A is wrong because the Map-Notify goes to the *old* xTR (Edge 1), not to every ITR. B is wrong because Edge 3 has nothing to register; the laptop isn't behind it. C would leave traffic black-holed for a day, which is exactly what SMR avoids.
</details>

## 13.4 VXLAN — Layer 2 Over Layer 3

**VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN, RFC 7348)** encapsulates a **complete Ethernet frame** inside a UDP packet so it can cross a routed network. The two endpoints of a VXLAN tunnel are **VTEPs**.

**Story Time 📖:** a shipping container. A container (the VXLAN packet) can carry anything that fits, here a whole Ethernet frame with its own MACs and VLAN-ish label. Lorries, trains and ships (underlay routers) only read the label on the outside of the container (the outer IP header) and never open it. The container's number (the VNI) tells the receiving port which customer the goods belong to.

### Why VXLAN Exists

1. **The VLAN ID is only 12 bits** — 4,094 usable segments. A multi-tenant data center or cloud runs out fast.
2. **Workloads need Layer 2 adjacency across a routed fabric** — live migration (12.3), clusters, and legacy apps that assume a shared subnet — without stretching spanning tree across the data center.
3. **Routed underlays are better** — ECMP across all links, no blocked ports, fast convergence (13.2).

VXLAN gives you Layer 2 *service* over a Layer 3 *network*.

### The Header

![VXLAN encapsulation and header](images/c13_vxlan_header.png)

| Field | Size | Purpose |
|-------|------|---------|
| Outer Ethernet | 14 B | Hop-by-hop MACs across the underlay |
| Outer IP | 20 B | Source VTEP → destination VTEP |
| Outer UDP | 8 B | **Destination port 4789**; source port is a hash of the inner frame |
| VXLAN header | 8 B | Flags + **24-bit VNI** |
| Inner frame | — | The original Ethernet frame, untouched |

**Total overhead: 50 bytes** (54 if the outer frame carries an 802.1Q tag). Underlay links therefore need a larger MTU, typically **9000 or 9216 jumbo**, or at minimum 1550, otherwise full-size 1500-byte frames from hosts get dropped.

**Why is the VNI 24 bits?** Because 2²⁴ = **16,777,216** segments ends the scarcity problem for good. Each **VNI (VXLAN Network Identifier)** is one Layer 2 segment, just as each VLAN ID was. VTEPs map local VLANs to VNIs: VLAN 10 on leaf 1 and VLAN 210 on leaf 2 can both be VNI 10010, so VLAN numbers become merely *local*.

**Why put it in UDP rather than straight into IP?** For **load balancing**. Underlay routers spread traffic over ECMP paths by hashing the 5-tuple. If every VXLAN packet between two VTEPs had the same outer header, all their flows would hash onto one path. By setting the **UDP source port from a hash of the inner frame's headers**, each inner flow gets a different outer 5-tuple, so it spreads across the fabric, while packets of a single flow stay in order on one path. *UDP is the cheapest header that carries a field routers already hash on.*

### VTEPs

A **VTEP (VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint)** encapsulates and decapsulates. It has a local IP in the underlay (usually a loopback) and one or more VNIs. VTEPs can be hardware (a leaf switch such as a Nexus 9000 or Catalyst 9000) or software (a hypervisor vSwitch).

**How a frame crosses the fabric, step by step.** VM-A (MAC `00aa.bb01.0001`, IP `10.10.0.11`) on Leaf 1 sends to VM-B (MAC `00aa.bb01.0002`, IP `10.10.0.12`) on Leaf 2. Both are in VLAN 10, mapped to **VNI 10010**. Leaf 1's VTEP address is `10.0.0.11`, Leaf 2's is `10.0.0.12`. Leaf 1 already knows where VM-B's MAC is (how it knows is the next topic):

1. VM-A sends an ordinary 1500-byte Ethernet frame, `00aa.bb01.0001 → 00aa.bb01.0002`, VLAN 10, into Leaf 1.
2. Leaf 1 maps VLAN 10 → VNI 10010 and looks up the destination MAC in VNI 10010: "behind VTEP `10.0.0.12`".
3. Leaf 1 adds an 8-byte VXLAN header (VNI 10010), a UDP header (destination port **4789**, source port from a hash of the inner frame), and an outer IP header `10.0.0.11 → 10.0.0.12`. The original VLAN tag is not carried; the VNI replaces it.
4. The spine switches route the outer packet using the underlay routing table (OSPF or IS-IS learned the two loopbacks), picking one of several equal-cost paths from the UDP source-port hash.
5. Leaf 2 sees UDP 4789 to its own VTEP address, strips the outer headers, reads VNI 10010, maps it to its *local* VLAN for that VNI, and delivers the original frame to VM-B. VM-B can't tell it ever left the switch.

**Worked example — the MTU sum.** The frame from step 1 is 1514 bytes on the wire (1500 payload + 14 Ethernet header). After step 3 the outer IP packet is 1500 (inner payload) + 14 (inner Ethernet) + 8 (VXLAN) + 8 (UDP) + 20 (outer IP) = **1550 bytes**. A spine link left at the default 1500 MTU can't carry it. VTEPs must not fragment VXLAN packets (RFC 7348), and switch hardware drops oversize packets rather than fragmenting them, so the frame is lost. Small pings work and big transfers fail, the same symptom as GRE in Chapter 12. Hence jumbo MTU on every underlay link.

### The Control-Plane Question: How Does a VTEP Learn Where MACs Are?

VXLAN itself only defines the encapsulation. A VTEP still needs to know *"MAC 00aa.bb01.0203 in VNI 10010 is behind VTEP 10.0.0.12"*, and to handle broadcasts, unknown unicast and multicast (**BUM** traffic).

| Approach | How BUM traffic is handled | How MACs are learned | Trade-off |
|----------|---------------------------|----------------------|-----------|
| **Flood and learn — multicast underlay** | Each VNI maps to a multicast group; BUM is sent to the group | Data plane: like a switch, learn the source MAC + source VTEP from received packets | Simple, but needs PIM in the underlay (Chapter 10) and still floods |
| **Flood and learn — ingress replication** | The VTEP unicasts a copy to every other VTEP in a configured list | Data plane learning | No multicast needed, but more replication load |
| **BGP EVPN** | Ingress replication or multicast, with peers discovered via BGP (route type 3) | **Control plane:** VTEPs advertise MAC and IP addresses in MP-BGP (route type 2); prefixes as type 5 | Scales, little flooding, ARP suppression, distributed anycast gateway. The data-center standard |
| **LISP** (SD-Access) | Fabric handles it; flooding is optional per pool | Edges register endpoints with the LISP control plane node | Campus-optimized; pull-based |

**How EVPN fills the table, step by step** (same VMs as above):

1. VM-B sends its first frame (a gratuitous ARP when it boots, for example). Leaf 2 learns `00aa.bb01.0002 / 10.10.0.12` on a local port.
2. Leaf 2 advertises an EVPN **route type 2** in BGP: "MAC `00aa.bb01.0002`, IP `10.10.0.12`, VNI 10010, next hop `10.0.0.12`".
3. The route reflector (usually the spines) passes it to every leaf.
4. Leaf 1 installs the MAC against remote VTEP `10.0.0.12` *before VM-A has sent a single frame to it*.
5. When VM-A ARPs for `10.10.0.12`, Leaf 1 already knows the answer and replies itself (ARP suppression), so the broadcast never crosses the fabric.

With flood-and-learn, step 4 only happens after a frame from VM-B has actually reached Leaf 1 through the tunnel, typically the reply to an ARP that Leaf 1 first flooded to every VTEP in VNI 10010.

**Why is BGP EVPN preferred over flood-and-learn?** Because flood-and-learn repeats the oldest Layer 2 behaviour (flood to everyone until you learn) across a whole fabric, and it needs every VTEP to observe traffic before it knows anything. EVPN **tells** every VTEP where every MAC and IP is as soon as it appears, so unknown-unicast flooding mostly disappears, VTEPs can answer ARP locally (**ARP suppression**), and the same default gateway can exist on every leaf (**anycast gateway**). *Control-plane learning replaces guessing with knowing.*

### 🔬 VXLAN-GPO — How SD-Access Carries Policy

SD-Access uses a VXLAN variant with the **Group Policy Option (VXLAN-GPO)**, which uses some reserved header bits to carry a **16-bit Scalable Group Tag (SGT)**. The destination edge can then enforce group-based policy (Chapter 14) without looking anything up. *One header carries the segment (VNI = virtual network) and the identity group (SGT).*

**📝 Exam-style questions — 13.4**

**Q1.** Hosts in a VXLAN fabric send full 1500-byte IP packets, and the outer frames are untagged. What is the minimum underlay MTU needed so these packets aren't dropped?

- **A.** 1500
- **B.** 1524
- **C.** 1550
- **D.** 9216, because VXLAN requires jumbo frames

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** 1500 + 14 (inner Ethernet) + 8 (VXLAN) + 8 (UDP) + 20 (outer IP) = 1550. Jumbo MTU is recommended, but 1550 is the minimum. **Why not the others:** A leaves no room for the 50 bytes of overhead. B is the GRE figure (24 bytes of overhead). D is common practice, not a requirement.
</details>

**Q2.** Why does VXLAN put its header inside UDP and set the UDP source port from a hash of the inner frame?

- **A.** So that underlay routers, which hash the 5-tuple for ECMP, spread different inner flows across different paths while keeping each flow on one path
- **B.** So that VTEPs can retransmit lost frames
- **C.** Because UDP encrypts the inner frame
- **D.** Because the destination VTEP uses the source port to identify the VNI

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Without the varying source port, all traffic between two VTEPs would have the same outer header and land on one path. **Why not the others:** B is wrong because UDP has no retransmission. C is false; UDP doesn't encrypt anything. D is wrong because the VNI is in the VXLAN header itself.
</details>

**Q3.** Which two statements describe BGP EVPN as a VXLAN control plane? (Choose two.)

- **A.** It needs PIM in the underlay for every VNI.
- **B.** VTEPs learn remote MAC addresses only from data traffic.
- **C.** VTEPs advertise MAC and IP addresses to each other in BGP route type 2.
- **D.** It limits the fabric to 4,094 segments.
- **E.** Leaf switches can answer ARP requests locally (ARP suppression).

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C, E.** EVPN *tells* every VTEP where each MAC and IP is, so a leaf can answer ARP itself instead of flooding. **Why not the others:** A describes flood-and-learn with a multicast underlay; EVPN can use ingress replication. B describes flood-and-learn. D is the VLAN limit; VNIs are 24-bit (about 16.7 million).
</details>

**Q4.** Leaf 1 maps VLAN 10 to VNI 10010. Leaf 2 maps VLAN 210 to VNI 10010. Can a host in VLAN 10 on Leaf 1 talk at Layer 2 to a host in VLAN 210 on Leaf 2?

- **A.** No, because the VLAN IDs must match on every leaf.
- **B.** Yes, because the VNI defines the Layer 2 segment across the fabric and VLAN numbers are only locally significant.
- **C.** Only if a router routes between VLAN 10 and VLAN 210.
- **D.** Only if both leaves carry the original 802.1Q tag inside the VXLAN packet.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** Each VTEP maps its local VLAN to the VNI on the way in and from the VNI back to its own local VLAN on the way out. **Why not the others:** A is the old VLAN-trunking rule that VXLAN removes. C is wrong because they're the same Layer 2 segment, so no routing is needed. D is wrong because the original VLAN tag isn't carried; the VNI replaces it.
</details>

---

## 13.5 LISP vs VXLAN at a Glance

**Why compare them:** the two are easy to blur because both are overlays, both use a 24-bit segment ID and both ride UDP. The difference is the job. LISP mainly answers *where is it?* (a lookup service), and VXLAN mainly answers *how do I carry it?* (an envelope). SD-Access uses LISP for the first and VXLAN for the second.

| Topic | LISP | VXLAN |
|-------|----------|-----------|
| Main job | **Control plane** — the EID-to-RLOC mapping system (it also defines its own data plane) | **Data plane** — the encapsulation |
| Encapsulates | IP packets (Layer 3) | Ethernet frames (Layer 2) |
| UDP port | 4342 control / 4341 data | **4789** |
| Overhead (IPv4 underlay) | 36 bytes | **50 bytes** |
| Segment ID | Instance ID (24-bit) | VNI (24-bit) |
| Learning model | Pull, on demand | Flood-and-learn, or a control plane (BGP EVPN / LISP) |
| Where you'll meet it | SD-Access control plane, multihomed branches, mobility | Data-center fabrics (EVPN), SD-Access data plane |

**Exam trap:** "Which protocol does SD-Access use for its data plane?" — **VXLAN** (with GPO). "Control plane?" — **LISP**. "Underlay routing?" — **IS-IS** (when Catalyst Center's LAN automation builds it). "Policy plane?" — **TrustSec/SGT**. Learn the four as a set; questions usually test whether you can keep them apart.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 13.5**

**Q1.** Which option correctly matches each SD-Access plane to its technology?

- **A.** Data plane: LISP. Control plane: VXLAN. Underlay: OSPF. Policy plane: IPsec
- **B.** Data plane: IPsec. Control plane: OMP. Underlay: BGP. Policy plane: ACLs
- **C.** Data plane: VXLAN. Control plane: BGP EVPN. Underlay: EIGRP. Policy plane: VRFs
- **D.** Data plane: VXLAN (GPO). Control plane: LISP. Underlay: IS-IS. Policy plane: TrustSec/SGTs

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** LISP answers "where is it?", VXLAN carries it, IS-IS (built by LAN automation) connects the loopbacks, and SGTs decide who may talk to whom. **Why not the others:** A swaps LISP and VXLAN. B describes SD-WAN pieces (OMP, IPsec). C uses EVPN, the data-center control plane, not SD-Access's.
</details>

**Q2.** Two virtual networks in an SD-Access fabric both use 10.1.0.0/16. Which field keeps their mappings apart in the LISP mapping system, and which field does the same job in the VXLAN data plane?

- **A.** The LISP Instance ID; the VXLAN VNI
- **B.** The RLOC; the VXLAN UDP source port
- **C.** The Map-Reply TTL; the outer IP header
- **D.** The route distinguisher; the 802.1Q tag

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Both are 24-bit segment IDs. Each virtual network gets its own IID in LISP and its own VNI in VXLAN, so overlapping addresses never collide. **Why not the others:** B: the RLOC is a location and the source port is for ECMP hashing. C: a TTL and a header don't identify segments. D: the RD does this job in MPLS VPNs, not in LISP, and the 802.1Q tag isn't carried across the fabric.
</details>

<a name="chapter-14"></a>
# Chapter 14: Catalyst SD-WAN & SD-Access

> **Blueprint:** ENCOR 1.2 — Explain the working principles of the Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN solution (1.2.a control and data plane elements, 1.2.b benefits and limitations); ENCOR 1.3 — Explain the working principles of the Cisco SD-Access solution (1.3.a control and data plane elements, 1.3.b traditional campus interoperating with SD-Access)

These are Cisco's two big **controller-based architectures** for the enterprise: **SD-WAN** for connecting sites across any transport, and **SD-Access** for the campus. Both apply the same idea from the CCNA guide's SDN chapter (22.2): separate the *brain* (management and control) from the *muscle* (forwarding), centralize the brain, and express what you want as **policy** rather than box-by-box CLI.

They're also where Chapters 12 and 13 come together. SD-WAN is built on **IPsec tunnels** and **VRF-style segmentation**; SD-Access is built on **LISP + VXLAN + VRFs**.

> **Names changed in 2023.** Cisco renamed the SD-WAN components. Learn the new names, but recognise the old ones, because documentation and many exam-prep sources still use them: **SD-WAN Manager = vManage**, **SD-WAN Controller = vSmart**, **SD-WAN Validator = vBond**. **Catalyst Center = DNA Center.**

---

## 14.1 Why SD-WAN? The Problem With the Traditional WAN

The classic enterprise WAN was **MPLS** circuits from one provider to every branch: reliable, but expensive, slow to order and rigid. Meanwhile:

- Applications moved **to the cloud** (Microsoft 365, SaaS, IaaS), but branch traffic was still backhauled to the data center first, adding latency.
- **Broadband and 4G/5G** became cheap and fast, but each is unreliable on its own.
- Every branch router was configured by hand, so policy drifted from site to site.

**SD-WAN's answer:** treat every transport — MPLS, internet, LTE — as a pool of interchangeable paths, build **encrypted tunnels over all of them**, measure each path continuously, and let a **central policy** decide which application uses which path.

**Story Time 📖:** a traditional WAN is a company that sends every parcel by one expensive courier on one fixed route, and every branch office writes its own shipping rules on a notepad. SD-WAN is a modern logistics firm. It has contracts with several carriers (MPLS, broadband, 4G), tracks every carrier's delivery times live, writes the shipping rules once at head office, and for each parcel picks whichever carrier is meeting the promised delivery time right now. Urgent medical supplies (voice) always get the carrier that's on time today; bulk catalogues (backups) take the cheapest.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 14.1**

**Q1.** A company's branches reach Microsoft 365 by sending all traffic over MPLS to the data center first, then out to the internet. Users complain about slow cloud applications. Which traditional-WAN problem does this describe?

- **A.** MPLS circuits can't carry encrypted traffic.
- **B.** Each branch router has too many routing protocols.
- **C.** Cloud traffic is backhauled through the data center, adding latency.
- **D.** Broadband circuits are too unreliable to be used at all.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Applications moved to the cloud, but the WAN design still sent branch traffic home first. SD-WAN fixes this with direct internet access and measured paths. **Why not the others:** A is false; MPLS can carry encrypted traffic. B isn't the issue described. D overstates it: broadband is unreliable *on its own*, which SD-WAN handles by combining transports.
</details>

**Q2.** Which statement best summarizes the Catalyst SD-WAN approach?

- **A.** Treat MPLS, internet and LTE as a pool of paths, build encrypted tunnels over all of them, measure every path continuously, and let central policy choose a path per application.
- **B.** Replace every transport with a single high-capacity MPLS circuit managed by Cisco.
- **C.** Configure each branch router by hand, but with a faster CLI.
- **D.** Send each application over the cheapest transport, regardless of path quality.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Transport independence, encryption, measurement and central policy are the four ideas behind it. **Why not the others:** B is the old single-provider model SD-WAN moves away from. C keeps the box-by-box problem. D ignores the measured SLAs that application-aware routing uses.
</details>

## 14.2 Catalyst SD-WAN Components

![Catalyst SD-WAN components and planes](images/c14_sdwan_planes.png)

| Component (former name) | Plane | Job |
|-------------------------|-------|-----|
| **SD-WAN Manager** (vManage) | **Management** | Single GUI and REST API: configuration templates/configuration groups, policy authoring, monitoring, software upgrades, certificates. Pushes config to devices over NETCONF |
| **SD-WAN Validator** (vBond) | **Orchestration** | The **first point of contact**. Authenticates every new device, tells it where the Controllers and Managers are, and helps with **NAT traversal** (it sees each device's public, post-NAT address). Must have a public, reachable IP |
| **SD-WAN Controller** (vSmart) | **Control** | The routing brain. Runs **OMP** with every WAN Edge, acting like a BGP route reflector: receives routes and TLOCs, applies **centralized control policy**, and redistributes them. Also distributes data-plane encryption keys |
| **WAN Edge** (cEdge — Catalyst 8000/8300/8500, ISR 1000/4000 on IOS XE; vEdge on legacy Viptela OS) | **Data** | The branch/DC routers. Build IPsec tunnels to each other, forward traffic, enforce data policy, measure paths |

**Story Time 📖 (the four roles):** think of an airline. The **Validator** is the passport desk at the entrance: it checks your identity and tells you which gate to go to, and you only go back to it if you have to rejoin. The **Controller** is air traffic control: it knows where every plane is and tells each pilot which routes are open. The **Manager** is head office: it writes the timetable and the rules, and watches the dashboards. The **WAN Edges** are the planes: they actually carry the passengers. If air traffic control's radio goes quiet for a while, planes already in the air keep flying their filed routes (graceful restart, 14.4), but no new routes can be issued.

**Why split it into four roles?** Each one has a different scaling and security need. The Validator must sit on the public internet so devices behind NAT can reach it, but it holds no routes. The Controllers need to be highly available and scale with the number of edges. The Manager is a heavyweight database and GUI that people log in to. Separating them means a busy GUI never slows routing, and an exposed orchestrator never holds the routing table. *Separate planes, separate failure domains.*

**Where the controllers run:** on-premises (VMs in your data center), in a private cloud, or **Cisco-hosted (cloud-delivered)**, where Cisco runs the Manager, Controllers and Validators for you and you only own the WAN Edges. The architecture and roles are identical in every case; only who operates the controller VMs changes.

### How a New WAN Edge Joins (Zero-Touch Provisioning)

1. The router boots with no configuration, gets an IP via DHCP on its WAN port, and contacts the **PnP Connect** cloud service (or a configured Validator address).
2. PnP Connect redirects it to the organisation's **Validator**.
3. The Validator authenticates the device by **certificate and serial number** (it must be on the authorised device list uploaded from Cisco's Plug and Play portal), then tells it the addresses of the **Controllers** and **Manager**.
4. The edge builds **permanent control connections** to the Controllers and Manager. The connection to the Validator is torn down once onboarding is done (it's transient).
5. The Manager pushes the device's configuration; the Controller starts sending routes and policy via OMP.

**Onboarding prerequisites, the usual reasons a device never joins:**

- **Organization name** must match exactly (case-sensitive) on every component, because it is embedded in the certificates each side checks.
- **The device must be on the authorised WAN Edge list** (its chassis/serial number), uploaded to the SD-WAN Manager and synced to the Validators and Controllers. An unknown serial is rejected at the Validator.
- **A trusted root CA chain** must be installed, so each side can validate the others' certificates (Cisco's PKI by default, or an enterprise CA).
- The edge needs a **unique system IP and site ID**, the **Validator's address** (or reachability to PnP Connect), and working DNS/NTP: certificate checks fail if the clock is wrong.

### Control Connections: DTLS or TLS

All control traffic runs inside **DTLS** (Datagram TLS, over UDP, the default) or **TLS** (over TCP) tunnels, authenticated with certificates in both directions. Nothing is trusted just because it's on the right subnet. The default base port is **12346** (UDP for DTLS). Devices with several control connections use **port offsets** above it, and **port hopping** moves to 12366, 12386, 12406 and 12426 if a NAT or firewall blocks the base port. Firewalls in front of controllers must allow this range.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 14.2**

**Q1.** Which Catalyst SD-WAN component is the first point of contact for a new WAN Edge, authenticates it, tells it where the Controllers and Managers are, helps with NAT traversal, and must have a publicly reachable IP address?

- **A.** SD-WAN Manager
- **B.** SD-WAN Controller
- **C.** WAN Edge
- **D.** SD-WAN Validator

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** The Validator (formerly vBond) is the orchestration plane. Its connection to an edge is transient: once onboarding is done it is torn down. **Why not the others:** A, the Manager (vManage), is the management GUI and API. B, the Controller (vSmart), runs OMP. C, the WAN Edge, is the router being onboarded.
</details>

**Q2.** A new WAN Edge never completes onboarding. Which two are likely causes? (Choose two.)

- **A.** The BFD hello interval is set to 1 second.
- **B.** The organization name configured on the edge differs in case from the one on the controllers.
- **C.** The control connections use DTLS instead of TLS.
- **D.** The edge's serial number isn't on the authorized WAN Edge list.
- **E.** The edge has two transport colors.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B, D.** The organization name is embedded in the certificates and must match exactly, and the Validator rejects any serial number it doesn't know. **Why not the others:** A is the default BFD hello, and BFD only matters after tunnels exist. C is wrong because DTLS is the default. E is normal; most edges have several colors.
</details>

**Q3.** In which plane does the SD-WAN Controller operate, and which protocol does it run with the WAN Edges?

- **A.** Management plane; NETCONF
- **B.** Control plane; OMP
- **C.** Data plane; IPsec
- **D.** Orchestration plane; DTLS

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** The Controller (formerly vSmart) is the routing brain. It runs OMP with every edge and acts much like a BGP route reflector. **Why not the others:** A describes the Manager, which pushes configuration over NETCONF. C describes the WAN Edges. D describes the Validator; DTLS is the transport for all control connections, not a routing protocol.
</details>

**Q4.** A firewall in front of a branch blocks UDP 12346. What does Catalyst SD-WAN do to keep the control connections up?

- **A.** Port hopping moves the connection to another port in the range (12366, 12386, 12406, 12426).
- **B.** It falls back to IKE on UDP 500.
- **C.** It switches to NETCONF on TCP 830.
- **D.** It sends the control traffic unencrypted over port 80.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Port hopping tries the next base ports when a NAT or firewall blocks one, which is why firewalls in front of controllers must allow the whole range. **Why not the others:** B is wrong because SD-WAN control connections use DTLS or TLS, not IKE. C is how the Manager pushes configuration, not a fallback for control connections. D is false; control traffic is always authenticated and encrypted.
</details>

## 14.3 OMP and TLOCs — How Routes and Paths Are Shared

**OMP (Overlay Management Protocol)** runs between each WAN Edge and the Controllers, never edge to edge. It carries three kinds of route:

| OMP route type | What it advertises |
|----------------|--------------------|
| **OMP routes** (vRoutes) | The service-side prefixes a site can reach — its LANs, learned via connected, static, OSPF, EIGRP or BGP and redistributed into OMP |
| **TLOC routes** | The site's transport attachment points, and how to reach them |
| **Service routes** | Network services (firewall, IPS) available at a site, for service chaining |

A **TLOC (Transport Locator)** identifies one WAN attachment point of one router. It is the tuple:

**TLOC = System IP + Color + Encapsulation**

- **System IP** — a unique router ID, like an OSPF router ID (not necessarily routable).
- **Color** — a label for the transport type: `mpls`, `biz-internet`, `public-internet`, `lte`, `private1`... Colors decide which TLOCs try to build tunnels to each other and whether to use public (post-NAT) or private addresses.
- **Encapsulation** — IPsec (normal) or GRE.

**Worked example — two branches, two transports each.** Branch 20 has an MPLS circuit and a broadband circuit; Branch 30 has broadband and LTE:

| Router | System IP | TLOC (color) | Transport address |
|--------|-----------|--------------|-------------------|
| Branch 20 | 1.1.1.20 | `mpls` | 172.31.20.2 (provider private) |
| Branch 20 | 1.1.1.20 | `biz-internet` | 203.0.113.20 (public) |
| Branch 30 | 1.1.1.30 | `biz-internet` | 198.51.100.30 (public) |
| Branch 30 | 1.1.1.30 | `lte` | 100.64.7.9 (behind carrier NAT) |

By default each TLOC tries to build an IPsec tunnel to every remote TLOC, so Branch 20 attempts four tunnels: mpls↔biz-internet, mpls↔lte, biz-internet↔biz-internet and biz-internet↔lte. The two from the MPLS TLOC stay down, because a private MPLS circuit has no route to internet addresses. Engineers usually add the **`restrict`** keyword to the `mpls` color so it only tries to build tunnels to other `mpls` TLOCs and doesn't waste time on attempts that can never come up. BFD then shows the two working internet-side tunnels as up.

**Why TLOCs instead of just IP addresses?** Because a WAN interface's IP can change (DHCP on broadband, NAT, a new circuit), and the overlay shouldn't care. An OMP route says *"10.20.0.0/16 is reachable via TLOC {System IP 1.1.1.20, color biz-internet}"*. If that circuit's public address changes, only the TLOC route changes; the prefixes stay valid. *Notice that's exactly LISP's split from 13.3 — identity (the prefix) is separated from location (the TLOC).*

**📝 Exam-style questions — 14.3**

**Q1.** Which three values make up a TLOC?

- **A.** Site ID, VPN ID and public IP address
- **B.** System IP, OMP route and BFD session
- **C.** System IP, color and encapsulation
- **D.** Organization name, serial number and color

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** A TLOC identifies one WAN attachment point of one router. **Why not the others:** A mixes in the VPN ID and an IP address, which can change; avoiding that dependency is the point of TLOCs. B lists things that use TLOCs. D lists onboarding values.
</details>

**Q2.** Why does Catalyst SD-WAN advertise prefixes as reachable "via a TLOC" instead of via a WAN interface's IP address?

- **A.** TLOCs are shorter, so OMP updates are smaller.
- **B.** IP addresses can't be carried in OMP.
- **C.** A TLOC encrypts the prefix, while an IP address would expose it.
- **D.** A WAN address can change (DHCP, NAT, a new circuit), and only the TLOC route then needs updating; the prefixes stay valid.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** This separates identity (the prefix) from location (the TLOC), the same idea as LISP's EID and RLOC. **Why not the others:** A isn't the reason. B is false; TLOC routes themselves carry the transport addresses. C is false; a TLOC is an identifier, not encryption.
</details>

**Q3.** Branch 20 has TLOCs with colors `mpls` and `biz-internet`. Branch 30 has `biz-internet` and `lte`. The `mpls` color on Branch 20 is configured with `restrict`. How many tunnels does Branch 20 attempt to build to Branch 30?

- **A.** 1
- **B.** 2
- **C.** 3
- **D.** 4

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** With `restrict`, the `mpls` TLOC only tries other `mpls` TLOCs, and Branch 30 has none. The `biz-internet` TLOC still tries both remote TLOCs: biz-internet↔biz-internet and biz-internet↔lte. **Why not the others:** D is the count *without* `restrict` (every local TLOC to every remote TLOC). A and C don't match either case.
</details>

## 14.4 The Data Plane

**The problem it solves:** OMP has told every edge *what* is reachable and *through which TLOCs*. The data plane now has to carry user traffic securely between sites, notice when a path dies or gets worse, and move the right applications off it.

**How a route becomes a forwarding path, step by step** (Branch 20 LAN `10.20.0.0/16`, Branch 30 wants to reach it):

1. Branch 20 learns `10.20.0.0/16` from its LAN-side OSPF in service VPN 1 and redistributes it into OMP.
2. It sends an OMP route to the Controller: "VPN 1, `10.20.0.0/16`, reachable via TLOCs {1.1.1.20, mpls, ipsec} and {1.1.1.20, biz-internet, ipsec}". It also sends TLOC routes saying how to reach each TLOC (its public and private addresses) and its encryption keys.
3. The Controller applies any centralized control policy and reflects the routes to Branch 30.
4. Branch 30 installs `10.20.0.0/16` in VPN 1 with the next hops being the TLOCs it has a working (BFD-up) tunnel to.
5. A user at Branch 30 sends to `10.20.5.5`. Branch 30 encrypts the packet with Branch 20's key and sends it through the chosen IPsec tunnel. The VPN ID (1) is carried in the packet, so Branch 20 delivers it into VPN 1 and nowhere else.

- WAN Edges build **IPsec tunnels directly to each other**, one per pair of TLOCs that policy allows. By default this is a **full mesh** of tunnels across all colors; policy can restrict it to hub-and-spoke or regional topologies.
- **Encryption keys are distributed by the Controller over OMP** rather than negotiated pairwise with IKE. Each edge generates its keys, sends them to the Controller, and the Controller reflects them to the edges that need them. *Why? Pairwise IKE between 1,000 sites would mean about 500,000 negotiations; one channel to the Controller scales linearly.*
- **BFD** runs inside every tunnel, both to detect failure and to **measure loss, latency and jitter** continuously. The defaults are a **1 s hello** with a **multiplier of 7**, so a dead tunnel is declared down after about **7 seconds**. Tune the hello interval down per color if you need faster failover.
- **Application-Aware Routing (AAR)** uses those measurements. You define **SLA classes** ("voice: loss < 1%, latency < 150 ms, jitter < 30 ms") and map applications (identified by DPI, NBAR2) to them. If the current path breaks the SLA, traffic moves to one that meets it.

**Worked example — Application-Aware Routing in action.** Branch 30 has two tunnels to the data center: biz-internet and LTE. The voice SLA class is *loss < 1%, latency < 150 ms, jitter < 30 ms*:

| Measurement window | biz-internet | LTE | Voice uses |
|--------------------|--------------|-----|------------|
| 09:00 | 0.1% loss, 35 ms, 4 ms jitter | 0.3% loss, 70 ms, 12 ms jitter | biz-internet (both meet the SLA; policy prefers it) |
| 09:20 | 3% loss, 40 ms, 25 ms jitter | 0.3% loss, 72 ms, 11 ms jitter | **LTE** (biz-internet breaks the loss limit) |
| 09:50 | 0.1% loss, 36 ms, 5 ms jitter | 0.4% loss, 71 ms, 13 ms jitter | biz-internet again |

Meanwhile email (no strict SLA) can stay on biz-internet the whole time. Note the time scale. AAR acts on **averages over polling windows** (several minutes by default), so it moves traffic away from a path that is *degrading*. A path that dies outright is caught much faster by BFD (about 7 seconds), and traffic simply fails over to the remaining tunnels.

**Segmentation:** VPNs in SD-WAN are VRFs. **VPN 0** is the transport (underlay) VPN facing the WAN; **VPN 512** is out-of-band management; **service VPNs** (e.g. 1–511) carry user traffic. The VPN ID travels in the data packets, so segments stay separate end to end.

**What if the Controllers are unreachable?** The data plane keeps forwarding. OMP **graceful restart** lets edges keep using their last-known routes and keys (by default for up to 12 hours), so a controller outage isn't a site outage. New changes simply can't be made until the controllers come back.

### Policy: Centralized vs Localized

SD-WAN policy comes in two families, defined in SD-WAN Manager:

| Policy type | Family | Delivered to | Acts on | Example |
|-------------|--------|--------------|---------|---------|
| **Control policy** | Centralized | The **Controllers** | OMP routes and TLOCs (the topology) | Build hub-and-spoke instead of full mesh; prefer a data-center exit |
| **Data policy** | Centralized | Controllers, then to edges via OMP | Packets at the edges | Direct internet access for guest traffic; send a subnet through a firewall (service chaining) |
| **App-aware routing policy** | Centralized | Controllers, then to edges via OMP | Applications vs SLA classes | Voice must use a path with < 150 ms latency |
| **Localized policy** | Localized | **Directly to one device** by the Manager (NETCONF) | That device's interfaces and routing protocols | QoS shaping, ACLs, route filtering on the LAN-side OSPF |

**Why the split?** Centralized policy expresses *network-wide intent* ("branches talk only through hubs"), so it belongs on the Controller that sees every route. Localized policy is about *one box's interfaces* (queues, ACLs), so it's pushed straight to that box. A classic exam question: "Which policy changes the overlay topology?" Centralized **control** policy, because it manipulates OMP routes and TLOCs on the Controller.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 14.4**

**Q1.** How are data-plane IPsec keys distributed between WAN Edges in Catalyst SD-WAN, and why?

- **A.** Each edge sends its keys to the Controller over OMP, and the Controller reflects them to the edges that need them, so key exchange scales linearly instead of needing pairwise IKE between every pair of sites.
- **B.** Every pair of edges runs IKEv2, so each tunnel has its own negotiation.
- **C.** The Manager pushes the same pre-shared key to every edge over NETCONF.
- **D.** The Validator generates all keys during onboarding and never changes them.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Pairwise IKE between 1,000 sites would mean about 500,000 negotiations; one channel per edge to the Controller avoids that. **Why not the others:** B is the scaling problem SD-WAN avoids. C is wrong because keys come from the edges through the Controller, and a shared key would be weak. D is wrong because the Validator only handles onboarding.
</details>

**Q2.** With default BFD settings, how long does a WAN Edge take to declare an SD-WAN tunnel down after the path dies?

- **A.** About 150 ms
- **B.** About 1 second
- **C.** About 7 seconds
- **D.** About 12 hours

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** The defaults are a 1-second hello and a multiplier of 7. **Why not the others:** A is a typical tuned campus BFD value (50 ms × 3), not the SD-WAN default. B is the hello interval, not the detection time. D is the default OMP graceful-restart period, which applies when the *controllers* are lost.
</details>

**Q3.** Refer to the exhibit. The voice SLA class is loss < 1%, latency < 150 ms, jitter < 30 ms, and policy prefers biz-internet when both paths qualify. Which path does voice use at 09:20?

```
Window   biz-internet                     LTE
09:00    0.1% loss, 35 ms, 4 ms jitter    0.3% loss, 70 ms, 12 ms jitter
09:20    3% loss, 40 ms, 25 ms jitter     0.3% loss, 72 ms, 11 ms jitter
```

- **A.** biz-internet, because its latency is lower
- **B.** biz-internet, because its jitter is still under 30 ms
- **C.** Both paths equally, because one path meets the SLA
- **D.** LTE, because biz-internet now breaks the loss limit

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** A path must meet *every* SLA value. At 09:20 biz-internet has 3% loss, above the 1% limit, so Application-Aware Routing moves voice to LTE, which still meets all three. **Why not the others:** A and B judge one metric and ignore the loss. C is wrong because only one path qualifies.
</details>

**Q4.** An engineer wants branches to talk only through the hubs instead of building a full mesh of tunnels. Which kind of SD-WAN policy changes the overlay topology like this?

- **A.** Localized policy pushed to each WAN Edge
- **B.** Centralized control policy, applied on the Controllers to OMP routes and TLOCs
- **C.** Application-aware routing policy
- **D.** A data policy for direct internet access

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** Topology is decided by which OMP routes and TLOCs each edge receives, and that is what centralized control policy manipulates. **Why not the others:** A covers one device's interfaces (QoS, ACLs), not the network-wide topology. C picks between existing paths per application. D acts on packets at the edge, not on the topology.
</details>

## 14.5 SD-WAN Benefits and Limitations

| Benefits | Limitations |
|----------|-------------|
| **Transport independence** — MPLS, broadband and LTE are all usable, all encrypted | **Controller dependency** — the overlay needs Controllers and Validators for onboarding and changes; they must be designed for HA |
| **Application-aware path selection** based on measured SLAs | **Overhead** — IPsec + extra headers reduce usable MTU; BFD probes add a little traffic on every tunnel |
| **Centralized policy** — one place to define routing, QoS, security | **Complexity and new skills** — OMP, TLOCs, colors, templates are a new model to learn and troubleshoot |
| **Zero-touch provisioning** — ship a router, plug it in | **Licensing and cost** — subscription licences; savings depend on replacing MPLS |
| **Direct cloud / internet access** from branches (Cloud OnRamp for SaaS/IaaS) | **Internet transports have no SLA** — SD-WAN steers around problems; it can't create bandwidth that isn't there |
| **Built-in segmentation** (VPNs) and encryption | **Full-mesh scale** — tunnel counts grow as roughly n²; large designs need regional/hub topologies |

**📝 Exam-style questions — 14.5**

**Q1.** Which two are limitations of Catalyst SD-WAN? (Choose two.)

- **A.** Onboarding and changes depend on the Controllers and Validators, so they must be designed for high availability.
- **B.** Traffic can't be encrypted over broadband transports.
- **C.** Only one transport can carry traffic at a time.
- **D.** It can steer around a poor internet path, but it can't create bandwidth or an SLA the transport doesn't have.
- **E.** Every branch must still be configured by hand.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A, D.** Controller dependency and the lack of an SLA on internet transports are real limits. **Why not the others:** B is false; every tunnel is IPsec. C is false; all transports are used, and AAR picks per application. E is false; zero-touch provisioning and central templates are core benefits.
</details>

**Q2.** All SD-WAN Controllers become unreachable for two hours. What happens to existing traffic between branches?

- **A.** All tunnels go down immediately, because OMP sessions are lost.
- **B.** Traffic falls back to unencrypted forwarding over the internet.
- **C.** Edges keep forwarding with their last-known routes and keys thanks to OMP graceful restart (up to 12 hours by default), but no changes can be made.
- **D.** The Validators take over the Controllers' role automatically.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** A controller outage isn't a site outage; the data plane keeps working. **Why not the others:** A is what graceful restart prevents. B is false; nothing falls back to clear text. D is wrong because the Validator holds no routes and can't replace the Controllers.
</details>
