## 14.6 SD-Access — The Campus Fabric

**The problem it solves:** in a traditional campus, *who you are* is tied to *where you plugged in*. Your VLAN and subnet depend on the switch port, so your IP address changes as you move, and security rules written as IP ACLs must be updated on many switches whenever anything changes.

Traditional campus networks segment with VLANs and ACLs: every new group means new VLANs, new subnets, new ACL lines on many switches, and policy tied to IP addresses that change as users move. **SD-Access** replaces this with a **fabric** in which:

- **Identity drives policy.** A user or device authenticates (802.1X/MAB via **ISE**) and is placed in a **virtual network** and a **group** automatically, wherever it plugs in.
- **The same subnet can exist on every access switch**, so users keep their IP addresses while roaming.
- **Everything is automated** by **Catalyst Center** (Chapter 16).

### The Planes of the Fabric

| Plane | Technology | Role |
|-------|------------|------|
| **Underlay** | Routed IP, normally **IS-IS** (built by Catalyst Center LAN automation; OSPF possible for manual underlays) | Connects all fabric nodes' loopbacks. No VLANs and no STP between switches |
| **Overlay — control plane** | **LISP** (13.3) | Tracks which endpoint (EID) sits behind which edge switch (RLOC) |
| **Overlay — data plane** | **VXLAN-GPO** (13.4) | Carries endpoint traffic between fabric nodes, including the VN and the SGT |
| **Policy plane** | **Cisco TrustSec** — **SGTs** and SGACLs, from **ISE** | Decides who may talk to whom, by group |
| **Management plane** | **Catalyst Center** | Design, automation, assurance |

**📝 Exam-style questions — 14.6**

**Q1.** Which problem of the traditional campus does SD-Access address most directly?

- **A.** Switches can't run IS-IS.
- **B.** A user's VLAN, subnet and security policy depend on the port they plug into, so policy written as IP ACLs breaks when users move.
- **C.** Wireless and wired users can't share a building.
- **D.** Campus links can't run faster than 1 Gbps.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** SD-Access puts users in a virtual network and a group based on identity (802.1X/MAB through ISE), wherever they connect. **Why not the others:** A is false, and IS-IS is the fabric's own underlay. C and D aren't problems the fabric was built to solve.
</details>

**Q2.** Which component provides the SD-Access policy plane?

- **A.** Cisco TrustSec: SGTs and SGACLs, defined in ISE
- **B.** LISP Map-Registers
- **C.** VXLAN VNIs
- **D.** IS-IS metrics

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** The policy plane decides who may talk to whom, by group. **Why not the others:** B is the control plane (where endpoints are). C is part of the data plane, and a VNI identifies a virtual network, not a permission. D is the underlay.
</details>

**Q3.** Which two statements describe the SD-Access underlay? (Choose two.)

- **A.** It carries every user VLAN as an 802.1Q trunk between switches.
- **B.** It runs spanning tree between all fabric nodes.
- **C.** It is a routed IP network, normally IS-IS built by Catalyst Center LAN automation.
- **D.** It must know every endpoint's IP address.
- **E.** It only needs to connect the fabric nodes' loopbacks; there are no VLANs and no STP between switches.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C, E.** The underlay is simple routing between loopbacks; everything endpoint-related lives in the overlay. **Why not the others:** A and B describe a traditional Layer 2 campus. D is wrong because endpoint locations are held by the LISP control plane node, not the underlay.
</details>

## 14.7 SD-Access Fabric Roles

![SD-Access fabric roles and the fusion router](images/c14_sda_roles.png)

| Role | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| **Control plane node** | The **LISP Map Server/Map Resolver**. Holds the *host tracking database*: every endpoint's identity and which edge it's behind. Often co-located with the border |
| **Edge node** | The access switch endpoints connect to. A LISP **xTR** and VXLAN VTEP. Authenticates endpoints, registers them with the control plane node, and provides the **anycast gateway**: the same gateway IP and MAC for a subnet on every edge |
| **Border node** | Connects the fabric to everything outside it: the data center, WAN, internet or a traditional network. Advertises external prefixes into the fabric and fabric prefixes out. Types: **internal** (known internal networks), **external** (default exit, e.g. to the internet), and **anywhere/internal + external** |
| **Intermediate node** | Any underlay switch between edges and borders. Just routes IP. It **knows nothing about the overlay** — it only sees VXLAN packets between loopbacks |
| **Fabric WLC** | Wireless controller integrated with the fabric. It handles the **control plane** for wireless clients (registering them with the control plane node), while AP **data** traffic is VXLAN-encapsulated straight to the edge switch. Wireless and wired then share the same policy model |
| **Extended node** | A small Layer 2 switch (e.g. Catalyst IE or compact switches) hanging off an edge, extending the fabric to places like factory floors |

**Story Time 📖 (anycast gateway):** imagine a company where every floor of every building has a reception desk with the *same* phone extension, 1000. Wherever you sit, dialling 1000 reaches the desk on your floor. You never need to learn a new number when you move desks. The anycast gateway is that: the same gateway IP and MAC (say `10.10.5.1`) on every edge switch, answered locally.

**How a packet crosses the fabric, step by step.** A laptop plugs into Edge 1 (RLOC loopback `192.168.255.1`) and sends to a printer on Edge 2 (RLOC `192.168.255.2`):

1. **Authenticate.** The laptop does 802.1X. ISE checks the user and returns: VN *Corporate*, SGT **10** (*Employees*). Edge 1 puts the port in the matching VLAN/VN.
2. **Get an address.** The laptop gets `10.10.5.25/24` by DHCP. Its default gateway is the anycast gateway `10.10.5.1`, which Edge 1 itself answers.
3. **Register.** Edge 1 sends a LISP Map-Register to the control plane node: "`10.10.5.25/32` (in the Corporate VN's instance ID) is behind `192.168.255.1`".
4. **Look up.** The laptop sends a packet to the printer at `10.10.7.40`. Edge 1 doesn't have it in its map-cache, so it asks the control plane node, which answers: "behind `192.168.255.2`". The printer authenticated on Edge 2 earlier and was assigned SGT **20** (*Printers*). Edge 2 knows that tag; Edge 1 doesn't need to.
5. **Encapsulate.** Edge 1 wraps the packet in VXLAN-GPO: the VNI for Corporate, **source SGT 10**, outer IP `192.168.255.1 → 192.168.255.2`.
6. **Carry.** Intermediate nodes route on the outer header using IS-IS routes to the loopbacks. They know nothing about the laptop or the printer.
7. **Enforce.** Edge 2 decapsulates, reads SGT 10, sees the destination is SGT 20, and checks the SGACL for *Employees → Printers* that it downloaded from ISE. Permit, so the printer receives the packet. Had the source been SGT 30 (*Guests*) with a deny rule, Edge 2 would drop it right there.

Nowhere in those steps did anyone write an ACL with an IP address in it.

**Why the anycast gateway?** Because in a traditional campus, a user's gateway lives on one distribution switch (with HSRP, Chapter 9). Roam to a different building and the subnet, and possibly the IP address, changes. In SD-Access, **every edge node owns the same gateway** for every subnet, so wherever an endpoint lands, its gateway is one hop away and its address stays valid. LISP tells the fabric where that endpoint now lives. *Mobility without stretching VLANs.*

### More Fabric Building Blocks

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Fabric in a box (FiaB)** | Border, control plane and edge roles all on **one switch** (or stack). For a small site that still wants the fabric's policy model |
| **INFRA_VN** | The VN that carries **fabric APs and extended nodes**. It maps to the **global routing table**, not a VRF, because APs need to reach the WLC and the underlay |
| **DEFAULT_VN** | A VN created by default for user endpoints when you don't need macro segmentation |
| **Extended node** | Layer 2 switch connected to an edge node. Ports are placed in VLANs that map to fabric VNs, but it **can't enforce SGACLs**; the edge node enforces for it |
| **Policy extended node** | A more capable extended node (selected Catalyst IE/compact models) that **can carry SGTs inline and enforce SGACLs** itself |

**Fabric APs.** Access points connect to an **edge node** and run in **local mode**. They sit in the **INFRA_VN**, so they reach the WLC in the global table. Control traffic (CAPWAP) goes to the fabric WLC as normal, but **client data does not**: the AP encapsulates each client's frames in **VXLAN straight to its edge switch**, which treats the wireless client like a wired one (same VN, same SGT enforcement, same anycast gateway). *Wireless becomes just another access port of the fabric.*

### Macro vs Micro Segmentation

| Level | Mechanism | Separates | Example |
|-------|-----------|-----------|---------|
| **Macro** | **Virtual Network (VN) = a VRF** | Whole routing domains; no communication between VNs unless deliberately routed outside the fabric | Corporate VN, Guest VN, IoT VN |
| **Micro** | **Scalable Group Tag (SGT)** within a VN | Groups inside the same VN, enforced by SGACLs | In the Corporate VN, *Contractors* can't reach *Finance-Servers* |

**Why two levels?** VRFs are strong walls but blunt. Every extra VN needs its own routing tables, and crossing between them requires a fusion device. SGTs are lightweight and plentiful, so you can write fine-grained "group A to group B" rules without new subnets or IP-based ACLs. *Use VNs for "these must never meet", and SGTs for "these share a network but have different permissions".*

**Why tag-based policy beats IP ACLs:** an IP ACL says "10.1.5.0/24 cannot reach 10.9.0.0/16". When users move, change subnet, or DHCP hands out new addresses, the rule is wrong. An SGT policy says "*Contractors* cannot reach *Finance-Servers*". The tag follows the authenticated identity, so the rule stays correct wherever the user connects. The ingress edge stamps the SGT into the VXLAN-GPO header, and the egress edge enforces the SGACL.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 14.7**

**Q1.** Which SD-Access node holds the host tracking database that maps every endpoint to the edge node it sits behind?

- **A.** Border node
- **B.** Intermediate node
- **C.** Catalyst Center
- **D.** Control plane node

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** The control plane node is the LISP Map Server/Map Resolver. **Why not the others:** A connects the fabric to outside networks (though the roles are often on the same box). B only routes the underlay and knows nothing about the overlay. C is the controller in the management plane, not the control plane node. That distinction is a classic exam trap.
</details>

**Q2.** A laptop with SGT 10 on Edge 1 sends to a printer with SGT 20 on Edge 2. Where is the SGACL for SGT 10 → SGT 20 enforced?

- **A.** On Edge 1, before the packet is encapsulated
- **B.** On every intermediate node along the path
- **C.** On Edge 2, after it decapsulates the packet and reads the source SGT from the VXLAN-GPO header
- **D.** On the control plane node, when Edge 1 queries it

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** The ingress edge stamps the source SGT into the header; the egress edge knows the destination's SGT (the printer authenticated there) and applies the policy it downloaded from ISE. **Why not the others:** A is wrong because Edge 1 doesn't need to know the printer's tag. B is wrong because intermediate nodes only route on the outer header. D is wrong because the control plane node answers location queries; it doesn't enforce policy.
</details>

**Q3.** How does a wireless client's data reach the network in an SD-Access fabric?

- **A.** The fabric AP encapsulates it in VXLAN straight to its edge switch, which treats the client like a wired one.
- **B.** It is tunneled in CAPWAP to the fabric WLC, which forwards it into the fabric.
- **C.** It is bridged onto a traditional VLAN trunked to the distribution layer.
- **D.** It goes to the control plane node, which forwards it to the destination edge.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** The WLC handles the control plane for wireless clients, but client data goes straight to the edge, so wired and wireless share the same VN, SGT enforcement and anycast gateway. **Why not the others:** B is the traditional centralized wireless model; in the fabric only CAPWAP *control* goes to the WLC. C describes a non-fabric campus. D is wrong because the control plane node never forwards user data.
</details>

**Q4.** In the Corporate virtual network, contractors must not reach the finance servers, but both groups must keep their current subnets. Which mechanism fits?

- **A.** Create a separate VN (VRF) for contractors.
- **B.** Assign scalable group tags and an SGACL between the two groups (micro-segmentation).
- **C.** Write IP ACLs on every edge node.
- **D.** Put the two groups in different LISP instance IDs inside the same VN.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** SGTs separate groups inside one VN, and the rule follows the user's identity rather than an IP address. **Why not the others:** A works but is the heavy macro option; VNs are for groups that must never meet, and they need a fusion device to cross. C ties policy to IP addresses that change. D is wrong because one VN has one instance ID.
</details>

## 14.8 Traditional Campus Interoperating With SD-Access

Very few organisations rip out the whole campus at once. The blueprint asks how the fabric connects to what's already there.

**1. Layer 3 handoff at the border, through a fusion router.** The border node hands each VN out as a separate VRF, usually over **802.1Q subinterfaces with eBGP per VRF (VRF-Lite)**, to an external **fusion router** (or firewall).

**Worked example — a fabric user gets DHCP through the fusion router.** The DHCP server `10.99.0.10` sits in the shared-services network, outside the fabric, in the global routing table:

1. A laptop in the *Corporate* VN broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER. Edge 1 (acting as DHCP relay) unicasts it towards `10.99.0.10` inside the Corporate VRF.
2. The border's Corporate VRF has a route to `10.99.0.0/24` only because the fusion router leaked that prefix into its own Corporate VRF and advertised it to the border over eBGP. So the border sends the packet out its Corporate subinterface (VLAN 3001) to the fusion router.
3. The fusion router has leaked `10.99.0.0/24` into its Corporate VRF and `10.10.5.0/24` into the global table, so it routes the request across to the DHCP server and the reply back again.
4. A laptop in the *Guest* VN gets DHCP through the same fusion router, but its VRF has no leaked route to the Corporate subnets, so Guests still can't reach Corporate users.

**Why is it called a "fusion" router?** Because the VNs are deliberately isolated, yet they all need **shared services** — DHCP, DNS, ISE, Catalyst Center, the internet. The fusion device **leaks routes between VRFs** (or a firewall routes between them under security policy), *fusing* the separate VNs with the shared-services and global routing tables at one controlled point. *Isolation inside the fabric, controlled sharing at the edge of it.*

**2. Layer 2 handoff (Layer 2 border).** A border node can bridge a fabric subnet to a **traditional VLAN** outside the fabric. Endpoints in the old network and in the fabric then share one subnet with one gateway (in the fabric). This is the migration tool: move users switch by switch, without readdressing hosts that are still on the old network.

**3. Routed connection to the existing core.** The traditional distribution/core simply becomes "outside" the fabric. Fabric prefixes are advertised to it from the border via BGP or redistributed into the existing IGP, and the legacy network's prefixes are imported into the fabric.

**4. Underlay coexistence.** Existing switches that support the fabric roles can be added; those that don't can act as intermediate nodes (pure IP routing) or stay outside the fabric entirely.

| Interop need | Tool | Typical design |
|--------------|------|----------------|
| Fabric users reach DHCP/DNS/ISE | Fusion router / firewall | Route leaking between VN VRFs and the shared-services VRF |
| Fabric reaches DC, WAN, internet | External border | VRF-Lite + eBGP per VN to fusion / WAN edge |
| Migrate a subnet without readdressing | Layer 2 border handoff | Fabric subnet bridged to legacy VLAN during the cutover |
| Legacy core keeps running | Border advertises fabric prefixes | BGP or IGP redistribution at the border |

### Connecting Fabric Sites: Transits

A large organisation runs several **fabric sites** (a campus, a branch, a data center), and something must join them. That joining network is a **transit**:

| Transit | How sites connect | What survives between sites |
|---------|-------------------|-----------------------------|
| **SD-Access transit** | Native fabric: VXLAN between site borders over an IP network, with **transit control plane nodes** acting as a LISP map server *between* sites | VN **and SGT** stay in the VXLAN header end to end. Single policy domain |
| **IP-based transit** | Borders hand off with **VRF-Lite + BGP** (or across an SD-WAN/MPLS network) | VNs survive as VRFs, but the VXLAN header is removed, so SGTs must be re-carried another way (inline tagging on the links, or SXP) |

**Why does SD-Access transit need its own control plane node?** Because each site's control plane node only knows its own endpoints. The **transit control plane node** aggregates the sites' prefixes, so a border can ask "which site has 10.9.4.0/24?" and tunnel straight there. *It's LISP again, one level up.*

**Exam trap:** the **control plane node** is not "the controller". The controller (management plane) is **Catalyst Center**. The control plane node is a *switch* running LISP MS/MR. Don't mix them up.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 14.8**

**Q1.** Why does an SD-Access deployment usually need a fusion router or firewall?

- **A.** The VNs are isolated VRFs, yet they all need shared services such as DHCP, DNS and ISE; the fusion device leaks routes between those VRFs and the shared-services table at one controlled point.
- **B.** It translates LISP into OMP for SD-WAN.
- **C.** It replaces the border node for internet access.
- **D.** It runs the IS-IS underlay for the fabric.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** It "fuses" the separate VNs with the shared services while keeping the VNs apart from each other. **Why not the others:** B is not its job. C is wrong; the border hands off to the fusion device, it doesn't get replaced by it. D is wrong because the fusion router sits outside the fabric.
</details>

**Q2.** An organization wants to move users into the fabric switch by switch, without readdressing hosts still on the old network. Which interoperability method fits?

- **A.** A routed connection from the border to the legacy core
- **B.** An SD-Access transit between sites
- **C.** A fusion router leaking routes between VRFs
- **D.** A Layer 2 handoff, bridging a fabric subnet to the traditional VLAN

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** Old and new endpoints share one subnet with one gateway in the fabric during the cutover. **Why not the others:** A connects separate subnets, so hosts would have to readdress. B joins fabric sites to each other. C gives access to shared services but doesn't stretch a subnet.
</details>

**Q3.** Two fabric sites are joined with an IP-based transit (VRF-Lite and BGP). What happens to the scalable group tags between sites?

- **A.** They are carried end to end in the VXLAN header, just as with an SD-Access transit.
- **B.** They are converted into BGP communities automatically.
- **C.** They are lost when the VXLAN header is removed at the border, so they must be carried another way, such as inline tagging or SXP.
- **D.** They are copied into the 802.1Q tag.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** VNs survive as VRFs, but the tag lived in the VXLAN header. **Why not the others:** A describes an SD-Access transit, which keeps VN and SGT in VXLAN. B and D are invented mechanisms.
</details>

## 14.9 SD-WAN and SD-Access Side by Side

**Why compare them:** exam questions love swapping one architecture's terms into the other ("Which protocol does the SD-WAN Controller use?" with LISP as a distractor). Seeing them side by side shows they solve the same problem in two places.

| Topic | Catalyst SD-WAN | SD-Access |
|-------|---------------------|---------------|
| Domain | WAN — connecting sites | Campus / branch LAN |
| Management | SD-WAN Manager | Catalyst Center |
| Control plane | OMP via SD-WAN Controllers | LISP via control plane nodes |
| Data plane | IPsec tunnels between WAN Edges | VXLAN-GPO between fabric nodes |
| Segmentation | VPNs (VRFs) | VNs (VRFs) + SGTs |
| Path / location abstraction | TLOC (System IP + color + encap) | RLOC (fabric node loopback) |
| Onboarding | Validator + PnP, certificates | Catalyst Center PnP / LAN automation |
| Policy | Centralized control and data policy, AAR | Group-based access control via ISE |

*The pattern repeats:* a central controller holds intent, a control protocol maps identities to locations, tunnels carry the data across a simple underlay, and VRFs plus tags keep the segments apart. Learn the pattern once and both architectures make sense.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 14.9**

**Q1.** Which protocol does the SD-WAN Controller use to distribute routes to the WAN Edges?

- **A.** LISP
- **B.** OMP
- **C.** BGP EVPN
- **D.** IS-IS

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** OMP runs between each edge and the Controllers. **Why not the others:** A is SD-Access's control plane. C is the data-center VXLAN control plane. D is the SD-Access underlay. Swapping one architecture's terms into the other is a favourite distractor.
</details>

**Q2.** In SD-Access, what plays the same role as the SD-WAN TLOC, identifying *where* traffic should be sent?

- **A.** The SGT
- **B.** The VNI
- **C.** The instance ID
- **D.** The RLOC (the fabric node's loopback)

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** Both are location identifiers that keep the endpoint's prefix separate from where it is attached. **Why not the others:** A is a group identity for policy. B and C identify the virtual network (segment), not the location.
</details>

<a name="chapter-15"></a>
# Chapter 15: Network Assurance Tools: Debugs, SNMP, Syslog, Flexible NetFlow, SPAN & IP SLA

> **Blueprint:** ENCOR 4.1 — Diagnose network problems using tools such as debugs, conditional debugs, traceroute, ping, SNMP, and syslog; ENCOR 4.2 — Configure and verify Flexible NetFlow; ENCOR 4.3 — Configure SPAN/RSPAN/ERSPAN; ENCOR 4.4 — Configure and verify IP SLA

**Network assurance** means being able to *prove* the network is doing what you intended, and to find out quickly when it isn't. The CCNA guide gave you ping, traceroute, syslog and SNMP as concepts (21.6, 17.5, 17.6). ENCOR expects you to use each one as a working diagnostic tool and to add four more: conditional debugs, Flexible NetFlow, traffic mirroring and IP SLA.

Each tool answers a different question:

| Question | Tool |
|----------|------|
| Can I reach it, and by which path? | **ping, traceroute** (extended) |
| What is the device doing internally, packet by packet? | **debug** — ideally *conditional* |
| What has the device been telling me happened? | **syslog** |
| How are its counters and health trending? | **SNMP** |
| Who is talking to whom, how much, using what? | **Flexible NetFlow** |
| What exactly is in the packets? | **SPAN / RSPAN / ERSPAN** + a packet analyzer |
| Is the path performing well right now, continuously? | **IP SLA** |

Chapter 32 returns to SNMP, logging, IP SLA and NetFlow at ENARSI **troubleshooting** depth. This chapter gets them configured and working.

---

## 15.1 Ping and Traceroute — Extended Versions

**The problem these solve:** someone says "I can't reach the server". Before you look at anything else, you need two facts: *does traffic get there and back?* and *if not, where does it stop?* Ping answers the first and traceroute answers the second. Both use **ICMP** (Internet Control Message Protocol), the small "status message" protocol that rides inside IP.

A basic `ping` sources from the outgoing interface with 5 × 100-byte packets. That is a very blunt question ("does *something* get there?"). The **extended** options let you ask much more precise questions:

```
R1# ping 10.2.2.2 source Loopback0 repeat 10 size 1500 df-bit
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 10, 1500-byte ICMP Echos to 10.2.2.2, timeout is 2 seconds:
Packet sent with a source address of 1.1.1.1
Packet sent with the DF bit set
MMMMMMMMMM
Success rate is 0 percent (0/10)
```

| Option | Question it answers |
|--------|---------------------|
| `source Loopback0` | Does the **far end have a route back** to this network? (A default ping sources from the exit interface, which may be reachable when your LANs aren't) |
| `repeat 1000` | Is there **intermittent** loss? Five packets can't show 1% loss |
| `size 1500 df-bit` | What MTU does the path support? `M` = "fragmentation needed but DF set" |
| `vrf NAME` | Test inside a VRF (12.6) |

**Ping result codes:** `!` reply · `.` timeout · `U` destination unreachable · `M` could not fragment · `Q` source quench · `&` TTL exceeded · `?` unknown packet type.

**Why does sourcing from a loopback catch so many problems?** Because routing is a two-way problem. A plain ping from R1 to R2 uses the link's own subnet, which R2 knows as directly connected, so it always works. Real user traffic comes from R1's LANs. If R2 has no route back to *those*, users fail while your basic ping succeeds. *Always test the way the traffic actually flows.*

**Worked example — finding the path MTU.** Users at a branch can open small web pages but large downloads stall. The branch reaches HQ over a GRE tunnel. **MTU** (Maximum Transmission Unit) is the largest packet a link can carry without splitting it, and the **DF** (Don't Fragment) bit tells routers "drop this rather than split it". So pinging with DF set and a growing size finds the biggest packet the whole path allows:

```
R1# ping 10.2.2.2 source Loopback0 size 1500 df-bit
MMMMM                                    ! 1500 is too big somewhere on the path
R1# ping 10.2.2.2 source Loopback0 size 1476 df-bit
!!!!!                                    ! 1476 fits
R1# ping 10.2.2.2 source Loopback0 size 1477 df-bit
MMMMM                                    ! 1477 does not: the path MTU is 1476
```

What the router did, and why: a router on the path had a 1476-byte limit (a 1500-byte link minus the 24 bytes of GRE plus outer IP header, Chapter 12). It could not split a DF packet, so it dropped it and sent back ICMP "fragmentation needed", which ping shows as `M`. The fix is on the tunnel (`ip tcp adjust-mss 1436`, so TCP never builds packets bigger than 1476 bytes, with `ip mtu 1476` set to match), not on the users' PCs. *One sweep of `size` with `df-bit` turns "large downloads stall" into a number.*

**Traceroute** (IOS sends UDP probes with increasing TTL) shows the path hop by hop, with these markers: `*` no reply within the timeout · `!H` host unreachable · `!N` network unreachable · `!P` protocol unreachable · `!A` administratively prohibited (an ACL). A trace that stops at one hop while the next hop's own pings work usually points at an ACL, or at a device configured not to send ICMP unreachables.

**How does traceroute know it has arrived?** Each intermediate router whose TTL expires answers with ICMP **time exceeded**. The destination itself isn't expiring anything; it receives a UDP probe aimed at a high port nobody listens on (33434 and up) and answers with ICMP **port unreachable**. That different reply is the signal that the trace is complete. If the destination filters UDP or doesn't send unreachables, the last line is `* * *` repeated to the 30-hop maximum, even though the host is reachable.

**Story Time 📖:** Every IP packet carries a **TTL** (Time To Live), a counter that each router lowers by 1. When it hits 0 the router throws the packet away and sends a note back saying "your packet died here". Traceroute abuses that on purpose. It's like sending a letter with the instruction "the 1st post office to touch this, send me a postcard", then another saying "the 2nd post office...", and so on. The postcards arrive from each post office in turn, and together they draw you the route.

**How it works, step by step** (R1 tracing to 10.3.3.3, three routers away):

1. R1 sends three UDP probes with **TTL 1**. R2 lowers TTL to 0, drops them, and replies with ICMP time exceeded from its own address. R1 prints line 1: R2's address and three round-trip times.
2. R1 sends three probes with **TTL 2**. R2 forwards them (TTL now 1), R3 drops them and replies. Line 2: R3.
3. TTL 3 reaches 10.3.3.3 itself. Nothing expires; the host finds no application on port 33434+ and replies **port unreachable**. Line 3, and the trace stops.

```
R1# traceroute 10.3.3.3 source Loopback0
  1 10.1.12.2 1 msec 1 msec 1 msec       ! R2 answered "time exceeded"
  2 10.1.23.3 2 msec 1 msec 2 msec       ! R3 answered "time exceeded"
  3 10.3.3.3 3 msec *  2 msec            ! destination answered "port unreachable"
```

The single `*` in line 3 is normal: many devices rate-limit ICMP replies, so one probe of three goes unanswered. A whole line of `* * *` followed by more hops that *do* answer usually means one router simply doesn't send time-exceeded messages; the path still works.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 15.1**

**Q1.** R1 and R2 are directly connected, and R2 has no ACLs. From R1, `ping 10.2.2.2` succeeds, but `ping 10.2.2.2 source Loopback0` (Loopback0 is 1.1.1.1 and is up) returns `.....`. What is the most likely cause?

- **A.** The R1–R2 link has an MTU mismatch
- **B.** R2 has no route back to 1.1.1.1
- **C.** Loopback0 cannot be used as a ping source until `ip unnumbered` is configured
- **D.** R1 has no route to 10.2.2.2

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** A plain ping leaves from the exit interface, whose subnet R2 knows as directly connected, so the reply always finds its way home. Sourcing from Loopback0 makes R2 reply to 1.1.1.1, and if R2 has no route to that address the replies are dropped, which ping shows as timeouts. **Why not the others:** A, both pings cross the same link with the same 100-byte size, so an MTU problem would hit both. C, any up interface with an IP address can be a ping source; no extra command is needed. D, if R1 had no route to 10.2.2.2, the plain ping would fail too.
</details>

**Q2.** Refer to the exhibit. What do the results show?

```
R1# ping 10.2.2.2 source Loopback0 size 1476 df-bit
!!!!!
R1# ping 10.2.2.2 source Loopback0 size 1477 df-bit
MMMMM
```

- **A.** 1477-byte packets are timing out because of congestion
- **B.** The path MTU is 1477 bytes, and the DF packets are being fragmented
- **C.** The path MTU is 1476 bytes; a router could not forward the larger DF packet and returned "fragmentation needed"
- **D.** R2 has an ACL that blocks ICMP packets larger than 1476 bytes

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** `M` means "could not fragment": a router on the path needed to split the packet, the DF bit forbade it, so it dropped the packet and sent back ICMP fragmentation-needed. The largest size that works, 1476, is the path MTU (typical of a GRE tunnel over a 1500-byte link). **Why not the others:** A, a timeout shows as `.`, not `M`. B, DF packets are never fragmented, and the 1477-byte test failed. D, an ACL drop shows as `.` or `U`; `M` specifically reports a fragmentation problem.
</details>

**Q3.** How does IOS traceroute know it has reached the destination?

- **A.** The destination replies with ICMP time exceeded
- **B.** The destination replies with an ICMP echo reply
- **C.** The TTL reaches the 30-hop maximum
- **D.** The destination replies with ICMP port unreachable to the UDP probe

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** IOS sends UDP probes to high ports (33434 and up) that nothing listens on. Routers along the way answer with time exceeded as the TTL runs out, but the destination doesn't expire the probe; it finds no application on that port and answers port unreachable, which ends the trace. **Why not the others:** A, time exceeded comes from the routers in between, not from the destination. B, IOS traceroute doesn't send echo requests, so it gets no echo reply. C, 30 hops is the limit a trace reaches when it never gets a port unreachable back, for example because the destination filters UDP.
</details>

## 15.2 Debugs — and Doing Them Safely

**The problem debugs solve:** `show` commands give you the *result* (the neighbor isn't there). They don't tell you *why*. To see why, you need to watch the protocol's own decisions as they happen: "I received a hello, I rejected it, here's the reason."

`debug` makes IOS print events from a process as they happen: `debug ip ospf adj`, `debug ip bgp updates`, `debug crypto ikev2`. It is the most detailed tool you have, and the most dangerous.

**Story Time 📖:** A debug is like asking a busy shop cashier to also say out loud, and write down, every single thing they do. With three customers that's helpful. With three hundred, the cashier spends all their time talking and writing, and the queue stops moving. The router's CPU is that cashier.

**Why are debugs dangerous?** Debug output is generated by the **CPU**. A debug that fires per packet (`debug ip packet` on a busy router) can drive the CPU to 100%, and the router may then drop routing protocol hellos, lose neighbors and lock you out of the console. *A debug can cause a bigger outage than the one you were investigating.*

**Safe debugging habits:**

```
R1(config)# no logging console                ! don't send debug output to the slow console
R1(config)# logging buffered 1000000 debugging ! to RAM instead - read: show logging
R1(config)# service timestamps debug datetime msec   ! so you can correlate events
R1# terminal monitor                          ! see log output on an SSH/VTY session
R1# undebug all                               ! (or: no debug all) - the stop button
```

**Why does `terminal monitor` matter?** Log and debug messages go to the console by default. If you're connected over SSH, you see **nothing** until you enter `terminal monitor`. It applies only to your current session, so you must repeat it on each login. *"I turned on debug and nothing happened" is usually a missing `terminal monitor`.*

### Conditional Debugs — Narrowing the Firehose

A **debug condition** limits debug output to traffic that matches a filter, such as an interface, an IP address or a peer:

```
R1# debug condition interface GigabitEthernet0/1   ! only events on this interface
R1# debug condition ip 10.1.1.50                    ! only events involving this host
R1# debug ip ospf adj
R1# show debug condition                          ! lists the active conditions
R1# undebug all
R1# no debug condition all                          ! conditions persist - clear them too
```

Many feature debugs also accept their own filters, for example an ACL with `debug ip packet 101 detail`, or a neighbor with `debug ip bgp 10.0.0.2 updates`.

**How a conditional debug works, step by step:**

1. You set one or more conditions (`debug condition interface Gi0/1`). Nothing prints yet; a condition is only a filter.
2. You turn on a debug (`debug ip ospf hello`). The process now generates its event messages.
3. Before each message is printed, IOS checks it against the conditions. Messages about Gi0/1 pass; messages about the other interfaces are thrown away.
4. Only the matching lines reach the log buffer or your session.

Not every debug honours every condition type, so check `show debug condition` and confirm the output really is narrowed before you trust it on a busy box.

**Worked example.** A core router has 40 OSPF neighbors. One of them, on Gi0/1, never forms an adjacency. Debugging OSPF hellos on all 40 would produce a line per hello per neighbor, so you narrow it to the one interface:

```
R1# debug condition interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1# debug ip ospf hello
OSPF-1 HELLO Gi0/1: Rcv hello from 2.2.2.2 area 0 10.1.12.2
OSPF-1 HELLO Gi0/1: Mismatched hello parameters from 10.1.12.2
OSPF-1 HELLO Gi0/1: Dead R 120 C 40, Hello R 30 C 10
R1# undebug all
R1# no debug condition all
```

Reading it: `R` is what was **received** from the neighbor and `C` is what is **configured** here. The neighbor sends hellos every 30 s with a 120 s dead time (the OSPF non-broadcast defaults), and R1 expects 10 and 40. So the neighbor's interface is probably set to a different OSPF network type. The exact prefix on each line varies a little by release, but the `R`/`C` comparison is the part to look for. Three lines of output, one clear answer, and the CPU barely noticed.

**Exam trap:** debug conditions **stay in place** after `undebug all`. If you forget to clear them, the next engineer's debug silently shows only part of the picture.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 15.2**

**Q1.** An engineer must debug an OSPF adjacency problem on a busy core router over SSH. Which two actions reduce the risk to the router? (Choose two.)

- **A.** Run `debug ip packet` without an ACL to capture everything in one pass
- **B.** Enter `terminal monitor` on the console to slow the output down
- **C.** Send output to RAM with `logging buffered` and turn off `logging console`
- **D.** Set `logging console debugging` so the output is not stored in RAM
- **E.** Set `debug condition interface` for the affected interface before enabling the debug

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C, E.** Debug output is generated by the CPU, and the console is the slowest, most expensive place to send it, so buffering to RAM keeps the router responsive. A debug condition throws away messages about other interfaces, so only the lines you need are produced and stored. **Why not the others:** A, a per-packet debug with no filter is exactly what drives a busy router's CPU to 100%. B, `terminal monitor` only makes log output appear on your own VTY session; it doesn't reduce anything, and it's pointless on the console. D, sending debugs to the console is the most dangerous choice of all.
</details>

**Q2.** Refer to the exhibit. What does the output tell you?

```
R1# debug condition interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1# debug ip ospf hello
OSPF-1 HELLO Gi0/1: Mismatched hello parameters from 10.1.12.2
OSPF-1 HELLO Gi0/1: Dead R 120 C 40, Hello R 30 C 10
```

- **A.** The neighbor sends 30 s hellos with a 120 s dead time, the defaults for non-broadcast and point-to-multipoint networks, so its interface probably uses a different OSPF network type
- **B.** R1 sends hellos every 30 s and the neighbor every 10 s
- **C.** The adjacency is failing because of an MTU mismatch
- **D.** The two routers have different authentication keys

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** `R` is what was **received** from the neighbor and `C` is what is **configured** on R1. The neighbor uses 30/120, the OSPF default for non-broadcast and point-to-multipoint networks, while R1 uses the broadcast/point-to-point 10/40, so the timers don't match and no adjacency forms. **Why not the others:** B reverses R and C. C, an MTU mismatch lets hellos through and gets stuck later in EXSTART/EXCHANGE. D, an authentication mismatch produces an authentication error, not a hello-parameter mismatch.
</details>

**Q3.** Yesterday an engineer ran `debug condition interface GigabitEthernet0/1`, investigated, and finished with `undebug all`. Today a colleague runs `debug ip ospf adj` on the same router. OSPF runs on four interfaces in area 0, and an adjacency is flapping on Gi0/2, but the debug only shows events for Gi0/1. Why?

- **A.** OSPF adjacency debugs only cover the first interface in the OSPF process
- **B.** The logging buffer is full and is discarding messages for the other interfaces
- **C.** The debug condition from yesterday is still in place, because `undebug all` does not remove conditions
- **D.** `terminal monitor` shows only messages for the interface the SSH session arrived on

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Debug conditions persist after `undebug all`. Yesterday's condition is still filtering every debug to Gi0/1, so Gi0/2's events are thrown away. Clear it with `no debug condition all`, and check with `show debug condition`. **Why not the others:** A, an OSPF debug covers every OSPF interface unless something filters it. B, a full buffer overwrites old messages; it doesn't pick an interface. D, `terminal monitor` displays all log output on the session, whatever interface you connected through.
</details>

## 15.3 Syslog

**The problem syslog solves:** problems often happen when nobody is watching: an interface flaps at 03:00, a BGP session resets, a fan fails. **Syslog** is how a device writes down what happened, so you can read it later and so a central server can collect it from every device in one place.

**Story Time 📖:** Syslog is a ship's logbook. Every notable event gets a line with the time, who reported it and how serious it was. The copy kept on board (the local buffer) is handy but goes down with the ship (a reload). The copy radioed to shore (the syslog server) survives. And the captain can decide that only serious entries get radioed, to keep the airwaves quiet.

Every IOS log message has a **severity** from 0 to 7. Lower numbers are more severe, and choosing a level includes **that level and everything more severe**.

| Level | Keyword | Example |
|-------|---------|---------|
| 0 | emergencies | System unusable |
| 1 | alerts | Immediate action needed (e.g. temperature) |
| 2 | critical | Critical condition (hardware failure) |
| 3 | errors | Interface errors, failed operations |
| 4 | warnings | Config warnings, approaching limits |
| 5 | notifications | Normal but significant: interface up/down, neighbor changes (`%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN`) |
| 6 | informational | ACL log hits, general info |
| 7 | debugging | Debug output |

*Mnemonic: **E**very **A**wesome **C**isco **E**ngineer **W**ill **N**eed **I**ce-cream **D**aily.*

**Reading a message.** Every IOS log line has the same shape:

```
*Oct 26 14:02:11.318 EST: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface Gi0/1, changed state to down
```

| Part | Here | Meaning |
|------|------|---------|
| Timestamp | `Oct 26 14:02:11.318 EST` | From `service timestamps` (a leading `*` means the clock isn't NTP-synchronized) |
| **FACILITY** | `LINK` | The subsystem that generated it (`LINEPROTO`, `OSPF`, `BGP`, `SYS`…) |
| **SEVERITY** | `3` | 0–7 as in the table above (here, errors) |
| **MNEMONIC** | `UPDOWN` | Short code for the event type |
| Description | `Interface Gi0/1, …` | The human-readable detail |

So `%FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC` tells you, before you read a word of the description, who is talking and how serious it is.

**Where messages go, and each destination's own level:**

| Destination | Command | Default level | Notes |
|-------------|---------|---------------|-------|
| Console | `logging console <level>` | debugging (7) | Slow serial line; heavy logging here can hurt CPU |
| VTY sessions | `logging monitor <level>` | debugging (7) | Only shown in a session that ran `terminal monitor` |
| Local buffer | `logging buffered <size> <level>` | debugging (7) | Read with `show logging`; lost on reload |
| Syslog server | `logging trap <level>` + `logging host` | informational (6) | The only destination that survives a reload |

Each destination filters independently. Sending debugs to the buffer but only warnings to the server is a normal design.

**Worked example — where does each message go?** R1 has this logging setup:

```
logging console warnings          ! console: levels 0-4
logging buffered 64000 informational  ! buffer: levels 0-6
logging trap notifications        ! server: levels 0-5
logging host 10.0.0.50
```

Gi0/1 goes down, and IOS generates two messages:

| Message | Severity | Console (0–4) | Buffer (0–6) | Server (0–5) |
|---------|----------|---------------|--------------|--------------|
| `%LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface Gi0/1, changed state to down` | 3 | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| `%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface Gi0/1, changed state to down` | 5 | No | **Yes** | **Yes** |

How the router decides: for each destination, it compares the message's severity number with that destination's level. If the message number is **less than or equal to** the configured level, it is sent. 3 ≤ 4, so the LINK message reaches the console; 5 > 4, so the LINEPROTO message doesn't. *Remember "lower number = more serious, and a level includes everything more serious than itself".*

```
R1(config)# service timestamps log datetime msec localtime show-timezone
R1(config)# logging buffered 64000 informational  ! local RAM buffer, levels 0-6
R1(config)# logging host 10.0.0.50                ! syslog server, UDP 514
R1(config)# logging trap warnings                 ! send levels 0-4 to the server
R1(config)# logging source-interface Loopback0    ! consistent source IP
R1# show logging                                  ! settings + the local buffer
```

**Why set `logging source-interface`?** The syslog server identifies devices by source IP. Without it, a router's messages come from whichever interface faces the server, which can change after a reroute, so its logs appear under a different "device". A loopback is always the same.

**Why are timestamps essential?** Because troubleshooting is **correlating events across devices**: "BGP dropped on R1 at 14:02:11.318 — what happened on R2 at that moment?" Without accurate time (NTP, Chapter 8) and millisecond timestamps, logs from different devices can't be lined up. *Logs without synchronised timestamps are anecdotes.*

**📝 Exam-style questions — 15.3**

**Q1.** Refer to the exhibit. Interface Gi0/1 goes down and R1 generates `%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN`. Which destinations receive that message?

```
logging console warnings
logging buffered 64000 informational
logging trap notifications
logging host 10.0.0.50
```

- **A.** The console, the local buffer and the syslog server
- **B.** The local buffer and the syslog server only
- **C.** The local buffer only
- **D.** The syslog server only

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** The message is severity 5. Each destination accepts messages whose number is less than or equal to its level: the buffer takes 0–6 (5 passes), the server takes 0–5 (5 passes), and the console takes 0–4 (5 is too high a number, so it is blocked). **Why not the others:** A, the console's `warnings` level (4) excludes severity 5. C, `notifications` on the server includes level 5. D, the buffer's `informational` level (6) includes level 5.
</details>

**Q2.** Why do engineers configure `logging source-interface Loopback0`?

- **A.** It encrypts syslog messages between the router and the server
- **B.** It keeps the router's log messages after a reload
- **C.** It changes the syslog transport from UDP 514 to TCP
- **D.** The server identifies devices by source IP, and a loopback keeps that address the same whichever interface the messages leave through

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** Without it, messages are sourced from whichever interface faces the server, which can change after a reroute, so the same router's logs appear under a different "device". A loopback never goes down and never changes. **Why not the others:** A, syslog sourcing has nothing to do with encryption. B, only the server copy survives a reload, whatever the source address is; the local buffer is lost either way. C, the source interface doesn't change the transport protocol or port.
</details>

**Q3.** A router logs `*Oct 26 14:02:11.318 EST: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface Gi0/1, changed state to down`. What do the leading `*` and the number 3 tell you?

- **A.** The clock isn't NTP-synchronized, and the message is severity 3 (errors)
- **B.** The message is debug output, and severity 3 means warnings
- **C.** The message has been repeated, and severity 3 means notifications
- **D.** The clock is synchronized to NTP, and severity 3 means critical

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** A leading `*` marks a timestamp from a clock that isn't NTP-synchronized, which matters when you try to line up logs from several devices. In `%LINK-3-UPDOWN`, the middle field is the severity, and 3 is errors. **Why not the others:** B, debug output is severity 7, and warnings is 4. C, the `*` doesn't mean repetition, and notifications is 5. D, it's the opposite: the `*` means **not** synchronized, and critical is 2.
</details>

## 15.4 SNMP

**The problem SNMP solves:** you have 500 devices and you want graphs of every interface's traffic, CPU and memory, plus an alert the moment a link drops. Logging into each one to type `show` commands can't do that. **SNMP** (Simple Network Management Protocol) gives a central server a standard way to *ask* every device for numbers, and gives devices a way to *tell* the server when something happens.

SNMP lets a **manager** (the **NMS**, Network Management Station) read and write **MIB** variables on an **agent** (the SNMP software on the device). Agents listen on **UDP 161**; traps and informs go to the manager on **UDP 162**.

**Story Time 📖:** Think of the device as a filing cabinet with thousands of numbered drawers, each holding one value (a counter, a temperature, an interface name). The MIB is the cabinet's index. The manager is a clerk who phones up and says "read me drawer 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10.3" (a **poll**). A **trap** is the cabinet phoning the clerk unprompted: "drawer 'link status' just changed!" A trap is a shout across the room; an **inform** is a shout that waits for "got it" and repeats itself until it hears it.

**MIBs and OIDs.** A **MIB** (Management Information Base) is a structured definition of what can be read or set: interface counters, CPU load, routing table entries. Every individual variable has an **OID** (Object Identifier), a dotted path through a global tree. For example `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10` is `ifInOctets` (under iso.org.dod.internet.mgmt.mib-2.interfaces). Standard MIBs live under `1.3.6.1.2.1` (mib-2); vendor MIBs under `1.3.6.1.4.1` (enterprises; Cisco is `.9`). Appending an index selects one instance: `…10.3` is the input octet counter of interface index 3.

| Operation | Direction | What it does |
|-----------|-----------|--------------|
| **Get** | Manager → agent | Read one OID |
| **GetNext** | Manager → agent | Read the *next* OID in the tree (how tables are walked) |
| **GetBulk** (v2c+) | Manager → agent | Read many next OIDs in one request |
| **Walk** | Manager tool | Repeated GetNext/GetBulk to dump a whole subtree (`snmpwalk`) |
| **Set** | Manager → agent | Write a value (needs RW access) |
| **Trap / Inform** | Agent → manager | Unsolicited notification of an event |

**How a poll works, step by step** (SNMPv2c, community `R3ad0nly`, the config shown below):

1. The NMS at 10.0.0.50 sends a **GetRequest** to R1 on UDP 161, carrying the community string and the OID `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10.3` (ifInOctets for interface index 3).
2. R1's agent looks up the community string, then checks the request's source address against the ACL attached to that community (20). If either check fails, it silently drops the request, so the NMS just sees a timeout.
3. The agent reads the live counter and sends a **GetResponse** back with the value.

**Worked example — turning counters into a graph.** SNMP counters only ever count up. The NMS polls `ifInOctets` on Gi0/0 every 300 seconds:

| Poll time | ifInOctets value |
|-----------|------------------|
| 10:00:00 | 1,000,000,000 |
| 10:05:00 | 1,075,000,000 |

Difference: 75,000,000 bytes in 300 s. × 8 bits = 600,000,000 bits ÷ 300 s = **2,000,000 bit/s, or 2 Mbps** average inbound. That's every traffic graph you've ever seen: two readings, a subtraction, a division. *SNMP gives raw counters; the NMS does the maths.* It's also why a 5-minute poll can't show a 10-second burst: the burst is averaged away. (On fast links, NMSs poll the 64-bit `ifHCInOctets` instead, because a 32-bit counter wraps back to 0 after about 4.3 GB, which a 10 Gbps link fills in under 4 seconds.)

**How a trap works, step by step:** Gi0/1 goes down → the agent builds a `linkDown` notification naming the interface → it sends it once to 10.0.0.50 on UDP 162 → done. If that one UDP packet is lost, the NMS never hears about it, which is why NMSs still poll to catch missed events.

| Version | Security | Notes |
|---------|----------|-------|
| **v1 / v2c** | **Community string**, sent in clear text | v2c added GetBulk and informs. Read-only (RO) or read-write (RW) communities |
| **v3** | **Users and groups**, with authentication and encryption | The only version you should deploy today |

### SNMPv3 Security Levels

**Why v3 exists:** in v1/v2c the community string *is* the password, and it crosses the network in clear text in every packet. Anyone who captures one poll can read the device, and an RW community lets them change it. v3 replaces communities with named **users**, proves each message really came from that user (**auth**, a keyed hash) and can encrypt the contents (**priv**). The level names say which of those you get:

| Level | Authentication | Encryption | Keyword |
|-------|----------------|------------|---------|
| **noAuthNoPriv** | Username only | No | `noauth` |
| **authNoPriv** | HMAC-SHA (MD5 is legacy) | No | `auth` |
| **authPriv** | HMAC-SHA (MD5 is legacy) | **Yes** (AES; DES/3DES are legacy) | `priv` |

### Traps vs Informs

- **Trap** — the agent sends a notification and forgets it. If the UDP packet is lost, the event is lost.
- **Inform** — the manager must **acknowledge** it, and the agent retransmits until it does. Reliable, but uses more memory and traffic.

**How an inform works, step by step:** the link goes down → the agent sends an InformRequest to the NMS on UDP 162 and **keeps a copy in memory** → the NMS replies with a Response (the acknowledgement) → the agent deletes its copy. If no Response arrives before the timeout, the agent sends the same inform again, up to its retry limit, and only then gives up. `show snmp` shows counters of informs sent, retried and dropped.

**Why not always use informs?** Because during a big failure, when hundreds of events fire, the device must hold every unacknowledged inform in memory and keep retransmitting, possibly toward a manager it can no longer reach. Informs are for events you can't afford to lose; traps are fine for high-volume, lower-value ones.

### Configuring SNMPv2c (Read-Only, Restricted)

You'll still see v2c on older estates and in exam exhibits. The only protection a community string has is the ACL attached to it:

```
R1(config)# access-list 20 permit host 10.0.0.50                  ! the NMS only
R1(config)# snmp-server community R3ad0nly RO 20                  ! RO + ACL
R1(config)# snmp-server host 10.0.0.50 version 2c R3ad0nly        ! trap destination
R1(config)# snmp-server enable traps
```

**Why the ACL matters:** the community string crosses the network in clear text. Anyone who captures it can poll the device, and with an RW community, change its configuration. Restricting the community to the NMS address is the minimum; v3 is the real fix.

### Configuring SNMPv3 (authPriv)

```
R1(config)# snmp-server view ALL-MIB iso included             ! what the group can see
R1(config)# snmp-server group NMS-GRP v3 priv read ALL-MIB    ! group requires authPriv
R1(config)# snmp-server user nms-admin NMS-GRP v3 auth sha AuthPass#1 priv aes 128 PrivPass#1
R1(config)# snmp-server host 10.0.0.50 version 3 priv nms-admin   ! where to send traps
R1(config)# snmp-server enable traps                          ! or enable specific ones
R1# show snmp user
R1# show snmp group
```

**Informs over v3 need one more step.** For a trap, the *sending* router is the authoritative SNMP engine, so the user above (keyed to the router's own engine ID) works. For an **inform**, the *receiver* is authoritative, because it must acknowledge. The router therefore needs the manager's engine ID and a copy of the user localized to it:

```
! (global configuration mode)
snmp-server engineID remote 10.0.0.51 800000090300AABBCCDDEE01
snmp-server user nms-admin NMS-GRP remote 10.0.0.51 v3 auth sha Auth#1 priv aes 128 Priv#1
snmp-server host 10.0.0.51 informs version 3 priv nms-admin
```

Configure the `engineID remote` **before** the remote user: the user's keys are computed from that engine ID. Skip it, and the informs are sent but never acknowledged, so the router keeps retransmitting them and the manager never logs a single event.

**A quirk worth knowing:** SNMPv3 users **don't appear in `show running-config`**. Their keys are localized and hashed, so you verify them with `show snmp user`. This surprises people the first time they check a config backup.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 15.4**

**Q1.** Which two statements about SNMP traps and informs are true? (Choose two.)

- **A.** Traps are sent to the manager on UDP 161
- **B.** An inform must be acknowledged by the manager, and the agent retransmits it until it is, up to its retry limit
- **C.** Informs are sent by the manager to poll the agent
- **D.** Traps are more reliable than informs because they use TCP
- **E.** Informs use more memory on the agent, because it holds a copy of each one until it is acknowledged

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B, E.** An inform waits for a Response from the manager and is resent if none arrives, so the agent must keep a copy in memory until then. That's the price of reliability, and why traps are still used for high-volume events. **Why not the others:** A, traps and informs go to the manager on UDP 162; the agent listens on 161. C, informs are notifications from the agent; polls are Get requests from the manager. D, SNMP runs over UDP, and a trap is sent once with no acknowledgement, so it's the less reliable of the two.
</details>

**Q2.** An NMS polls `ifInOctets` on a WAN interface every 5 minutes. It reads 2,000,000,000 at 10:00:00 and 2,150,000,000 at 10:05:00. What was the average inbound rate?

- **A.** 0.5 Mbps
- **B.** 1.2 Mbps
- **C.** 4 Mbps
- **D.** 40 Mbps

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** The difference is 150,000,000 bytes. × 8 = 1,200,000,000 bits, ÷ 300 seconds = 4,000,000 bit/s = 4 Mbps. **Why not the others:** A is the bytes-per-second figure (500,000 bytes/s) read as megabits, which forgets the × 8. B treats the 1.2 billion bits moved over the whole five minutes as if it were a rate; those bits still have to be divided by the 300 seconds. D is a factor of ten too high.
</details>

**Q3.** Refer to the exhibit. The NMS at 10.0.0.51 never logs an inform from R1, and R1 keeps retransmitting them. The NMS can poll R1 successfully with `nms-admin`. What is missing?

```
snmp-server group NMS-GRP v3 priv
snmp-server user nms-admin NMS-GRP v3 auth sha Auth#1 priv aes 128 Priv#1
snmp-server host 10.0.0.51 informs version 3 priv nms-admin
snmp-server enable traps
```

- **A.** `snmp-server engineID remote` for 10.0.0.51, and a copy of the user created with `remote 10.0.0.51`
- **B.** The group must use `auth` instead of `priv` for informs
- **C.** A community string with an ACL permitting 10.0.0.51
- **D.** The `snmp-server host` line must use the `traps` keyword instead of `informs`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** For an inform, the receiver is the authoritative SNMP engine because it must acknowledge. R1 therefore needs the manager's engine ID and a user localized to it; without them the informs can't be validated, so they're never acknowledged and R1 retransmits forever. Polls work because for a Get the router is authoritative. **Why not the others:** B, informs work at any v3 level; dropping encryption fixes nothing. C, v3 uses users, not community strings. D, switching to traps would stop the retransmissions only by giving up acknowledgement; it wouldn't make the configuration correct.
</details>

**Q4.** An auditor flags `snmp-server community R3ad0nly RO 20`. What is the main risk that SNMPv3 removes?

- **A.** SNMPv2c doesn't support GetBulk, so polling is slow
- **B.** The ACL on a read-only community is ignored, so any host can poll
- **C.** SNMPv2c traps are encrypted but polls are not
- **D.** The community string crosses the network in clear text in every packet, so anyone who captures one can use it; v3 adds per-user authentication and encryption

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** In v1/v2c the community string is the password, and every poll carries it unencrypted. v3 replaces it with named users, authenticates each message with a keyed hash and can encrypt it. **Why not the others:** A, GetBulk was added in v2c. B, the ACL (20 here) is applied, and it's the only protection a community has. C, nothing in v2c is encrypted.
</details>

---

## 15.5 Flexible NetFlow

SNMP tells you an interface is 90% busy. **NetFlow** tells you **who** is using it: which hosts, which applications, how many bytes. A **flow** is a set of packets sharing the same **key fields**, classically the 7-tuple: source/destination IP, source/destination port, protocol, ToS and input interface.

**Flexible NetFlow (FNF)** is the modern IOS XE implementation. You choose exactly which fields define a flow and which are collected. It is built from four parts:

| Component | Job | Command |
|-----------|-----|---------|
| **Flow record** | Which fields are **keys** (`match`, define a flow) and which are **non-key** (`collect`, measured per flow) | `flow record` |
| **Flow exporter** | Where to send flow data, how, and in what format | `flow exporter` |
| **Flow monitor** | Ties a record to one or more exporters; holds the **cache** | `flow monitor` |
| **Interface** | Applies the monitor, input and/or output | `ip flow monitor … input` |

**Story Time 📖:** NetFlow is your phone bill, not a wiretap. The itemised bill lists every call: who called whom, when, for how long. It never records what was said. That's exactly enough to spot "someone called an overseas number for six hours at 3 a.m.", and it costs almost nothing to keep. When you need to hear the actual words, you need a recording: that's SPAN (15.6).

**Why the key/non-key distinction?** Key fields decide *what counts as a separate flow*. Add `match transport destination-port` and HTTPS and SSH between the same hosts become separate flows. Non-key fields are just *measurements* recorded about each flow: bytes, packets, timestamps. *Keys determine the granularity of the answer; non-keys determine what you learn about each flow.*

**How the flow cache works, step by step:**

1. A packet arrives on an interface with a flow monitor applied.
2. The router reads the **key fields** from it (with the record below: source/destination IP, protocol, source/destination port, input interface).
3. It looks those keys up in the **cache**, a table held in memory.
   - **No entry yet:** a new flow entry is created, with packets = 1, bytes = this packet's size, first and last timestamps = now.
   - **Entry exists:** packets +1, bytes + this packet's size, last timestamp = now.
4. An entry is **expired** (removed from the cache and exported) when the flow ends (TCP FIN or RST), when no packet has matched it for the **inactive timeout** (15 s default), when it has existed for the **active timeout** (1800 s default), or when the cache is full.
5. The exporter packs expired entries into NetFlow v9 or IPFIX packets and sends them to the collector over UDP. Because v9/IPFIX are template-based, it first sends a **template** saying which fields each record contains, so the collector knows how to read them.

**Worked example.** PC 10.1.1.25 opens one HTTPS session to 52.96.10.4 and sends three packets of 1500, 1500 and 600 bytes, all from source port 51544:

| After packet | Cache entry (10.1.1.25:51544 → 52.96.10.4:443, TCP, Gi0/0) |
|--------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| 1 | new entry: pkts 1, bytes 1500 |
| 2 | same keys, update: pkts 2, bytes 3000 |
| 3 | same keys, update: pkts 3, bytes 3600 |

Now the PC opens a **second** session (new source port 51545) to the same server. One key differs, so it becomes a **second** entry. If your record had *not* matched on source port, both sessions would merge into one entry. That's the key-field choice in action.

### Configuring It (Try It!)

```
flow record REC-WAN
 match ipv4 source address            ! key fields - define the flow
 match ipv4 destination address
 match ipv4 protocol
 match transport source-port
 match transport destination-port
 match interface input
 collect counter bytes long           ! non-key fields - measured per flow
 collect counter packets long
 collect timestamp absolute first
 collect timestamp absolute last
!
flow exporter EXP-COLLECTOR
 destination 10.0.0.60                ! the NetFlow collector
 source Loopback0
 transport udp 2055                   ! collector's port (2055, 9995, 9996 are common)
 export-protocol netflow-v9           ! or ipfix
!
flow monitor MON-WAN
 record REC-WAN
 exporter EXP-COLLECTOR
 cache timeout active 60              ! export long-lived flows every 60 s
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip flow monitor MON-WAN input
 ip flow monitor MON-WAN output
```

### Verifying

```
R1# show flow monitor MON-WAN cache format table
IPV4 SRC ADDR  IPV4 DST ADDR  TRNS SRC PORT  TRNS DST PORT  IP PROT  bytes long  pkts long
=============  =============  =============  =============  =======  ==========  =========
10.1.1.25      52.96.10.4             51544            443        6    18422190      13021
10.1.1.40      10.2.0.10              62011             22        6       41250        310

R1# show flow exporter EXP-COLLECTOR statistics    ! are packets actually being sent?
R1# show flow interface GigabitEthernet0/0         ! which monitors are applied where
R1# show flow monitor MON-WAN statistics           ! cache size, active/added/aged flows
```

**Why `cache timeout active`?** A flow is normally exported when it **ends** (TCP FIN/RST, or inactive for 15 seconds by default). A two-hour file transfer would then appear on the collector only after it finished, so for two hours the graphs would show nothing. The active timeout forces long flows to be exported in slices (default 1800 s; 60 s is common), so the collector sees traffic as it happens.

**Common FNF problems:** monitor applied in only one direction (half the conversation is missing); the exporter's source interface has no route to the collector; a collector expecting a different port or format (v5 vs v9 vs IPFIX). **NetFlow v5** has a *fixed* format (IPv4 only, no templates); **v9 and IPFIX** are *template-based*, which is what makes flexible records possible.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 15.5**

**Q1.** A flow record matches only on IPv4 source and destination address and collects bytes and packets. The team wants HTTPS and SSH between the same two hosts to appear as separate flows. Which line should be added to the record?

- **A.** `collect transport destination-port`
- **B.** `match transport destination-port`
- **C.** `collect counter bytes long`
- **D.** `cache timeout active 60`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** `match` lines are key fields, and key fields decide what counts as a separate flow. Adding the destination port as a key splits port 443 and port 22 traffic into different cache entries. **Why not the others:** A, `collect` makes the port a non-key field: it's recorded for each flow, but the two sessions still merge into one entry. C is already a measurement and doesn't change flow identity. D is a flow monitor command about export timing, not about what defines a flow.
</details>

**Q2.** A two-hour file transfer appears on the NetFlow collector only after it finishes, so the graphs show nothing while it runs. Which change fixes this?

- **A.** `cache timeout inactive 3600` under the flow monitor
- **B.** `export-protocol ipfix` under the flow exporter
- **C.** `ip flow monitor MON-WAN output` on the interface
- **D.** `cache timeout active 60` under the flow monitor

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** A flow is normally exported when it ends or goes idle. The active timeout (default 1800 s) forces long-lived flows to be exported in slices, so with 60 s the collector sees the transfer minute by minute. **Why not the others:** A, the inactive timer covers idle flows; a busy transfer is never idle, and raising it only delays exports further. B, the export format doesn't change when flows are exported. C adds the other direction of traffic but doesn't make long flows export sooner.
</details>

**Q3.** `show flow monitor MON-WAN cache` shows flows, but the collector receives nothing. Which two problems could explain this? (Choose two.)

- **A.** The exporter's source interface has no route to the collector
- **B.** The monitor is applied in the input direction only
- **C.** The collector listens on a different UDP port or expects a different export format
- **D.** The flow record matches on `interface input`
- **E.** The inactive timeout is still at its default of 15 seconds

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A, C.** The cache is filling, so the monitor and record work; the failure is in getting records to the collector. Either the exported packets can't reach it, or they arrive where it isn't listening or in a format it doesn't expect. `show flow exporter ... statistics` tells you whether packets are being sent. **Why not the others:** B would give you only half of each conversation, not nothing. D is a normal key field. E is the normal default and causes idle flows to be exported, not withheld.
</details>
