## 15.6 SPAN, RSPAN and ERSPAN — Copying Traffic to an Analyzer

NetFlow summarizes traffic; sometimes you need the **actual packets**, for Wireshark, an IDS (Intrusion Detection System) or a recorder. A switch normally forwards a frame only to its destination port, so a laptop plugged into a spare port sees almost nothing. You have to tell the switch to **mirror** traffic to a monitoring port. **SPAN** stands for Switched Port ANalyzer.

**Story Time 📖:** SPAN is a photocopier in the mail room. Every letter going to or from one desk is still delivered normally, but a photocopy of it is also dropped into your tray. RSPAN sends the photocopies to another building through a private internal mail route (a dedicated VLAN). ERSPAN puts them in a sealed envelope and posts them through the public mail (GRE over IP) to anywhere. *The analogy breaks in one place:* a real photocopier waits for you, but a SPAN port that's too slow for the volume of copies just throws the extras away.

![SPAN, RSPAN and ERSPAN compared](images/c15_span.png)

| Type | Source and destination | Transport for the copies |
|------|------------------------|--------------------------|
| **SPAN** (local) | Same switch | Internal |
| **RSPAN** (remote) | Different switches, same Layer 2 domain | A dedicated **RSPAN VLAN** across trunks |
| **ERSPAN** (encapsulated remote) | Anywhere reachable by IP | **GRE** across a routed network |

### Local SPAN

```
SW1(config)# monitor session 1 source interface Gi1/0/1 both    ! rx, tx, or both
! VLANs can be sources too (monitor session 2 source vlan 10 rx), but a session's
! sources must be all ports or all VLANs, never a mix
SW1(config)# monitor session 1 destination interface Gi1/0/24   ! the analyzer port
SW1# show monitor session 1
Session 1
---------
Type                     : Local Session
Source Ports             :
    Both                 : Gi1/0/1
Destination Ports        : Gi1/0/24
    Encapsulation        : Native
          Ingress        : Disabled
```

**How the copy path works:** a frame arrives on Gi1/0/1 (an **rx**, received, copy is taken) → the switch forwards the original normally → when a frame *leaves* Gi1/0/1 a **tx**, transmitted, copy is taken → the hardware queues every copy to Gi1/0/24 → the analyzer receives them. `Encapsulation: Native` means the copies go out untagged (add `encapsulation replicate` to keep the original VLAN tags), and `Ingress: Disabled` means Gi1/0/24 ignores anything the analyzer sends.

**Worked example — will the capture be complete?** Gi1/0/1 is a 1 Gbps server port. During the problem it receives 700 Mbps and sends 600 Mbps. With source `both`, the copies total 700 + 600 = **1.3 Gbps**, but Gi1/0/24 is also 1 Gbps. About 300 Mbps of copies are dropped, with no error message. Wireshark then flags "previous segment not captured" for packets that were actually delivered fine, and you can waste a day chasing loss that only exists in the capture. Fixes: mirror only `rx` (or only `tx`), limit a trunk source to the VLANs you care about (`monitor session 1 filter vlan 10`), or use a 10 Gbps destination port.

### RSPAN

```
! On EVERY switch the copies cross:
vlan 999
 remote-span                          ! marks it as RSPAN - no MAC learning in this VLAN
!
! Source switch
SW1(config)# monitor session 1 source interface Gi1/0/1 both
SW1(config)# monitor session 1 destination remote vlan 999
!
! Destination switch
SW2(config)# monitor session 1 source remote vlan 999
SW2(config)# monitor session 1 destination interface Gi1/0/24
```

**Why must the VLAN be flagged `remote-span`?** Because mirrored frames still carry their **original** MAC addresses. In a normal VLAN, intermediate switches would learn those MACs on the wrong port (the mirror path) and could start forwarding *real* traffic for those hosts along it. In an RSPAN VLAN, MAC learning is disabled, so the copies simply flood along to the destination. The RSPAN VLAN must also be **allowed on every trunk** in the path.

**RSPAN walk-through:** SW1 copies Gi1/0/1's frames → it puts the copies into VLAN 999 and sends them up its trunk → the middle switch receives them in VLAN 999, learns no MACs, and floods them out its other trunks allowed for VLAN 999 → SW2 takes everything arriving in VLAN 999 and delivers it to Gi1/0/24. If any trunk on the way doesn't allow VLAN 999 (`switchport trunk allowed vlan`), the copies stop there and the analyzer sees nothing.

### ERSPAN (IOS XE)

**Why ERSPAN exists:** RSPAN only works where VLAN 999 can stretch, so the source and analyzer must sit in the same Layer 2 domain. Modern campuses route between distribution blocks, and the analyzer may be in a data centre across a WAN. ERSPAN wraps each copied frame in **GRE** (Generic Routing Encapsulation, the same tunnel header as Chapter 12) inside an ordinary IP packet, so the copies can be routed anywhere the source can reach.

```
! Source router/switch
monitor session 10 type erspan-source
 source interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1 both
 no shutdown                          ! ERSPAN sessions are shut by default
 destination
  erspan-id 100                       ! must match on the receiver
  ip address 10.9.9.9                 ! the receiving device or analyzer
  origin ip address 10.1.1.1          ! source of the GRE packets
!
! Destination switch (if a switch, not an analyzer, decapsulates)
monitor session 20 type erspan-destination
 destination interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24
 no shutdown
 source
  erspan-id 100
  ip address 10.9.9.9
```

Many analyzers (Wireshark, commercial probes) can receive and decode ERSPAN directly, so a destination session isn't always needed.

### SPAN Rules and Limits

- A **destination port** stops being a normal switch port: it doesn't forward ordinary traffic or take part in STP, and by default it ignores incoming traffic.
- **Oversubscription:** mirroring `both` directions of a 1 Gbps port can produce up to 2 Gbps of copies, more than a 1 Gbps destination can carry. The excess is **silently dropped**, so your capture may be missing packets.
- The number of monitor sessions is limited by platform, often to just a few per switch. Check the platform's limits before you rely on another one being free.
- Mirroring adds load; ERSPAN adds GRE overhead to the network it crosses (so mind the MTU).
- A port can't be both a source and a destination, and an EtherChannel member can't be a destination.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 15.6**

**Q1.** SPAN source Gi1/0/1 (both directions) is a 1 Gbps server port receiving 700 Mbps and sending 600 Mbps. The destination Gi1/0/24 is also 1 Gbps. Wireshark reports "previous segment not captured", but the server shows no retransmissions. What explains this?

- **A.** The session mirrors only received traffic, so half of each conversation is missing
- **B.** SPAN copies are encrypted, so Wireshark can't decode some of them
- **C.** 700 + 600 = 1.3 Gbps of copies exceed the 1 Gbps destination, and the excess copies are silently dropped
- **D.** The destination port takes part in STP and blocks some frames

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Mirroring both directions creates copies of everything received and sent. The destination can only carry 1 Gbps, so about 300 Mbps of copies are discarded with no error. The real traffic was delivered fine; only the capture is incomplete. Fix it by mirroring one direction, filtering VLANs, or using a faster destination port. **Why not the others:** A, the session uses `both`. B, SPAN copies the frames exactly as they are; it doesn't encrypt anything. D, a SPAN destination port doesn't take part in STP.
</details>

**Q2.** Traffic on SW1 must be mirrored to an analyzer on SW3 through SW2 using RSPAN VLAN 999. Which two requirements apply? (Choose two.)

- **A.** VLAN 999 needs an SVI with an IP address on each switch
- **B.** VLAN 999 must be configured with `remote-span` on every switch the copies cross
- **C.** SW3 must run an ERSPAN destination session
- **D.** VLAN 999 must be allowed on every trunk in the path
- **E.** SW1 and SW3 must be in different Layer 2 domains

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B, D.** The `remote-span` flag turns off MAC learning in that VLAN, so the copies (which carry the original MAC addresses) don't corrupt the switches' MAC tables. The copies travel as ordinary VLAN 999 frames, so every trunk on the way must allow the VLAN or they stop there. **Why not the others:** A, RSPAN is pure Layer 2; no IP addressing is involved. C, ERSPAN is a different, GRE-based mechanism. E, it's the opposite: RSPAN needs both switches in the same Layer 2 domain.
</details>

**Q3.** Refer to the exhibit. The analyzer at 10.9.9.9 receives nothing, although the switch can ping 10.9.9.9 from 10.1.1.1. What is the most likely fix?

```
monitor session 10 type erspan-source
 source interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1 both
 destination
  erspan-id 100
  ip address 10.9.9.9
  origin ip address 10.1.1.1
```

- **A.** Enter `no shutdown` under the monitor session
- **B.** Change `erspan-id 100` to match the VLAN of Gi1/0/1
- **C.** Create VLAN 100 with `remote-span`
- **D.** Change the source direction from `both` to `rx`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** ERSPAN sessions are shut down by default, and this one has no `no shutdown`, so nothing is sent. **Why not the others:** B, the ERSPAN ID only has to match on the sender and receiver; it has nothing to do with VLANs. C, ERSPAN carries copies in GRE across IP; it doesn't use an RSPAN VLAN. D would cut the volume of copies, but a shut session sends nothing in either direction.
</details>

---

## 15.7 IP SLA — Measuring the Path Continuously

Ping tells you about **now**, when you happen to run it. **IP SLA** (Service Level Agreement) makes the router run probes **continuously, on a schedule**, keep statistics, and (combined with tracking) **react** when performance degrades.

**Why that matters:** your ISP's link can stay physically up while the ISP's network behind it is broken. The interface says "up/up", the default route stays in the table, and every user is cut off. Only a test that actually crosses the ISP's network, repeated all day, notices.

**Story Time 📖:** IP SLA is a nurse doing hourly observations. Nobody waits for the patient to complain; the nurse takes a pulse on a timetable, writes it on the chart, and calls the doctor when a reading crosses a line. The probe is the pulse check, `frequency` is the timetable, `show ip sla statistics` is the chart, and the **track** object (below) is the call to the doctor.

**How an operation runs, step by step** (operation 10 below):

1. Every `frequency` seconds (10), R1 sends one ICMP echo to 8.8.8.8 out of Gi0/0.
2. It waits up to `timeout` (1000 ms) for the reply.
3. It sets the **return code**: **OK** if the reply came back within `threshold` (300 ms); **Over threshold** if it came back but took longer; **Timeout** if it never came.
4. It updates the statistics (latest RTT, success and failure counts).
5. Anything tracking the operation reads the new return code and decides whether it is up or down.

```
R1(config)# ip sla 10
R1(config-ip-sla)#  icmp-echo 8.8.8.8 source-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-ip-sla-echo)#  frequency 10            ! probe every 10 s (default 60)
R1(config-ip-sla-echo)#  threshold 300           ! ms - above this, "over threshold"
R1(config-ip-sla-echo)#  timeout 1000            ! ms to wait for a reply
R1(config)# ip sla schedule 10 life forever start-time now
```

```
R1# show ip sla statistics 10
IPSLA operation id: 10
        Latest RTT: 14 milliseconds
Latest operation start time: 10:42:31 UTC Mon Oct 26 2026
Latest operation return code: OK
Number of successes: 412
Number of failures: 3
Operation time to live: Forever

R1# show ip sla configuration 10
R1# show ip sla summary
```

**Why `life forever`?** An operation that's configured but not **scheduled** never runs, and the default life is 3600 seconds, after which it silently stops. Forgetting the schedule, or leaving the default life, is the classic "my IP SLA does nothing" problem.

### Operation Types You Should Recognise

| Operation | Measures | Needs a responder? |
|-----------|----------|--------------------|
| `icmp-echo` | Reachability and round-trip time | No — any device that answers ping |
| `udp-jitter` | Delay, **jitter**, loss in each direction, MOS for voice | **Yes** — `ip sla responder` on the far Cisco device |
| `tcp-connect` | Can a TCP session be opened to a port (application up?) | No for well-known ports; yes otherwise |
| `http` | Web response time | No |
| `udp-echo` | UDP round trip | Usually |

**Why does `udp-jitter` need a responder?** Because measuring **one-way** delay and jitter requires timestamps from *both* ends. A plain ping only shows the round trip. The **IP SLA responder** timestamps each probe on arrival and departure, and subtracts its own processing time, so the measurements reflect the network rather than the far router's CPU.

**Jitter** is the *variation* in delay between packets. Voice copes with steady delay but sounds broken when delay jumps around. Example: four packets take 20, 22, 40 and 21 ms one way. The average delay (about 26 ms) is fine, but the jumps (2, 18 and 19 ms) are what the far phone's jitter buffer must absorb. A one-way jitter of 30 ms or more is a common warning level for voice.

**How a udp-jitter operation runs:** R1 first sends a small **control message** to R2's responder on **UDP 1967**, asking it to listen on UDP 16384 for the next few seconds → the responder opens that port → R1 sends a train of timestamped probes (with `codec g711ulaw`, 1000 packets of 172 bytes, 20 ms apart, by default) → the responder stamps each one with its arrival and departure times and returns it → R1 computes one-way delay, jitter and loss in each direction. One-way delay figures are only accurate if both routers' clocks are synchronized with NTP (Chapter 8).

### Try It — udp-jitter for Voice Quality

```
R2(config)# ip sla responder                         ! far end: answer and timestamp probes
!
R1(config)# ip sla 20
R1(config-ip-sla)#  udp-jitter 10.2.2.2 16384 codec g711ulaw source-ip 10.1.1.1
R1(config-ip-sla-jitter)#  frequency 30
R1(config)# ip sla schedule 20 life forever start-time now
!
R1# show ip sla statistics 20
```

The `codec g711ulaw` keyword makes the probe mimic a G.711 call (packet size and interval), so the statistics include a **MOS** (Mean Opinion Score) and **ICPIF** voice-quality estimate alongside one-way latency, jitter and loss in each direction. If R2's responder is missing, every operation fails with a **timeout** return code, even though R2 answers pings.

### From Measurement to Action

On its own, IP SLA only measures. Linked to a **track object**, it can change routing:

```
track 1 ip sla 10 reachability
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.254 track 1   ! primary default - removed if probe fails
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.254 10         ! floating backup (CCNA guide 15.5)
```

**`state` or `reachability`?** Two ways to turn a probe into up/down, and the difference is the **threshold**:

| Track keyword | Up when the return code is | Down when |
|---------------|----------------------------|-----------|
| `track 1 ip sla 10 reachability` | OK **or Over threshold** | Timeout or other failure |
| `track 1 ip sla 10 state` | **OK only** | Over threshold, timeout, failure |

So with `threshold 300`, a path answering in 450 ms keeps a `reachability` track **up** (it's slow but reachable) but takes a `state` track **down** (it's failing its SLA). Pick `state` when "too slow" should trigger failover, and `reachability` when only "dead" should.

```
R1# show track 1
Track 1
  IP SLA 10 reachability
  Reachability is Up
    3 changes, last change 00:41:12
  Latest operation return code: OK
  Latest RTT (millisecs) 14
  Tracked by:
    Static IP Routing 0
```

Read it as: what it tracks, its current state, **how often it has flapped** (the change counter), the latest probe result, and **what depends on it** (here, a static route).

**Worked example — the failover, second by second.** Using operation 10 (`frequency 10`), track 1 (`reachability`) and the two default routes above:

1. **Normal:** probes return OK. Track 1 is Up, so the primary default (AD 1) is in the routing table and the backup (AD 10) waits.
2. **The ISP's core fails at 10:00:03.** Gi0/0 stays up/up. The 10:00:10 probe gets no reply within 1000 ms, so its return code is **Timeout**.
3. Track 1 sees the failure and goes **Down**. IOS logs `%TRACK-6-STATE: 1 ip sla 10 reachability Up -> Down`.
4. The static route tied to `track 1` is withdrawn, so the floating route is installed.
5. **The ISP recovers.** The next OK probe brings track 1 Up, and the primary route (AD 1 beats AD 10) returns.

```
R1# show ip route static | include 0.0.0.0        ! step 1: primary in use
S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 198.51.100.254
R1# show ip route static | include 0.0.0.0        ! step 4: backup in use
S*    0.0.0.0/0 [10/0] via 203.0.113.254
```

Users lost about 10 seconds of connectivity instead of hours. To stop a flapping path bouncing the routes back and forth, add `delay down 5 up 30` under the track: it must stay down 5 s before acting, and stay up 30 s before failing back.

This is how a router fails over when an ISP's *link* stays up but the ISP's *network* is broken, which an interface-down check would never notice. Chapter 9 uses the same tracking to lower HSRP priority, and Chapter 32 covers troubleshooting tracking and jitter operations at ENARSI depth.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 15.7**

**Q1.** An engineer configures `ip sla 10` with `icmp-echo 8.8.8.8`, `frequency 10` and `threshold 300`, and ties `track 1 ip sla 10 reachability` to the primary default route. `show ip sla statistics 10` shows no start time and no successes. What is wrong?

- **A.** The threshold is lower than the round-trip time
- **B.** `frequency` must be at least 60 seconds
- **C.** The track must use `state` instead of `reachability`
- **D.** The operation was never scheduled; add `ip sla schedule 10 life forever start-time now`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** An IP SLA operation that's configured but not scheduled never runs, so it has no start time and no results. (Leaving the default life of 3600 s is the related trap: it stops after an hour.) **Why not the others:** A, a slow reply would still record a start time and an "Over threshold" result. B, 10 seconds is a valid frequency (60 is only the default). C changes how results are interpreted, but there are no results to interpret.
</details>

**Q2.** Operation 10 has `threshold 300`. The primary default route must be removed when the path is down **or** when replies take longer than 300 ms. Which track configuration meets this?

- **A.** `track 1 ip sla 10 reachability`
- **B.** `track 1 ip sla 10 state`
- **C.** `track 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 line-protocol`
- **D.** `track 1 ip sla 10 reachability` with `delay down 5 up 30`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** `state` is up only when the return code is OK, so "Over threshold" (slow) and Timeout (dead) both take it down. **Why not the others:** A, `reachability` stays up for "Over threshold", so a 450 ms path wouldn't trigger failover. C watches only the local interface, which can stay up while the ISP's network is broken or slow. D just adds damping to the same `reachability` behaviour.
</details>

**Q3.** A `udp-jitter` operation from R1 to R2 fails every time with a Timeout return code, although R1 can ping R2. What is the most likely cause?

- **A.** R2 needs its own `ip sla schedule` for the operation
- **B.** The operation must use `codec g729a`
- **C.** R2 is missing `ip sla responder`
- **D.** The probe's destination port must be 1967

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** `udp-jitter` needs the far Cisco device to run the IP SLA responder, which agrees to listen on the probe port and timestamps every probe. Without it, nothing answers the probes, so every operation times out, even though ping works. **Why not the others:** A, the operation is scheduled on R1 only. B, the codec only shapes the probe stream; any codec fails without a responder. D, UDP 1967 is the responder's control port; the probe port (16384 in the guide's example) is set in the operation.
</details>

**Q4.** Why does a `udp-jitter` operation need a responder when `icmp-echo` doesn't?

- **A.** One-way delay and jitter need timestamps from both ends, and the responder stamps each probe and removes its own processing time
- **B.** The responder encrypts the probes so they aren't dropped by firewalls
- **C.** Without a responder, R1 cannot measure even the round-trip time
- **D.** The responder sends the results to the NMS by SNMP

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** A round trip can be measured from one end, but delay and jitter in each direction need the far end to say when each probe arrived and left. Subtracting the responder's own processing time makes the figures reflect the network, not the far router's CPU. **Why not the others:** B, the responder doesn't encrypt anything. C, `icmp-echo` measures round-trip time with no responder at all. D, results are read on the source router (`show ip sla statistics`), not pushed by the responder.
</details>

---

## 15.8 Choosing the Right Tool

**Why this matters:** ENCOR 4.1 says *diagnose*, so exam questions give you a symptom and ask which tool finds the cause. Each tool has a cost (CPU, setup time, disk space) and answers one kind of question. Pick by the question, not by habit.

| Symptom | First tool | Then |
|---------|-----------|------|
| "Site B is unreachable" | Extended ping **sourced from the LAN**, traceroute | Routing table on each hop; ACLs at the hop where the trace stops |
| "OSPF neighbor keeps flapping" | `show logging` (look for `%OSPF-5-ADJCHG`) | Conditional `debug ip ospf adj` on that interface |
| "The WAN link is full — by what?" | **Flexible NetFlow** cache / collector | QoS (Chapter 11) or a conversation with the top talker |
| "VoIP calls are choppy" | **IP SLA udp-jitter** | QoS marking/queuing on the path |
| "The app vendor wants a packet capture" | **SPAN / ERSPAN** to Wireshark | Analyze the handshake and retransmissions |
| "CPU and interface trends over a month" | **SNMP** polling to the NMS | Thresholds and alerts |
| "Failover didn't happen when the ISP broke" | `show track`, `show ip sla statistics` | Check the schedule, life and the target used |

**Worked example — one complaint, four tools.** "The ERP app at Site B is slow every morning around 09:00."

1. **Syslog first** (cheap, already collected): `show logging` on Site B's router shows no interface flaps or neighbor changes at 09:00. So it isn't an outage.
2. **SNMP graphs** (already polled): the WAN interface's inbound traffic sits at 98% of the 100 Mbps link from 08:55 to 09:40 every weekday. So it's congestion.
3. **Flexible NetFlow** (who is using it?): the cache during that window shows 10.20.5.14 → 10.1.9.30 on TCP 445 carrying 85% of the bytes. That's a file server copying to a PC, probably a scheduled sync.
4. **IP SLA udp-jitter** (prove the impact and the fix): jitter and loss during the window confirm the damage. After the sync is moved to 22:00, or put in a low-priority QoS class (Chapter 11), the next morning's statistics are clean.

No debug and no packet capture were needed. *Broad tools found the right place; narrow tools would only have been needed if the broad ones had pointed at a single misbehaving device.*

*The habit to build:* go from broad and cheap tools (logs, counters, flows) to narrow and expensive ones (debugs, captures). Start the expensive ones only once you know where to point them.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 15.8**

**Q1.** Users report choppy VoIP calls between two sites every afternoon. Which tool measures one-way jitter and loss in each direction, continuously?

- **A.** Flexible NetFlow
- **B.** SNMP polling of interface counters
- **C.** SPAN to a packet analyzer
- **D.** IP SLA `udp-jitter`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** `udp-jitter` sends a stream that mimics a voice call, on a schedule, and reports one-way delay, jitter, loss and a MOS estimate in each direction. **Why not the others:** A shows who is using the link, not voice quality. B shows how busy interfaces are, averaged over the poll interval. C captures packets at one point in time and one place; it doesn't measure the path continuously.
</details>

**Q2.** A WAN link runs at 98% every morning. The manager wants to know which hosts and applications are using it, without capturing any payload. Which tool should you use?

- **A.** SNMP polling of `ifInOctets`
- **B.** Flexible NetFlow
- **C.** A conditional `debug ip packet`
- **D.** SPAN to Wireshark

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** NetFlow records who talked to whom, on which ports, and how many bytes, without keeping any payload: the phone bill, not the recording. **Why not the others:** A proves the link is full but not who is filling it. C is CPU-heavy and impractical at link-saturating volumes. D captures payloads, which the manager specifically doesn't want, and a SPAN port would struggle with that volume anyway.
</details>

---

<a name="chapter-16"></a>
# Chapter 16: Cisco Catalyst Center: Traditional & AI-Powered Workflows

> **Blueprint:** ENCOR 4.5 — Describe how Cisco Catalyst Center (formerly Cisco DNA Center) is used to apply network configuration, monitoring, and management using traditional and AI-powered workflows

**Cisco Catalyst Center** (called **DNA Center** until 2023) is Cisco's controller for the enterprise campus, branch and wireless network. It's the management plane of SD-Access (Chapter 14), but it manages traditional networks too. You met it in the CCNA guide as "the controller" (22.2). ENCOR wants you to describe *how it is used*: how intent becomes configuration, how monitoring becomes **assurance**, and what its AI features actually do.

> **A note on product claims.** Catalyst Center's features, especially the AI ones, change with every release and depend on licensing (most AI features require the **Advantage** tier, and some need cloud connectivity). This chapter describes the capabilities and the ideas behind them. Check Cisco's current release notes before you rely on a specific feature in production.

---

## 16.1 From Box-by-Box to Intent

**The traditional way:** an engineer works out what is needed ("a new floor needs a voice VLAN with QoS"), translates it into CLI, then logs in to each switch and types it, hoping every box ends up consistent. Monitoring is a separate set of tools (SNMP graphs, syslog server, NetFlow collector) that each show one slice, and correlating them is a manual job.

**Intent-based networking (IBN)** turns that around:

1. **Express the intent** (*what* you want: "voice gets priority on every access port at this site").
2. **Translate and activate.** The controller works out the per-device configuration and pushes it to every device consistently.
3. **Assure.** Continuously collect telemetry and verify the network *is* behaving as intended. When it isn't, explain why and suggest a fix.

**Story Time 📖:** traditional management is giving a driver turn-by-turn directions from memory and hoping they arrive. Intent-based networking is a satnav. You state the destination (the intent), it works out every turn (the configuration), and then it keeps watching your position. If you drift off route or hit traffic, it notices and suggests a new route (assurance). *Where it breaks:* a satnav re-routes on its own, while Catalyst Center mostly *suggests* fixes and leaves the decision to change the network with you.

**Why does the "assure" step matter so much?** Because pushing configuration was never the hard part; scripts could already do that. The hard part is knowing whether the network is actually *delivering* what you asked for, right now, for every user. A config that was pushed successfully can still produce terrible voice quality. *IBN closes the loop: intent → config → verification → back to intent.*

| Aspect | Traditional CLI management | Catalyst Center (controller-based) |
|--------|----------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Unit of work | One device | A site, a group, a policy |
| Consistency | Depends on the engineer's discipline | Templates and intent enforced everywhere; drift is flagged |
| New device | Console cable, manual config | **Plug and Play** — zero-touch |
| Software upgrades | Device by device, manual checks | **SWIM** — golden images, automated pre/post checks |
| Monitoring | Separate SNMP, syslog, NetFlow tools | **Assurance** — correlated health scores per device, client, application |
| Troubleshooting | Engineer's experience + `show` commands | Guided issues with suggested actions, path trace, AI baselines |
| Integration | Screen-scraping CLI | **Intent API** (REST), webhooks, ITSM integration (Chapter 20) |

**📝 Exam-style questions — 16.1**

**Q1.** Which sequence correctly orders the intent-based networking loop?

- **A.** Assure → express the intent → translate and activate
- **B.** Express the intent → translate and activate → assure, then back to the intent
- **C.** Translate and activate → express the intent → assure
- **D.** Express the intent → assure → translate and activate

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** State *what* you want, let the controller work out and push the per-device configuration, then continuously verify the network is delivering it. **Why not the others:** A and D try to verify before anything has been deployed. C pushes configuration before anyone has said what it should achieve.
</details>

**Q2.** Why does intent-based networking treat assurance as an essential step rather than an optional extra?

- **A.** Because Catalyst Center can't push configuration without first collecting telemetry
- **B.** Because assurance replaces the need for configuration templates
- **C.** Because SNMP is the only way to configure devices
- **D.** Because a configuration that was pushed successfully can still fail to deliver what was intended, so the network's actual behaviour must be checked continuously

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** Pushing configuration was never the hard part; scripts could already do that. The hard part is knowing that users are actually getting what was asked for, right now. **Why not the others:** A is false; provisioning doesn't depend on assurance data. B is wrong; assurance verifies configuration, it doesn't replace it. C is false; Catalyst Center mostly configures devices over SSH, and NETCONF where supported.
</details>

## 16.2 The Four Workflows

**Why workflows:** every network change has the same life: decide what you want, decide who may do what, roll it out, then check it works. Catalyst Center gives each stage its own area, so the menus follow the job: **Design → Policy → Provision → Assurance**, plus a platform layer for integration.

![Catalyst Center workflows and the assurance loop](images/c16_workflow.png)

### Discovery and Inventory — Getting Existing Devices In

PnP (below) handles *new* devices. An existing network gets into Catalyst Center through **Discovery**:

1. **Choose how to find devices:** a **CDP** or **LLDP** crawl outward from a seed device (with a hop limit), or an **IP address range/subnet** scan.
2. **Supply credentials**, because Catalyst Center must log in to and poll what it finds: **CLI** (SSH username, password, enable secret), **SNMP** (v2c read/write communities or v3 users), and optionally **NETCONF** (port 830) and HTTP(S) credentials.
3. **Discovered devices land in the Inventory** with their reachability status ("Reachable", "Unreachable", "Authentication failed"), software version, platform and role. From there you **assign them to a site** in the hierarchy, which applies that site's settings.

**Why do so many discoveries end in "Authentication failed" or "Unreachable"?** Because Discovery is just SSH and SNMP under the hood. Wrong CLI credentials, an SNMP community that doesn't match (or an SNMP ACL that doesn't permit the Catalyst Center address), or SSH not enabled on the device all stop it. *Catalyst Center manages a device only as well as it can log in to it.*

### Design — Describe the Network You Want

- **Network hierarchy:** Areas → Buildings → Floors (with floor maps for wireless). Everything else (settings, policies, reports) attaches to a place in this hierarchy, and child sites inherit from parents.
- **Network settings:** AAA servers, DHCP, DNS, NTP, syslog, SNMP and NetFlow collectors, time zone, banners, all defined once per site.
- **IP address pools:** IP Address Management (IPAM) built in, or integrated with an external IPAM.
- **Image repository:** which software version is the **golden image** for each device family.
- **Wireless:** SSIDs, RF profiles.

**Why define settings once at the site level?** So a new switch dropped into "Building 3" automatically gets the right NTP server, syslog collector and AAA configuration. *Settings become a property of the place, not something someone has to remember to type.*

### Policy — Describe Who Can Do What

- **Group-based access control** with **ISE**: define scalable groups (SGTs) and the policy matrix between them (14.7).
- **Virtual networks** for SD-Access macro-segmentation.
- **Application policy (QoS):** classify applications as business-relevant, default or business-irrelevant, and Catalyst Center generates the matching QoS configuration (classification, marking, queuing) per platform (Chapter 11).

### Provision — Make It Real

- **Plug and Play (PnP):** a new device boots with no configuration and finds Catalyst Center through **DHCP option 43**, a DNS lookup of **`pnpserver.<domain>`**, or Cisco's cloud **PnP Connect** redirect. It then receives its image and Day-0 configuration automatically.
- **Templates:** Day-N configuration written in **Velocity** or **Jinja2**, with variables filled in per device or site, and pushed consistently.
- **SWIM (Software Image Management):** mark a golden image, and Catalyst Center flags non-compliant devices, distributes the image, runs **pre-checks** (flash space, config saved, startup config valid), activates it in a maintenance window, and runs **post-checks**.
- **LAN automation and fabric provisioning** for SD-Access: build the IS-IS underlay automatically and assign fabric roles (14.7).
- **Compliance:** compares running configurations, images and security advisories against the intended state, and flags drift.

**How PnP finds Catalyst Center, step by step** (option 43 method). A new switch is cabled to an access port in VLAN 99, whose DHCP server is a router:

```
ip dhcp pool PNP-VLAN99
 network 10.99.0.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 10.99.0.1
 option 43 ascii "5A1N;B2;K4;I10.10.10.50;J80"
```

1. The switch boots with no startup configuration, so the PnP agent starts and sends DHCPDISCOVER on its uplink.
2. It gets `10.99.0.x` plus option 43. Reading the string: `5A1N` = PnP, active, version 1, no debug; `B2` = the server address is IPv4; `K4` = use HTTP; `I10.10.10.50` = Catalyst Center's address; `J80` = port 80.
3. The switch contacts `10.10.10.50` and appears in Catalyst Center as an *Unclaimed* device, identified by its serial number.
4. An engineer (or a pre-staged rule matching that serial) **claims** it to a site, for example *Leeds / Building 1 / Floor 2*, and picks a template and image.
5. Catalyst Center upgrades the image if needed, pushes the Day-0 configuration, and the switch moves into the Inventory as managed.

If option 43 is missing, the switch tries the DNS name `pnpserver.<domain>` (using the domain name from DHCP), and then the PnP Connect cloud service.

**Worked example — one template, two switches.** A Day-N template written in Velocity:

```
hostname $hostname
interface Vlan$mgmt_vlan
 ip address $mgmt_ip 255.255.255.0
#foreach ($port in [1..24])
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/$port
 switchport access vlan $data_vlan
 switchport voice vlan $voice_vlan
#end
```

Provisioned to two switches with different variable values:

| Variable | LEEDS-AS-01 | YORK-AS-01 |
|----------|-------------|------------|
| `$mgmt_vlan` / `$mgmt_ip` | 99 / 10.99.1.11 | 99 / 10.99.2.11 |
| `$data_vlan` / `$voice_vlan` | 10 / 110 | 20 / 120 |

Each switch gets 24 identically structured port configurations; only the numbers differ. Nobody types 48 interface blocks by hand, so nobody mistypes one.

**Why do PnP and templates together matter so much?** Because the costliest part of rolling out 300 branch switches isn't buying them. It's the engineer time spent consoling into each one, and the configuration errors that slip in. With PnP and templates, a non-technical person at the site plugs the switch in, and it gets exactly the same validated configuration as every other site.

### Assurance — Prove It Works

Catalyst Center continuously collects telemetry — **streaming telemetry**, **SNMP**, **syslog**, **NetFlow**, wireless data from controllers and APs, and data from ISE and other integrations — and correlates it into **health scores** and **issues**.

| Health score | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| **8–10** | Good |
| **4–7** | Fair |
| **1–3** | Poor |
| — | No data (shown grey, not scored) |

- **Device health** combines KPIs such as CPU, memory, interface errors, reachability and (for APs) radio utilization and interference.
- **Client health** combines onboarding (association, authentication, DHCP) and connectivity (RSSI, SNR, data rate) for each wired and wireless client.
- **Network health** is the **percentage of devices that are healthy** (score 8–10) — overall and per site and category. *Example:* the York site has 20 devices; 18 score 8–10, one scores 6 (high CPU) and one scores 2 (unreachable uplink). Network health for York is 18 ÷ 20 = **90%**, and the two unhealthy devices appear as issues you can click into.
- **Application health** uses NBAR/AVC data: throughput, latency, packet loss and jitter per application.

**Issues** are detected problems with context: *what* happened, *where*, *when*, the impact (how many clients), and **suggested actions** (often a guided set of checks that Catalyst Center can run for you).

**Tools inside Assurance:**

- **Path Trace** — pick a source and destination, and Catalyst Center computes the hop-by-hop path from its knowledge of the topology, routing and configuration, including ACLs that would block the flow.
- **Intelligent Capture** — packet-level and RF data for a specific wireless client, captured by the AP.
- **Sensor tests** — dedicated sensors (or APs in sensor mode) that act as synthetic clients, testing onboarding, DNS, DHCP, web access and more, on a schedule.
- **Time travel** — scroll health back in time to see the state *when the user complained*, not just now.

**Why is "time travel" so valuable?** Because most user complaints arrive after the fact: "the Wi-Fi was terrible during the 10 o'clock meeting". With traditional tools you'd see a healthy network at 2 p.m. and close the ticket. With stored, correlated history you can look at that client, AP and moment directly. *Assurance turns "can't reproduce" into evidence.*

### Platform — Talk to Everything Else

The **Intent API** (northbound REST) exposes most of Catalyst Center's functions, so scripts, ITSM tools (e.g. ServiceNow) and orchestrators can drive and query it. Event notifications can be pushed out by webhook, email or syslog. Chapter 20 covers the API and its response codes.

---

### How Catalyst Center Talks to Devices (Southbound)

Intent is turned into device changes, and telemetry collected, over ordinary management protocols:

| Protocol | Used for |
|----------|----------|
| **SSH / CLI** | Pushing configuration (templates, provisioning) and running show commands for inventory and compliance. The workhorse |
| **NETCONF** (SSH, port 830) | Model-driven configuration on IOS XE devices that support it (Chapter 20) |
| **SNMP** | Polling device status and counters for inventory and assurance; receiving traps |
| **Syslog, NetFlow, streaming telemetry** | Event and flow data feeding Assurance |
| **HTTPS / RESTCONF and controller APIs** | Talking to wireless controllers, ISE (pxGrid/ERS) and other integrated systems |

*Northbound, Catalyst Center offers the Intent API (REST) to your scripts (Chapter 20). Southbound, it is still mostly SSH and SNMP to the devices, which is why device credentials and reachability are the first things to check when provisioning fails.*

**📝 Exam-style questions — 16.2**

**Q1.** A Catalyst Center discovery finds several switches but marks them "Authentication failed". What is the most likely cause?

- **A.** The CLI credentials or SNMP community in the discovery job don't match the devices, or an SNMP ACL on the devices doesn't permit Catalyst Center.
- **B.** The switches have no DHCP option 43 configured.
- **C.** The switches aren't running the golden image.
- **D.** The switches haven't been claimed in the PnP workflow.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Discovery is SSH and SNMP underneath; Catalyst Center manages a device only as well as it can log in to it. **Why not the others:** B and D are about Plug and Play for *new* devices, not discovering existing ones. C is a SWIM compliance issue, not a login failure.
</details>

**Q2.** Refer to the exhibit. A new switch with no startup configuration gets a DHCP lease from this pool. What does it do next?

```
ip dhcp pool PNP-VLAN99
 network 10.99.0.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 10.99.0.1
 option 43 ascii "5A1N;B2;K4;I10.10.10.50;J80"
```

- **A.** Downloads a configuration file from TFTP server 10.10.10.50
- **B.** Contacts Catalyst Center at 10.99.0.1 over HTTPS on port 443
- **C.** Contacts Catalyst Center at 10.10.10.50 over HTTP on port 80 and appears as an Unclaimed device, identified by its serial number
- **D.** Looks up `pnpserver.<domain>` in DNS, because option 43 is ignored when a default router is set

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** In the option 43 string, `B2` = an IPv4 server address, `K4` = HTTP, `I10.10.10.50` = the server and `J80` = port 80. The device then waits to be claimed to a site. **Why not the others:** A is wrong because PnP talks to Catalyst Center over HTTP(S), not TFTP. B uses the default gateway's address and the wrong protocol and port. D is wrong because the DNS lookup is the fallback used only when option 43 is missing.
</details>

**Q3.** Which two methods can a new device use to find Catalyst Center through Plug and Play? (Choose two.)

- **A.** An SNMP trap from Catalyst Center
- **B.** DHCP option 43
- **C.** A CDP announcement from its neighbour
- **D.** A NETCONF hello from Catalyst Center
- **E.** A DNS lookup of `pnpserver.<domain>`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B, E.** The third method is a redirect from Cisco's cloud PnP Connect service. **Why not the others:** A and D are things Catalyst Center does with devices it already manages. C is something Catalyst Center's *discovery* can use to crawl an existing network, not how a new device finds the controller.
</details>

**Q4.** A site has 25 devices: 20 have a health score of 8–10, 3 score 4–7 and 2 score 1–3. What network health does Catalyst Center show for the site?

- **A.** 92%
- **B.** 8 out of 10
- **C.** 88%
- **D.** 80%

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** Network health is the percentage of devices that are healthy, meaning a score of 8–10: 20 ÷ 25 = 80%. **Why not the others:** A counts the "fair" devices as healthy (23 ÷ 25). B treats network health as an average score, which it isn't. C doesn't match any correct calculation.
</details>

## 16.3 AI-Powered Workflows

The v1.2 blueprint specifically asks about **AI-powered workflows**. The core idea: the network already produces vastly more telemetry than people can read, so machine learning and reasoning engines turn that data into **baselines, anomalies, root causes and natural-language answers**.

### AI Network Analytics — Learned Baselines and Anomaly Detection

A traditional alert uses a **static threshold**: "alert when DHCP response time > 500 ms". That threshold is always wrong somewhere. Too low for a busy Monday morning at headquarters, too high for a quiet branch.

**AI Network Analytics** sends anonymized telemetry to Cisco's cloud ML service, which learns a **dynamic baseline** for *your* network: what is normal for this KPI, at this site, at this time of day and week. Then it:

- **Detects anomalies** — deviations from the learned normal (for example, onboarding failures at one site far above what's usual for a Tuesday at 9 a.m.), rather than crossings of a fixed line.
- **Peer comparison** — compares a site or AP with similar ones ("this building's roaming times are worse than your other buildings").
- **Trends and insights** — longer-term patterns, such as recurring interference or growing capacity pressure.

**Story Time 📖:** a static threshold is a doctor who flags every patient with a resting heart rate above 90. A baseline is your own doctor, who knows your normal is 55, so a reading of 80 is worth a look for you, while 85 is normal for someone else. Same number, different meaning, because "normal" depends on who and when.

**Why do learned baselines beat static thresholds?** A static threshold produces two kinds of noise: *false alarms* where "high" is normal, and *missed problems* where a large deviation still sits below the line. A baseline asks "is this unusual **here and now**?", which is the question an experienced engineer actually asks. *It cuts alert fatigue while catching subtle problems earlier.*

### Machine Reasoning Engine (MRE) — Automated Root-Cause Analysis

The **Machine Reasoning Engine** encodes troubleshooting knowledge from Cisco experts (TAC, engineering) as **reasoning workflows**. Given an issue, it gathers the relevant data from devices (configs, `show` output, state) and works through the logical steps an expert would, to reach a **root cause and a recommended fix**.

Typical uses include:

- **Network Reasoner** tools — guided checks such as diagnosing high CPU, an interface that is down, or a failed ping between devices.
- **Security advisories** — checking whether a published Cisco PSIRT vulnerability actually applies to each device's *configuration*, not just its software version.
- **Compliance and best-practice checks** across the network.

**Why "reasoning" rather than ML?** Because many problems have a *known* logical diagnosis ("BGP is down → is the neighbor reachable? → are the AS numbers right? → is there an ACL on TCP 179?"). Learning that from data would be pointless when experts can write it down. MRE automates **known expertise**; ML finds **unknown patterns**. Catalyst Center uses both.

### AI Endpoint Analytics

Identifies and classifies endpoints (IP phones, cameras, medical devices, printers, IoT) using deep packet inspection, network probes and ML clustering. It suggests labels for unknown devices so they can be placed in the correct **group** for policy (14.7, with ISE).

### Natural-Language Operations — the AI Assistant

Cisco has added a generative-AI **AI Assistant** to Catalyst Center and other management platforms. Operators can ask questions in plain language ("which sites had the most client onboarding failures this week?", "why is this AP unhealthy?") and receive summarized answers, explanations of issues and suggested next steps. Cisco has also introduced **AI Canvas**, a collaborative workspace in which AI agents help with troubleshooting across Cisco's platforms ("AgenticOps"). Availability, scope and licensing vary by release.

**What's different from traditional workflows?** The engineer no longer needs to know *which page or command* holds the answer. They state the question, and the system finds and correlates the data. The engineer's judgement still matters: AI output is a starting point that must be verified, especially before any change is made.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 16.3**

**Q1.** Why does AI Network Analytics use a learned baseline instead of a static threshold such as "alert when DHCP response time is over 500 ms"?

- **A.** A static threshold can't be configured in Catalyst Center.
- **B.** Baselines need no telemetry, so they work on unmanaged devices.
- **C.** What's normal differs by site and by time of day and week, so a fixed threshold raises false alarms in some places and misses real problems in others.
- **D.** Baselines are calculated on each switch, so no data leaves the device.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** A baseline asks "is this unusual here and now?", which cuts alert fatigue and catches subtle deviations. **Why not the others:** A is false. B is backwards; baselines are learned *from* telemetry. D is wrong because AI Network Analytics sends anonymized telemetry to Cisco's cloud ML service.
</details>

**Q2.** What is the key difference between the Machine Reasoning Engine (MRE) and AI Network Analytics?

- **A.** MRE automates *known* expert troubleshooting logic (for example, checking whether a PSIRT advisory applies to a device's configuration), while AI Network Analytics finds *unknown* patterns in telemetry.
- **B.** MRE is a natural-language chat interface, while AI Network Analytics classifies endpoints.
- **C.** MRE needs no device data, while AI Network Analytics logs in to devices.
- **D.** They are two names for the same cloud ML service.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Many problems have a known logical diagnosis that experts can write down; learning it from data would be pointless. **Why not the others:** B describes the AI Assistant and AI Endpoint Analytics. C is wrong because MRE gathers configs, `show` output and state from devices. D is wrong; Catalyst Center deliberately uses both approaches.
</details>

**Q3.** Which Catalyst Center feature suggests labels for unknown devices on the network, such as cameras or medical devices, so they can be placed in the correct group for policy?

- **A.** Path Trace
- **B.** AI Endpoint Analytics
- **C.** SWIM
- **D.** Intelligent Capture

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** It classifies endpoints using deep packet inspection, network probes and ML clustering, feeding group-based policy with ISE. **Why not the others:** A computes the hop-by-hop path between two endpoints. C manages software images. D captures packet and RF data for one wireless client.
</details>

## 16.4 Traditional vs AI-Powered — Same Problem, Two Workflows

**Scenario:** users at the Leeds office report that Wi-Fi "keeps dropping" every morning.

| Step | Traditional workflow | AI-powered Catalyst Center workflow |
|------|----------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Detect | Wait for complaints | **AI baseline** flags abnormal disconnects at that site at 08:30–09:30, before most tickets arrive |
| Scope | Ask users which floor; check WLC logs | **Issue** lists the affected clients, APs and floor; client health over time |
| Correlate | Compare syslog times with RF graphs by hand | Peer comparison shows only this building; insights show co-channel interference rising at the same times |
| Root cause | Engineer's experience, maybe a site visit | Guided checks / **MRE** reasoning plus RF data point to channel planning on two APs |
| Fix | Change channels on the WLC by hand | Apply an RF profile change in **Design**, provision it to the site |
| Verify | Wait for complaints to stop | Assurance shows client health back to 8–10 the next morning (**time travel** to compare) |

*The point:* the network and the engineer haven't changed. What's changed is how quickly the evidence is assembled, and that the system can see a problem *before* users report it.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 16.4**

**Q1.** A user reports that the Wi-Fi was poor during a meeting three hours ago, but everything looks healthy now. Which Assurance capability lets you see the client's and AP's state at the time of the complaint?

- **A.** Path Trace
- **B.** Time travel
- **C.** Sensor tests
- **D.** SWIM post-checks

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** Stored, correlated history lets you look at that client, AP and moment directly, turning "can't reproduce" into evidence. **Why not the others:** A shows the current path between two endpoints. C runs synthetic tests from now on; it can't look back. D checks devices after a software upgrade.
</details>

**Q2.** Users at one office report that Wi-Fi "keeps dropping" every morning between 08:30 and 09:30. With AI-powered Assurance, what lets Catalyst Center notice these morning disconnects before most users open tickets?

- **A.** An AI baseline that flags disconnects far above what is normal for that site at that time
- **B.** A static SNMP trap threshold on the WLC
- **C.** A Velocity template pushed to every AP
- **D.** The PnP Connect cloud service

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** The anomaly is a deviation from the learned normal for that site and time, so it shows up without anyone complaining. **Why not the others:** B is the traditional static-threshold approach the scenario contrasts with. C pushes configuration; it doesn't detect anything. D is for onboarding new devices.
</details>

## 16.5 Exam-Ready Summary

| Term | One-line meaning |
|------|------------------|
| **Catalyst Center** | Cisco's enterprise controller (formerly DNA Center); management plane for SD-Access and traditional networks |
| **Design / Policy / Provision / Assurance** | The four lifecycle workflows: describe the network, define access/QoS policy, push it, prove it works |
| **PnP** | Zero-touch onboarding via DHCP option 43, DNS `pnpserver`, or PnP Connect |
| **Templates** | Velocity/Jinja2 configuration with variables, applied consistently |
| **SWIM** | Golden images, automated distribution and activation with pre/post checks |
| **Health score** | 1–10 per device/client/application; 8–10 good, 4–7 fair, 1–3 poor |
| **Path Trace** | Computed hop-by-hop path between two endpoints, including ACL checks |
| **AI Network Analytics** | Cloud ML — learned baselines, anomaly detection, peer comparison, trends |
| **Machine Reasoning Engine** | Expert knowledge encoded as automated root-cause workflows |
| **AI Endpoint Analytics** | ML-assisted endpoint classification for group policy |
| **AI Assistant** | Natural-language questions and guided answers about the network |
| **Intent API** | Northbound REST API (Chapter 20) |
