<a name="chapter-17"></a>
# Chapter 17: Device Access Control, AAA, ACLs & CoPP

> **Blueprint:** ENCOR 5.1.a — Lines and local user authentication; ENCOR 5.1.b — Authentication and authorization using AAA; ENCOR 5.2.a — ACLs; ENCOR 5.2.b — CoPP

At CCNA you learned that a router should have passwords, that AAA has three A's, and that ACLs filter traffic (CCNA guide 18.4, Chapter 19). At CCNP the question changes from *"what is it?"* to *"how do I lock down a device so that the right people get exactly the right access, it keeps working when the AAA server dies, and nobody can knock it over by flooding its CPU?"* This chapter builds that answer in four layers: **the lines** you log in through, **who you are** (local users and AAA), **what traffic is allowed through** the box (ACLs), and **what traffic is allowed to the box's own brain** (CoPP).

**Chapter 31** takes the same features into troubleshooting depth for ENARSI. Here we build them correctly.

---

## 17.1 The Doors Into a Device — Console, AUX and VTY Lines

**The problem:** a router's CLI can change everything the network does. So the first security question is *how can someone even reach a command prompt?* If any of those paths is left open, every other control in this chapter can be walked around.

Every Cisco device has **lines**: the doors an administrator can walk through to get a CLI (Command-Line Interface).

| Line | What it is | Typical numbering | Reach |
|------|------------|-------------------|-------|
| **Console** (`line con 0`) | Physical serial/USB port on the device | Exactly one | You must be standing there (or on a terminal server) |
| **AUX** (`line aux 0`) | Auxiliary serial port, historically for a modem | One (many platforms no longer have it) | Out-of-band dial-in |
| **VTY** (`line vty 0 4`, `0 15`, …) | Virtual terminals for Telnet/SSH sessions | 5 or 16+ — one per simultaneous remote session | Anywhere with IP reachability |

**Why are VTYs numbered as a range?** Because each one is a *slot* for one remote session. `line vty 0 4` is five slots, so five admins can be connected at once; a sixth is refused. Newer IOS XE images have `vty 0 15` or more. **The trap:** if you configure `line vty 0 4` but the device also has `line vty 5 15`, those extra eleven lines keep their *old* settings — possibly Telnet with a weak password. *Always check `show running-config | section line vty` to see every VTY block, not just the first one.*

### Hardening the lines

```
R1(config)# line con 0
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 10 0          ! log out an idle session after 10 min 0 s
R1(config-line)# logging synchronous        ! stop log messages chopping your typing
R1(config-line)# login local                ! authenticate against the local user database
!
R1(config)# line aux 0
R1(config-line)# transport input none       ! nothing can open a session through AUX
R1(config-line)# no exec                    ! and no EXEC shell even if something connects
!
R1(config)# ip access-list standard MGMT-HOSTS
R1(config-std-nacl)# permit 10.99.0.0 0.0.0.255   ! the management subnet only
!
R1(config)# line vty 0 15
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh        ! SSH only — Telnet sends passwords in clear text
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 10 0
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# access-class MGMT-HOSTS in ! only these sources may even attempt to log in
```

**Why `access-class` rather than an ACL on an interface?** Because the VTY is the thing you want to protect, no matter which interface the session arrives on. An interface ACL protects one door in the building; `access-class` protects the room itself. A router with ten interfaces and a loopback would need the same entry on all eleven; `access-class` does it once. *Note that `access-class ... in` checks the **source** of incoming sessions, and `access-class ... out` restricts where a user may connect to **from** the router (via `telnet`/`ssh` out of it).* If management sessions arrive in a VRF, add `vrf-also` (`access-class MGMT-HOSTS in vrf-also`), or the ACL silently doesn't apply to them.

**How an SSH login meets this config, step by step:**

1. A TCP connection arrives for port 22 on any of R1's addresses.
2. R1 picks a **free VTY** line (0–15). If all 16 are busy, the connection is refused.
3. `transport input ssh` is checked: SSH is allowed on this line (a Telnet attempt to port 23 would be refused here).
4. `access-class MGMT-HOSTS in` is checked against the **source** IP. Not permitted → the connection is closed before any login prompt appears.
5. `login local` asks for a username and password and checks them against the `username` lines.
6. The session starts. If it sits idle for 10 minutes (`exec-timeout 10 0`), R1 logs it out and frees the line.

**Worked example.** Two people try to SSH to R1:

| Source | Step 4 (`access-class`) | Step 5 (`login local`) | Result |
|--------|-------------------------|------------------------|--------|
| 10.99.0.15 (management PC) | permitted by `10.99.0.0 0.0.0.255` | `admin` + correct password | Logged in |
| 198.51.100.7 (internet) | no match → implicit deny | never reached | Connection closed; the attacker never even sees a `Username:` prompt to guess against |

**Why `exec-timeout` matters for security, not just tidiness.** An abandoned privileged session on a console is a logged-in root shell for whoever walks past next. `exec-timeout 0 0` (never time out) is a lab convenience you should never see in production.

### Three ways a line can authenticate (before AAA)

Without AAA, each line decides for itself how to check who you are. There are exactly three options, and the exam expects you to read them:

```
R1(config)# line con 0
R1(config-line)# password C0ns0le-Pw     ! the line has its own password...
R1(config-line)# login                   ! ...and "login" says "ask for it"
!
R1(config)# line vty 0 15
R1(config-line)# login local             ! ask for a username + password from "username" lines
!
R1(config)# line aux 0
R1(config-line)# no login                ! no prompt at all — whoever connects gets a shell
```

| Line config | Prompt you see | Checked against |
|-------------|----------------|-----------------|
| `password X` + `login` | `Password:` only | The line's own password |
| `login local` | `Username:` then `Password:` | The local `username ... secret` database |
| `no login` | Nothing | Nobody — open door |

**The two traps.** First, `login` **without** a `password` on a VTY line refuses every session with *"Password required, but none set"*. VTYs (unlike the console) won't let you in with no password configured. Second, `login local` with **no** `username` lines locks everyone out, because there is nothing to match. *`password` is a shared secret per door; `login local` is per-person identity, which is what accounting and audit need.*

**Landing straight in privileged mode.** By default a line session starts at level 1 (`R1>`). `privilege level 15` under a line drops everyone who logs in through that line straight into `R1#`:

```
R1(config)# line con 0
R1(config-line)# privilege level 15      ! console users start at level 15
```

It's convenient on a console in a locked room, and dangerous on VTYs with a shared line password, because then knowing one password means full control. With `login local`, the **user's** privilege (`username X privilege N`) decides the level instead.

### SSH prerequisites (recap from CCNA guide 6.6, with the CCNP extras)

```
R1(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# ip domain name corp.example
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 3072   ! RSA keys need hostname + domain first
R1(config)# ip ssh version 2
R1(config)# ip ssh time-out 60                     ! seconds to finish logging in
R1(config)# ip ssh authentication-retries 3
R1(config)# login block-for 120 attempts 5 within 60  ! brute-force brake (see below)
```

`login block-for 120 attempts 5 within 60` means: *if 5 logins fail within 60 seconds, refuse all logins for 120 seconds* ("quiet mode"). Pair it with `login quiet-mode access-class MGMT-HOSTS` so your management subnet can still get in while the device is shrugging off an attack.

**Worked example.** A password-guessing script hits R1. Its 1st to 5th wrong guesses arrive at 10:00:02, :09, :15, :21 and :30, all inside one 60-second window. On the 5th failure R1 logs `%SEC_LOGIN-1-QUIET_MODE_ON` and refuses every login for 120 seconds, until 10:02:30. The script now gets about 5 guesses every two minutes or so instead of hundreds per minute. Meanwhile an admin at 10.99.0.15 can still log in, because the quiet-mode ACL exempts the management subnet. `show login` displays the current state and the blocked time remaining.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 17.1**

**Q1.** Refer to the exhibit. A security audit finds Telnet sessions to SW1 from outside the management subnet. Why?

```
line vty 0 4
 transport input ssh
 access-class MGMT-HOSTS in
 login local
line vty 5 15
 transport input telnet
 password Cisco123
 login
```

- **A.** `access-class` filters only Telnet sessions, not SSH
- **B.** Lines 5–15 keep their own older settings, so sessions that land on them can use Telnet with no source restriction
- **C.** `transport input ssh` takes effect only after `ip ssh version 2` is configured
- **D.** VTY ACLs apply only to the first five lines by design

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** Each VTY range has its own settings. Hardening `vty 0 4` does nothing for `vty 5 15`, which still accepts Telnet with a shared password and has no `access-class`. That's why you check every VTY block with `show running-config | section line vty`. **Why not the others:** A, `access-class` filters sessions by source address whatever the protocol. C, `transport input ssh` is effective as soon as it's configured. D, an `access-class` applies to every line it's configured on; here it simply isn't configured on 5–15.
</details>

**Q2.** Only hosts in 10.99.0.0/24 may open management sessions to R1, which has ten interfaces and a loopback, all reachable. What is the most efficient way to enforce this?

- **A.** Apply an extended ACL inbound on all eleven interfaces
- **B.** Configure `ip access-group MGMT-HOSTS in` under `line vty 0 15`
- **C.** Configure `access-class MGMT-HOSTS in` under `line vty 0 15`
- **D.** Configure `access-class MGMT-HOSTS out` under `line vty 0 15`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** `access-class ... in` protects the VTY lines themselves, so it applies to sessions arriving through any interface, configured once. **Why not the others:** A works but needs the same entry on eleven interfaces, and it's easy to miss one. B, `ip access-group` is an interface command, not a line command. D, `access-class ... out` controls where a user may connect **to** from the router, not who may connect in.
</details>

**Q3.** Refer to the exhibit. No `password` is configured under the VTY lines. What happens when an administrator opens a Telnet session to R1?

```
line vty 0 15
 transport input telnet
 login
```

- **A.** The session is refused with "Password required, but none set"
- **B.** The administrator gets a level 1 shell with no prompt
- **C.** The administrator is asked for a username from the local database
- **D.** The administrator lands in privileged EXEC mode

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** `login` means "check the line's own password". On a VTY with no password set, IOS refuses every session rather than letting people in. **Why not the others:** B describes `no login`, the open door. C describes `login local`. D would need `privilege level 15` on the line, and the session never gets that far.
</details>

**Q4.** R1 has `login block-for 120 attempts 5 within 60` and `login quiet-mode access-class MGMT-HOSTS`. A script fails five logins within 30 seconds. What happens next?

- **A.** Only the script's source address is blocked, for 60 seconds
- **B.** The VTY lines are shut down until an administrator clears them
- **C.** All logins, including those from the management subnet, are refused for 120 seconds
- **D.** All logins are refused for 120 seconds, except from sources permitted by MGMT-HOSTS

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** Five failures inside 60 seconds trigger quiet mode, which refuses all logins for 120 seconds. The quiet-mode access-class exempts the management subnet, so administrators can still get in during the attack. **Why not the others:** A, quiet mode blocks everyone not exempted, not just the attacker, and it lasts 120 s (the 60 s is the window for counting failures). B, quiet mode ends by itself. C ignores the exemption that `login quiet-mode access-class` provides.
</details>

---

## 17.2 Local Users, Privilege Levels and Password Hashes

**The problem:** not everyone who logs in should be able to do everything. A NOC (Network Operations Centre) operator who watches interfaces shouldn't be able to erase the config. And the passwords themselves sit in the config file, which gets backed up, emailed and pasted into tickets, so how they're stored matters as much as how strong they are.

**Story Time 📖:** Privilege levels are the floors of an office building with a keycard lift. Level 1 is the lobby: you can look around (`show` a few things) but not touch anything. Level 15 is the top floor with every key. Levels 2–14 are empty floors you can fit out yourself, moving chosen commands onto them, then giving someone a card that stops at floor 5.

### Privilege levels

IOS has **16 privilege levels, 0–15**:

| Level | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| **0** | Almost nothing — `logout`, `enable`, `disable`, `help`, `exit` |
| **1** | User EXEC (`R1>`) — the default after login |
| **2–14** | Unused by default — you can move commands into them |
| **15** | Privileged EXEC (`R1#`) — everything |

```
R1(config)# username noc privilege 5 algorithm-type scrypt secret N0c-Viewer!
R1(config)# privilege exec level 5 show running-config   ! level 5 may RUN the command...
R1(config)# username admin privilege 15 algorithm-type scrypt secret Adm1n-Str0ng!
```

A user created at `privilege 15` lands straight in `R1#` on login. A level-5 user gets `R1#` too (any level above 1 shows `#`) but can only run commands assigned to levels 0–5. Check where you are with `show privilege`.

**Worked example — the `noc` user's session** (with the config above and `login local` on the VTYs):

```
R1# show privilege
Current privilege level is 5
R1# show running-config               ! allowed: moved to level 5 above
R1# configure terminal
              ^
% Invalid input detected at '^' marker.   ! level 15 command - not on this user's floor
R1# reload
% Unknown command or computer name, or unable to find computer address
```

IOS doesn't say "access denied". Commands above your level behave as if they **don't exist**, which is why the error is `Invalid input`, or, for a single unknown word like `reload`, `Unknown command or computer name` (IOS tries an unknown single word as a host name to Telnet to; with `ip domain-lookup` on, you first see a `Translating "reload"` delay). How it decides: every command has a level (most `show` commands are 1, `configure terminal` and `reload` are 15). You may run a command only if its level is **less than or equal to** your current level.

> **Exam trap — the near-empty running config.** Moving `show running-config` to level 5 lets the NOC user *run* it, but below level 15 the output only includes the commands that user is **allowed to configure**. A level-5 user with no configuration commands sees little more than the `version` line, `end`, and a few headers. It's a classic "why can't my NOC see the config?" question. The fixes: assign `show running-config view full` to the level (the `view full` option shows the whole config regardless of the user's level), or grant `file privilege 5` so a level-5 user can read the config as a file with `more system:running-config`. With AAA, command authorization (17.4) is the cleaner answer.

**Separate enable passwords per level.** `enable secret` can be set per level, and `enable N` asks for that level's password:

```
R1(config)# enable algorithm-type scrypt secret level 5 Lvl5-Pw!   ! the level-5 enable secret
R1> enable 5                 ! prompts for the level-5 secret; lands at level 5
R1# show privilege
Current privilege level is 5
```

Plain `enable` with no number means `enable 15`. This is how small shops gave a NOC "a bit more than user mode" before AAA, and it still shows up in exam exhibits.

**Why do local custom privilege levels fall out of favour at scale?** Because they're per-device. Maintaining `privilege exec level 5 ...` lines identically on 800 switches is exactly the problem AAA command authorization (17.4) solves centrally. *Local levels are a fine fallback; they are a poor primary policy.*

### Password types — what the number in the config means

When you view the config, every password carries a **type** number that tells you how it's stored:

| Type | How it's stored | Command that produces it | Verdict |
|------|-----------------|--------------------------|---------|
| **0** | Clear text | `password X` (no service password-encryption) | Never |
| **7** | Vigenère-style reversible encoding | `service password-encryption` | Hides from shoulder-surfers only — reversible in seconds |
| **4** | SHA-256, but **unsalted with a single iteration** (a flawed implementation) | Old `enable secret` on some 15.x releases | Deprecated and removed — weaker than type 5 |
| **5** | MD5 hash (salted) | `secret X` on older IOS | Deprecated — too fast to brute-force |
| **8** | PBKDF2 with SHA-256 | `algorithm-type sha256 secret X` | Good |
| **9** | scrypt | `algorithm-type scrypt secret X` | Best — memory-hard |

```
R1(config)# enable algorithm-type scrypt secret En4ble-Str0ng!
R1# show running-config | include secret
enable secret 9 $9$nhEmQVczB7dqsO$X.HsgL6x1il0RxkOSSvyQYwucySCt7qFm4v7pqCxkKM
username admin privilege 15 secret 9 $9$7Mbz3XS/W/tKpe$ue8JC8/kk4lCSUbsZB3CKS5U7PmzKX...
```

**Why is a hash (types 5/8/9) fundamentally different from type 7?** Type 7 is *encoding*: the device has to turn it back into the original to use it, so anyone with the algorithm (it's public) can too. A hash is one-way: the device never needs the original. At login it hashes what you typed and compares hashes. To "crack" a hash an attacker has to guess passwords and hash every guess. **Why is scrypt (type 9) better than MD5 (type 5) when both are one-way?** Because cracking is a speed race. MD5 was designed to be *fast*, so a GPU can try billions of guesses per second. scrypt is deliberately *slow and memory-hungry*, so every guess costs real RAM, which makes massively parallel GPU cracking expensive. *The goal of a password hash is to be slow on purpose.*

**How a type 9 login check works, step by step:** you type `Adm1n-Str0ng!` → the router takes the **salt** stored in the config (the random characters between `$9$` and the next `$`) → it runs scrypt over salt + what you typed → it compares the result with the stored hash → equal means correct. The original password is never stored and never recovered. The salt means two users with the same password get different hashes, so an attacker can't crack one and recognise the other.

**Story Time 📖:** Type 7 is a note written in a simple code that comes with its own decoder ring, and everyone owns a copy of the ring. A hash is a fingerprint: you can check whether a finger matches it, but you can't grow a finger from the print. MD5 lets an attacker test billions of fingers a second; scrypt makes each test slow and expensive.

> **Exam trap:** `enable password` and `enable secret` can both exist; if they do, **`enable secret` wins** and `enable password` is ignored. And `service password-encryption` does **not** touch `secret` values. It only converts type 0 to type 7.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 17.2**

**Q1.** Refer to the exhibit. User `noc` can run `show running-config` but sees little more than the `version` line and `end`. What explains this, and what fixes it?

```
username noc privilege 5 algorithm-type scrypt secret N0c-Viewer!
privilege exec level 5 show running-config
```

- **A.** Level 5 users can't run any `show` commands; move the user to level 15
- **B.** `privilege exec` must name level 15 for `show` commands; change it to `level 15`
- **C.** Below level 15, `show running-config` shows only the commands the user may configure; assign `show running-config view full` to level 5
- **D.** `service password-encryption` hides the configuration from lower levels; disable it

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Moving the command to level 5 lets `noc` run it, but the output is filtered to commands that user is allowed to configure, which is almost none. `show running-config view full` displays the whole config regardless of level (granting `file privilege 5` is another option). **Why not the others:** A, level 5 can run any command assigned to levels 0–5, including this one. B, setting the command to level 15 would stop `noc` running it at all. D, password encryption only changes how passwords are stored.
</details>

**Q2.** A configuration backup was pasted into a public ticket. Which line should be treated as the most urgent to change?

- **A.** `username admin privilege 15 secret 9 $9$nhEmQVczB7dqsO$X.HsgL6x1il0RxkO...`
- **B.** `enable secret 9 $9$7Mbz3XS/W/tKpe$ue8JC8/kk4lCSUbsZB3...`
- **C.** `username ops privilege 15 secret 8 $8$dsYGNam3K1SIJO$7nv/35M/qr6t.dVc...`
- **D.** `username noc privilege 5 password 7 0822455D0A16`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** Type 7 is reversible encoding with a public algorithm, so anyone with the backup can recover that password in seconds. **Why not the others:** A and B are type 9 (scrypt) and C is type 8 (PBKDF2-SHA-256). All three are salted one-way hashes, so an attacker can only guess and test, which these algorithms make slow. They should still be rotated, but they aren't readable.
</details>

**Q3.** R1 has `enable password Cisco123` and an `enable secret` set to a different password. An administrator types `enable` and enters `Cisco123`. What happens?

- **A.** It is accepted, because `enable password` is checked first
- **B.** It is rejected, because `enable secret` takes precedence and `enable password` is ignored
- **C.** It is accepted only if `service password-encryption` is enabled
- **D.** It is accepted, because either password is valid

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** When both exist, only the `enable secret` is used. The old `enable password` is ignored, so typing it fails. **Why not the others:** A and D, IOS never falls back to `enable password` while a secret exists. C, `service password-encryption` only turns type 0 passwords into type 7; it doesn't change which password is checked.
</details>

**Q4.** Why is a type 9 (scrypt) secret stronger than a type 5 (MD5) secret, when both are one-way hashes?

- **A.** scrypt is deliberately slow and memory-hungry, so each guess costs an attacker far more than an MD5 guess
- **B.** scrypt can be decrypted by the router, which allows password recovery
- **C.** MD5 hashes are reversible, like type 7
- **D.** scrypt hashes are unsalted, so they are shorter and harder to steal

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Cracking a hash means guessing and hashing every guess. MD5 was built to be fast, so GPUs can test billions of guesses per second; scrypt makes every guess use real time and memory, which makes mass guessing expensive. **Why not the others:** B, neither type can be decrypted; the router compares hashes at login. C, MD5 is one-way; type 7 is the reversible one. D, type 9 is salted, which is what stops two identical passwords producing the same hash.
</details>

---

## 17.3 AAA — Turning It On and Building Method Lists

**The problem AAA solves:** local usernames live on each device. With 800 switches, adding a new engineer means 800 config changes, and removing one who leaves means 800 more, and the one you miss is a back door. **AAA** (Authentication, Authorization and Accounting) moves the decision to a central server, usually **Cisco ISE** (Identity Services Engine), so you change a person's access once and every device obeys.

- **Authentication** — *who are you?* (username and password, checked centrally)
- **Authorization** — *what may you do?* (privilege level, allowed commands)
- **Accounting** — *what did you do?* (a record of sessions and commands)

**Story Time 📖:** The router is a nightclub bouncer, and the AAA server is head office. When you arrive, the bouncer phones head office: "Is Jane on the list?" (authentication). Head office says yes, and that she's VIP (authorization: level 15). The bouncer writes in a book "Jane in at 22:04, out at 01:30" (accounting). If the phone line is dead, the bouncer falls back to a short paper list kept at the door (the **local** users). But if head office answers "Jane is banned", the bouncer does *not* then check the paper list. That last rule is ERROR vs FAIL, below, and it's the most-tested idea in this section.

![AAA conversation between an admin, the router and a TACACS+ server](images/c17_aaa_flow.png)

**How a TACACS+ login works, step by step** (admin `jsmith` SSHs to R1, which uses the config built below):

1. jsmith's SSH session reaches a VTY. The VTY uses the `default` login list: `group ADMIN-TACACS local`.
2. R1 opens a **TCP 49** connection from Loopback0 to the first server, ISE-1 (10.99.0.21). The whole TACACS+ payload is encrypted using the shared key.
3. R1 sends an authentication **START** with the username; ISE replies asking for the password (**GETPASS**); R1 relays what jsmith types in a **CONTINUE**.
4. ISE checks its identity store and replies **PASS** (or **FAIL**).
5. On PASS, if exec authorization is configured (17.4), R1 asks "may jsmith have a shell, at what level?" and ISE answers with `priv-lvl=15`.
6. If accounting is configured, R1 sends an accounting **START** record. When jsmith logs out, a **STOP** record follows with the session duration.

### `aaa new-model` changes everything at once

```
R1(config)# aaa new-model
```

The moment you enter this, **line-level `login` and `password` commands stop being used**. Every line that doesn't name its own list (console and VTYs alike) now authenticates through the `default` method list, and if you haven't defined one, the implicit default is **local**. The VTYs are where this bites, because that's where a remote admin is when it happens. *Why does that matter?* Because if you type `aaa new-model` on a remote router that has no local usernames, your next SSH session has nothing to authenticate against. **Always create a local privilege-15 user before `aaa new-model`.** That's the exam-style "locked yourself out" scenario, and in real life it's the one where you drive to the data centre.

### Defining servers and server groups (modern IOS XE syntax)

```
R1(config)# tacacs server ISE-1
R1(config-server-tacacs)# address ipv4 10.99.0.21
R1(config-server-tacacs)# key 0 T@cacsSharedKey
R1(config-server-tacacs)# single-connection          ! reuse one TCP session for many requests
!
R1(config)# tacacs server ISE-2
R1(config-server-tacacs)# address ipv4 10.99.0.22
R1(config-server-tacacs)# key 0 T@cacsSharedKey
!
R1(config)# aaa group server tacacs+ ADMIN-TACACS
R1(config-sg-tacacs+)# server name ISE-1             ! tried first
R1(config-sg-tacacs+)# server name ISE-2             ! tried if ISE-1 does not answer
R1(config-sg-tacacs+)# ip tacacs source-interface Loopback0
!
R1(config)# radius server ISE-R1
R1(config-radius-server)# address ipv4 10.99.0.21 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
R1(config-radius-server)# key 0 R@diusSharedKey
R1(config)# aaa group server radius ACCESS-RADIUS
R1(config-sg-radius)# server name ISE-R1
```

**Why put the source interface on a loopback?** The AAA server only answers devices it has been told about, identified by **source IP**. If the request leaves from whichever physical interface faces the server, a routing change can switch the source IP and the server will silently ignore the device. A loopback never goes down, so the device's identity never moves. *This is the same reason OSPF prefers a loopback for its router ID (CCNA guide 16.7).*

### Method lists — the ordered "how do I check this?" list

A **method list** is a named, ordered list of places to check:

```
R1(config)# aaa authentication login default group ADMIN-TACACS local
R1(config)# aaa authentication login CONSOLE local
R1(config)# aaa authentication enable default group ADMIN-TACACS enable
!
R1(config)# line con 0
R1(config-line)# login authentication CONSOLE      ! console uses the named list
! (VTYs use "default" automatically — no command needed)
```

| Part | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `login` | This list authenticates **logins** (as opposed to `enable`, `dot1x`, `ppp`) |
| `default` | Applied to **every line automatically** unless a line names another list |
| `CONSOLE` | A **named** list — only used where you apply it with `login authentication CONSOLE` |
| `group ADMIN-TACACS local` | Try the TACACS+ group first; then the local user database |

The methods you can put in a list, and what each one checks:

| Method keyword | Checks | Notes |
|----------------|--------|-------|
| `group tacacs+` | Every TACACS+ server defined globally | Generic — all servers, in config order |
| `group radius` | Every RADIUS server defined globally | Generic |
| `group NAME` | Only the servers in that named server group | Preferred: you control membership and order |
| `local` | Local `username` database, username matched **case-insensitively** | Password is always case-sensitive |
| `local-case` | Local database, username **case-sensitive** | `Admin` ≠ `admin` |
| `enable` | The enable secret | Common last resort in `aaa authentication enable` lists |
| `line` | The line's own `password` | Lets old per-line passwords act as a fallback |
| `none` | Nothing — always succeeds | Only as a deliberate last resort (e.g. console of a lab box) |

Methods are tried left to right, up to four, and the ERROR-vs-FAIL rule below decides when the router moves on.

**Why give the console its own `local`-only list?** Because the console is the door you use when the network is broken, and a broken network often means the AAA server is unreachable. If the console tries TACACS+ first, every login waits for timeouts before falling back. Some designs deliberately keep the console independent of the network.

### The rule everyone gets wrong — ERROR vs FAIL

**The next method in the list is tried only when the current one returns an ERROR, never when it returns a FAIL.**

| What the TACACS+ server does | Result | Does the router try `local` next? |
|------------------------------|--------|-----------------------------------|
| Doesn't answer (down, unreachable, wrong key → no valid reply) | **ERROR** | **Yes** |
| Answers "this user/password is wrong" | **FAIL** (reject) | **No** — login denied, list stops |

**Why is it designed this way?** Think about what fallback is *for*: keeping you in when the central server is **unavailable**. If a rejection from the server also fell through to `local`, then any account the security team disabled centrally could still log in with a stale local password. That would turn the backup door into a bypass. *The fallback is for an absent server, never for a server that said no.* This is also why the local fallback account should have a long, vaulted password and be audited: it's the one account that works when ISE is down.

**Worked example — three logins, one method list** (`aaa authentication login default group ADMIN-TACACS local`; local user `admin` exists; ISE-1 and ISE-2 in the group):

| Situation | What R1 does | Result |
|-----------|--------------|--------|
| ISE-1 up; jsmith types the right password | ISE-1 replies PASS | Logged in via TACACS+ |
| ISE-1 up; jsmith types the wrong password | ISE-1 replies FAIL | **Denied.** `local` is never tried |
| ISE-1 and ISE-2 both unreachable (WAN down); `admin` types the local password | ISE-1 times out (5 s default) → ERROR → tries ISE-2 → times out → ERROR → moves on to `local` | Logged in via the local account, after roughly a 10-second wait |
| Both unreachable; jsmith (a TACACS+-only account) tries | Both ERROR → `local` has no `jsmith` | Denied: only accounts that exist locally work during the outage |

The 10-second pause in row 3 is normal and worth expecting: it's the timeout for each server in turn. That's also why the console in the example above uses a `local`-only list.

> **Exam trap:** "The admin's TACACS+ account was disabled but they can still log in using the local account" is **impossible** while the TACACS+ server is reachable. If they can, the server must be unreachable (ERROR), so check reachability, keys and source interface (Chapter 31).

**📝 Exam-style questions — 17.3**

**Q1.** R1 uses `aaa authentication login default group ADMIN-TACACS local`. The TACACS+ server is reachable. User `jdoe` has been disabled on the server but still has a local account on R1, and types the local password. What happens?

- **A.** The server returns ERROR, so R1 tries `local` and `jdoe` logs in
- **B.** R1 tries `local` first because it's faster, and `jdoe` logs in
- **C.** The server returns FAIL, the login is denied, and `local` is never tried
- **D.** The server returns FAIL, so R1 tries `local` and `jdoe` logs in

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** The next method is tried only after an ERROR (no valid answer). A reachable server that rejects the user returns FAIL, which ends the list. Fallback exists for an absent server, never for a server that said no. **Why not the others:** A, a reachable server that answers gives FAIL, not ERROR. B, methods are tried strictly left to right. D is the bypass the ERROR-vs-FAIL rule is designed to prevent.
</details>

**Q2.** An engineer is connected by SSH to a remote router whose VTYs use `password` and `login`. The router has no `username` lines. The engineer enters only `aaa new-model` and logs out. What happens on the next SSH login?

- **A.** It still uses the line password, because no method list is defined
- **B.** It fails: the VTYs now use the `default` list, which with nothing defined means `local`, and no local users exist
- **C.** It succeeds with no password, because no method is defined
- **D.** It uses the enable secret instead

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** `aaa new-model` stops line `login`/`password` being used. With no `default` list defined, the implicit default is `local`, and with no usernames there's nothing to match, so the engineer is locked out. Always create a local privilege-15 user first. **Why not the others:** A, line passwords stop being used the moment AAA is enabled. C, an undefined list falls back to local, not to "allow". D, the enable secret only applies to `enable`, unless a list names the `enable` method.
</details>

**Q3.** The console must stay usable when every AAA server is unreachable, without waiting for server timeouts. Which configuration achieves this?

- **A.** `aaa authentication login default group ADMIN-TACACS local`
- **B.** `aaa authentication login CONSOLE group ADMIN-TACACS none`, applied to `line con 0`
- **C.** `aaa authentication login default none`
- **D.** `aaa authentication login CONSOLE local`, applied with `login authentication CONSOLE` under `line con 0`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** A named `local`-only list on the console never contacts a server, so it never waits for timeouts. **Why not the others:** A is the VTY list: the console would wait for every server to time out before falling back. B still waits for the servers, and `none` lets anyone in when they're down. C makes every line an open door.
</details>

**Q4.** After a routing change, TACACS+ logins to R1 fail, and the TACACS+ server logs requests from an unknown device, 10.0.13.1 (an R1 physical interface). Which two actions fix the problem and stop it recurring? (Choose two.)

- **A.** Configure `ip tacacs source-interface Loopback0` in the TACACS+ server group
- **B.** Change the TACACS+ transport to UDP 49
- **C.** Add `single-connection` to the server definition
- **D.** Register R1's Loopback0 address as the device on the TACACS+ server
- **E.** Change the method list to `group radius`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A, D.** The server answers only devices it knows by source IP. Sourcing from a loopback gives R1 one address that never changes with routing, and the server must know R1 by that address. **Why not the others:** B, TACACS+ uses TCP 49; there's no UDP option. C reuses one TCP session but doesn't change the source address. E swaps protocols, and the RADIUS server would have the same source-address problem.
</details>

---

## 17.4 Authorization and Accounting

**The problem:** after login, everyone authenticated by the server would otherwise get the same access. You want the help desk to run `show` commands, the network team to configure, and contractors to touch only their own switches, all decided centrally. And when something breaks at 03:12, you want to know who typed what.

Authentication proves who you are. **Authorization** decides what you may do. On a device you authorize two things:

```
R1(config)# aaa authorization exec default group ADMIN-TACACS local if-authenticated
R1(config)# aaa authorization commands 15 default group ADMIN-TACACS local if-authenticated
R1(config)# aaa authorization console        ! without this, the console skips authorization
R1(config)# aaa authorization config-commands
```

| Command | What gets authorized |
|---------|----------------------|
| `aaa authorization exec` | Whether you get a shell at all, **and at which privilege level** (the server returns e.g. `priv-lvl=15`) |
| `aaa authorization commands 15` | **Every single level-15 command**, one by one, as you type it (TACACS+ only — see why below) |
| `if-authenticated` | Last-resort method: "if they authenticated, allow it" — keeps you working if the server dies |

**Why does per-command authorization need TACACS+ rather than RADIUS?** Because RADIUS combines authentication and authorization into one exchange at login. It hands back a bundle of attributes and the conversation is over. TACACS+ keeps the three A's **separate**, so the device can ask a fresh question ("may `admin` run `configure terminal`?") for every command, long after login. *That separation is the whole reason TACACS+ is the device-administration protocol.*

**How command authorization works, step by step.** jsmith is logged in at level 15 and types `interface Gi0/1` then `shutdown`:

1. Before running `interface GigabitEthernet0/1`, R1 sends ISE an authorization **REQUEST**: user `jsmith`, `cmd=interface`, `cmd-arg=GigabitEthernet0/1`.
2. ISE checks jsmith's **command set** (for example, "help desk: permit `show *`, permit `interface *`, permit `shutdown`, permit `no shutdown`, deny everything else") and replies **PASS** or **FAIL**.
3. On PASS the command runs. On FAIL, R1 prints `Command authorization failed.` and nothing changes.
4. The same check repeats for `shutdown`. With command accounting on, R1 also sends a record of each command that ran.

**Worked example — what the accounting server records:**

| Time | User | Device | Source | Command |
|------|------|--------|--------|---------|
| 03:11:48 | jsmith | R1 (10.255.0.1) | 10.99.0.15 | `interface GigabitEthernet0/1` |
| 03:12:02 | jsmith | R1 (10.255.0.1) | 10.99.0.15 | `shutdown` |

That's the 03:12 outage solved in one search. (`if-authenticated` as the last method means that if every earlier method errors out, for example ISE becomes unreachable, a user who has already authenticated may keep working rather than being frozen out mid-change.)

**Accounting** records what happened:

```
R1(config)# aaa accounting exec default start-stop group ADMIN-TACACS
R1(config)# aaa accounting commands 15 default start-stop group ADMIN-TACACS
```

`start-stop` sends a record when something begins and when it ends (session duration). `stop-only` sends just the end. With `commands 15` accounting, the server keeps a line for every config command and who typed it. That's the answer to "who shut that interface at 03:12?"

### TACACS+ vs RADIUS — the CCNP version of the table

| Property | **TACACS+** | **RADIUS** |
|----------|-------------|------------|
| Transport | **TCP 49** | **UDP 1812** (auth) / **1813** (accounting); legacy 1645/1646 |
| Encryption | **Entire payload** | **Only the password** attribute |
| AAA separation | Authentication, authorization, accounting **separate** | Authentication + authorization **combined** |
| Per-command authorization | **Yes** | No |
| Origin | Cisco (now RFC 8907, informational) | IETF standard (RFC 2865/2866) |
| Primary job | **Device administration** | **Network access** — 802.1X, VPN, Wi-Fi (18.3, Chapter 31) |

**Why TCP for TACACS+ and UDP for RADIUS?** TACACS+ authorizes command by command, so a reliable, long-lived session (`single-connection`) suits it. RADIUS handles thousands of short, independent access requests (every laptop joining the network), and connectionless UDP with its own retries is lighter for that.

### Verifying

```
R1# test aaa group ADMIN-TACACS jsmith Secr3t! legacy
Sending password
User successfully authenticated
R1# show tacacs                 ! per-server: connection state, packets sent/received, errors
R1# show aaa servers            ! UP/DEAD state, request counts, response times
R1# show aaa sessions
R1# debug aaa authentication    ! Chapter 31 walks through reading this output
```

**📝 Exam-style questions — 17.4**

**Q1.** Why does per-command authorization require TACACS+ rather than RADIUS?

- **A.** RADIUS uses TCP, which is too slow to check every command
- **B.** TACACS+ encrypts only the password, so it's faster
- **C.** RADIUS cannot return a privilege level
- **D.** RADIUS combines authentication and authorization in one exchange at login, while TACACS+ keeps them separate so each command can be authorized later

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** Because TACACS+ separates the three A's, the device can ask a fresh question ("may jsmith run `shutdown`?") for every command, long after login. RADIUS hands back its attributes at login and the conversation is over. **Why not the others:** A, RADIUS uses UDP; TACACS+ is the TCP one. B, it's RADIUS that encrypts only the password; TACACS+ encrypts the whole payload. C, RADIUS can return a privilege level at login; what it can't do is authorize commands one by one.
</details>

**Q2.** Which command makes R1 ask the AAA server whether a user may have a shell at all, and at which privilege level?

- **A.** `aaa authorization exec default group ADMIN-TACACS local if-authenticated`
- **B.** `aaa authorization commands 15 default group ADMIN-TACACS local if-authenticated`
- **C.** `aaa accounting exec default start-stop group ADMIN-TACACS`
- **D.** `aaa authentication enable default group ADMIN-TACACS enable`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Exec authorization decides whether a shell starts and at what level (the server returns, for example, `priv-lvl=15`). **Why not the others:** B checks each level-15 command after the shell exists. C records sessions; it doesn't decide anything. D authenticates the `enable` command, which is a different step.
</details>

**Q3.** Which two statements about TACACS+ and RADIUS are true? (Choose two.)

- **A.** RADIUS encrypts the entire payload
- **B.** TACACS+ uses TCP 49 and encrypts the entire payload
- **C.** TACACS+ uses UDP 1812 for authentication
- **D.** RADIUS supports per-command authorization
- **E.** RADIUS is the usual protocol for network access such as 802.1X and VPN

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B, E.** TACACS+ is the device-administration protocol: TCP 49, whole payload encrypted, A's separate. RADIUS is the network-access protocol used by 802.1X, VPN and Wi-Fi. **Why not the others:** A, RADIUS encrypts only the password attribute. C, UDP 1812 is RADIUS authentication. D, per-command authorization needs TACACS+.
</details>

**Q4.** An interface was shut down at 03:12 and nobody admits to it. Which configuration would have recorded who did it?

- **A.** `aaa authorization config-commands`
- **B.** `aaa accounting exec default start-stop group ADMIN-TACACS`
- **C.** `aaa accounting commands 15 default start-stop group ADMIN-TACACS`
- **D.** `aaa authorization console`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Command accounting sends the server a record of every level-15 command with the user, device, source and time, which answers "who typed `shutdown` at 03:12?". **Why not the others:** A and D are authorization commands; they decide what's allowed but don't keep a record. B records when sessions start and stop, but not the commands typed in them.
</details>

---

## 17.5 ACLs at CCNP Depth

**The problem ACLs solve:** a router forwards anything it has a route for. That's its job, but it means that without a filter, every host that can reach your network can reach every service on it. An **ACL** (Access Control List) is the router's list of "who may send what to where".

**Story Time 📖:** An ACL is a bouncer with a numbered checklist. For each packet he reads from the top: "Line 10, does this match? No. Line 20? No. Line 30? Yes: deny." He acts on the **first** line that matches and never reads further. If he reaches the bottom without a match, the unwritten last line says "turn them away" (the implicit deny).

CCNA taught standard vs extended, wildcards, placement and the implicit deny (CCNA guide Chapter 19). CCNP adds four practical skills: **editing in place**, **object-groups**, **`established`**, and **IPv6 ACLs**. It also adds the habit of reading hit counters as a troubleshooting tool.

### Number ranges, for completeness

| Type | Numbers |
|------|---------|
| Standard IPv4 | 1–99, 1300–1999 |
| Extended IPv4 | 100–199, 2000–2699 |

On IOS XE, a numbered ACL and a named ACL are the same thing internally. `ip access-list extended 110` opens numbered ACL 110 in named-ACL mode, so you get sequence numbers for it too.

### Sequence numbers — editing without rewriting

```
R1# show access-lists EDGE-IN
Extended IP access list EDGE-IN
    10 permit tcp any host 203.0.113.10 eq 443 (18234 matches)
    20 permit tcp any host 203.0.113.10 eq 80 (512 matches)
    30 deny ip any any log (97 matches)
!
R1(config)# ip access-list extended EDGE-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 25 permit udp any host 203.0.113.53 eq domain   ! insert between 20 and 30
R1(config-ext-nacl)# no 20                                          ! remove one line only
R1(config)# ip access-list resequence EDGE-IN 10 10                 ! renumber 10, 20, 30 ...
```

**Why does this matter so much in production?** Before sequence numbers, changing one line of a numbered ACL meant removing the whole ACL and re-entering it. For the few seconds in between, an interface ACL that's been deleted either permits everything or doesn't exist. Inserting by sequence number changes **one rule atomically**. *The `(N matches)` counters are your first troubleshooting tool: a rule with 0 matches after a test either isn't being reached or doesn't match what you think it does.* Clear them with `clear ip access-list counters EDGE-IN` before you test.

**Worked example — walking packets through EDGE-IN** (after adding 25 and removing 20, before the resequence: lines 10, 25, 30):

| Packet arriving inbound | Line 10 (tcp → .10:443) | Line 25 (udp → .53:53) | Line 30 (deny ip any any log) | Result |
|-------------------------|-------------------------|------------------------|-------------------------------|--------|
| TCP 198.51.100.7 → 203.0.113.10:443 | **match** | — | — | permitted, line 10 counter +1 |
| UDP 198.51.100.7 → 203.0.113.53:53 | no | **match** | — | permitted, line 25 +1 |
| TCP 198.51.100.7 → 203.0.113.10:**80** | no | no | **match** | **denied** (line 20 was removed), logged |
| TCP 198.51.100.7 → 203.0.113.10:22 | no | no | **match** | denied, logged |

The third row is how you'd prove a change worked: clear the counters, test from outside, and see line 30's counter (and a `%SEC-6-IPACCESSLOGP` log message) increment for port 80.

### Object-groups — naming sets of things

When the same servers and ports appear in many rules, object-groups turn an ACL into readable policy:

```
R1(config)# object-group network WEB-SERVERS
R1(config-network-group)# host 10.20.0.10
R1(config-network-group)# host 10.20.0.11
R1(config-network-group)# 10.20.1.0 255.255.255.0          ! note: subnet MASK, not wildcard
!
R1(config)# object-group service WEB-PORTS
R1(config-service-group)# tcp eq 80
R1(config-service-group)# tcp eq 443
!
R1(config)# ip access-list extended TO-WEB
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 10 permit object-group WEB-PORTS any object-group WEB-SERVERS
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 20 deny ip any object-group WEB-SERVERS log
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 30 permit ip any any
```

**Why use object-groups if the device expands them into the same rules anyway?** Because humans maintain ACLs. Adding a third web server is now one line in `WEB-SERVERS`, and every rule that references the group picks it up. Without groups you'd hunt through the ACL for every rule mentioning the old servers and inevitably miss one. *Object-groups move the "what" (which hosts) away from the "policy" (what they may do).*

**Worked example — what line 10 really means.** `WEB-PORTS` holds 2 services and `WEB-SERVERS` holds 3 destinations, so line 10 stands for 2 × 3 = **6** ordinary rules: TCP to port 80 or 443 on 10.20.0.10, 10.20.0.11, or anything in 10.20.1.0/24. Add `host 10.20.0.12` to `WEB-SERVERS` and line 10 now covers 8 combinations, while line 20 also starts protecting the new server, without either ACL line being touched.

### `established` — the cheap return-traffic trick

```
R1(config)# ip access-list extended FROM-INTERNET
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp any 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 established
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip any any log
```

`established` matches TCP segments with the **ACK or RST** bit set. Every TCP segment *except the very first SYN* of a connection has ACK set. So this lets replies to inside-initiated sessions back in, while blocking new connections initiated from outside.

**Worked example.** Inside PC 10.1.1.25 browses to 52.96.10.4:

| Packet arriving from the internet | Flags | `established` matches? | Result |
|-----------------------------------|-------|------------------------|--------|
| 52.96.10.4:443 → 10.1.1.25:51544 (the server's reply) | SYN+ACK | yes (ACK set) | permitted |
| 52.96.10.4:443 → 10.1.1.25:51544 (data) | ACK | yes | permitted |
| 198.51.100.7:40000 → 10.1.1.25:3389 (someone trying RDP) | SYN only | no | denied by the next line |
| 198.51.100.7:40000 → 10.1.1.25:3389 (crafted probe) | ACK | **yes** | **permitted** — the weakness below |

**Why isn't this a firewall?** Because it's **stateless**. The router doesn't remember which connections actually exist; it just looks at flag bits, and an attacker can set ACK on a crafted packet to probe through. It also does nothing for UDP or ICMP replies. *It's a filter that trusts what the packet says about itself. A stateful firewall (18.4) remembers what really happened.*

### Placement at CCNP level

The CCNA placement rules still hold (extended near the source, standard near the destination). CCNP adds three refinements:

- **Infrastructure ACLs (iACLs)** at the network edge deny traffic *to your own device addresses* (loopbacks, link IPs) from the outside, except for what must reach them (BGP from your peer, for example). They protect the control plane before CoPP ever sees the packet.
- **Inbound beats outbound** where you have the choice: a packet denied inbound never consumes a route lookup.
- **`ip access-group` applies to transit traffic.** Outbound interface ACLs do **not** filter traffic the router itself generates. Protecting the router's own management uses `access-class` (17.1) and CoPP (17.6).

### IPv6 ACLs — the same idea with three differences

```
R1(config)# ipv6 access-list V6-EDGE-IN
R1(config-ipv6-acl)# permit tcp any host 2001:db8:20::10 eq 443
R1(config-ipv6-acl)# permit icmp any any nd-na              ! keep neighbor discovery working
R1(config-ipv6-acl)# permit icmp any any nd-ns
R1(config-ipv6-acl)# deny ipv6 any any log
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 traffic-filter V6-EDGE-IN in           ! not "access-group"
```

| Difference | IPv4 ACL | IPv6 ACL |
|------------|----------|----------|
| Types | Standard and extended | **Named extended only** |
| Address match | Wildcard masks | **Prefix lengths** (`2001:db8::/32`) |
| Applied with | `ip access-group` | **`ipv6 traffic-filter`** |
| Hidden lines at the end | `deny ip any any` | `permit icmp any any nd-na`, `permit icmp any any nd-ns`, **then** `deny ipv6 any any` |

**Why does IPv6 hide two permits before the implicit deny?** Because IPv6 has no ARP. Neighbor Discovery (NS/NA) is how neighbours find each other's MACs (CCNA guide 13.8), and it runs over ICMPv6. If the implicit deny blocked ND, any IPv6 ACL would break basic reachability on the link. **The trap:** those hidden permits sit *after* your last line. If you write your own explicit `deny ipv6 any any` at the end (to log it, say), you've placed it *above* the hidden ND permits, and you break neighbor discovery. *That's why the example above permits `nd-na` and `nd-ns` explicitly before its own deny.*

**Worked example of the trap.** An engineer writes `permit tcp any host 2001:db8:20::10 eq 443` then `deny ipv6 any any log`, and applies it inbound on the link to the upstream router. Web traffic works for a few minutes, then everything stops. Why: the upstream router's Neighbor Solicitations and Advertisements now hit the explicit deny. Once R1's neighbor cache entry for the upstream router expires and can't be refreshed, R1 can no longer resolve its MAC address, so nothing can be sent to it. `show ipv6 neighbors` shows the entry stuck at `INCMP` (incomplete), and the deny line's counter is climbing with ICMPv6 packets. Adding the two `nd-` permits above the deny fixes it. Chapter 31 covers IPv6 filtering troubleshooting.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 17.5**

**Q1.** Refer to the exhibit. ACL EDGE-IN is applied inbound on the internet interface. A packet arrives: TCP from 198.51.100.7 to 203.0.113.10 port 80. What happens?

```
Extended IP access list EDGE-IN
    10 permit tcp any host 203.0.113.10 eq 443
    25 permit udp any host 203.0.113.53 eq domain
    30 deny ip any any log
```

- **A.** It is denied by line 30, and a log message is generated
- **B.** It is permitted by line 10, because the destination host matches
- **C.** It is denied silently by the implicit deny
- **D.** It is permitted, because no line explicitly denies TCP port 80

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** The packet doesn't match line 10 (port 443 only) or line 25 (UDP), so it reaches line 30, which matches everything and logs. Line 30's counter goes up by one. **Why not the others:** B, line 10 needs both the host **and** port 443. C, the explicit line 30 matches first, so the implicit deny is never reached. D, ACLs stop at the first match, and the deny on line 30 matches all IP traffic.
</details>

**Q2.** An ACL inbound from the internet has `permit tcp any 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 established` followed by `deny ip any any log`. Which packet is permitted even though it shows this ACL's weakness?

- **A.** A TCP SYN from 198.51.100.7 to 10.1.1.25 port 3389
- **B.** A DNS reply over UDP from 8.8.8.8 to 10.1.1.25
- **C.** An ICMP echo reply from 52.96.10.4 to 10.1.1.25
- **D.** A crafted TCP segment with the ACK bit set from 198.51.100.7 to 10.1.1.25 port 3389

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** `established` only checks whether ACK or RST is set. It doesn't remember which connections exist, so an attacker who sets ACK on a crafted packet gets through, which is why it isn't a firewall. **Why not the others:** A, a plain SYN has no ACK, so it's denied (as intended). B and C aren't TCP, so they don't match the `established` line and are denied, which is the other weakness of this trick: it does nothing for UDP or ICMP replies.
</details>

**Q3.** Refer to the exhibit. Web traffic to 2001:db8:20::10 works for a few minutes after the ACL is applied, then all traffic through the interface stops. `show ipv6 neighbors` shows the upstream router as `INCMP`. What is the fix?

```
ipv6 access-list V6-EDGE-IN
 permit tcp any host 2001:db8:20::10 eq 443
 deny ipv6 any any log
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
 ipv6 traffic-filter V6-EDGE-IN in
```

- **A.** Apply the ACL with `ipv6 access-group` instead of `ipv6 traffic-filter`
- **B.** Add `permit icmp any any nd-na` and `permit icmp any any nd-ns` above the deny line
- **C.** Remove `log` from the deny line
- **D.** Convert the ACL to a standard IPv6 ACL

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** IPv6 ACLs hide two Neighbor Discovery permits **before** their implicit deny. An explicit `deny ipv6 any any` sits above those hidden permits, so NS/NA messages are dropped. When the cached neighbor entry expires it can't be refreshed (`INCMP`), and traffic to the upstream router stops. **Why not the others:** A, `ipv6 traffic-filter` is the correct command. C, logging doesn't change what's matched. D, IPv6 has no standard ACLs; they are all named extended.
</details>

**Q4.** Line 10 of an ACL is `permit object-group WEB-PORTS any object-group WEB-SERVERS`. WEB-PORTS holds `tcp eq 80` and `tcp eq 443`; WEB-SERVERS holds three entries. An engineer adds one more host to WEB-SERVERS. How many port/destination combinations does line 10 now permit?

- **A.** 5
- **B.** 6
- **C.** 8
- **D.** 9

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** The line expands to every service in WEB-PORTS for every destination in WEB-SERVERS: 2 × 4 = 8 after the new host is added. The ACL line itself wasn't touched, which is the point of object-groups. **Why not the others:** A adds the counts (2 + 3) instead of multiplying. B is the count before the new host (2 × 3). D is 3 × 3, which miscounts the ports.
</details>

## 17.6 Control Plane Policing (CoPP)

![CoPP sits between the forwarding hardware and the route processor](images/c17_copp.png)

**The problem CoPP solves:** a router can forward a flood of traffic *through* itself without breaking a sweat, yet be knocked over by a much smaller flood sent *to* itself. CoPP (Control Plane Policing) protects the router's own CPU, so that its routing protocols keep running whatever is thrown at it.

### Three planes, one weak spot

| Plane | What it does | Example traffic | Handled by |
|-------|--------------|-----------------|------------|
| **Data plane** | Forwards *through* the device | User packets | Forwarding hardware (ASIC/CEF) — fast |
| **Control plane** | Builds the forwarding tables | OSPF hellos, BGP updates, ARP, STP BPDUs | **The CPU** |
| **Management plane** | Lets people manage the device | SSH, SNMP, NTP, syslog | **The CPU** |

**Why does the CPU need its own protection?** A switch ASIC can forward tens or hundreds of gigabits per second. The CPU behind it can process only a few thousand packets per second. Any traffic *addressed to* the device, or that needs CPU handling (TTL expiry, ARP, IP options), is **punted** from the fast hardware up to that slow CPU. If an attacker, or just a loop or a misbehaving host, floods the box with SSH SYNs, pings or ARP, the CPU drowns. **When the CPU drowns, OSPF hellos go unanswered, neighbours time out, and the router drops off the network even though its forwarding hardware is idle.**

**Story Time 📖:** Picture a huge warehouse with conveyor belts (the forwarding hardware) moving thousands of parcels a second, and one manager in a small office upstairs (the CPU). Parcels addressed *to the manager* have to be carried up a narrow staircase. If someone posts ten thousand junk letters to the manager, the staircase jams, and the manager never receives the phone calls from the other warehouses (the routing protocol hellos) that keep the business running. CoPP is a bouncer at the foot of the staircase with a rule for each kind of visitor: "routing partners, come right up; staff from the management office, a steady stream; strangers with pings, one at a time; anyone else, a trickle."

### Building a CoPP policy with MQC

CoPP uses the same **Modular QoS CLI** (MQC) you'll use for QoS in Chapter 11: **class-map** (what), **policy-map** (what to do), **service-policy** (where). The "where" is the special `control-plane` configuration mode.

**Step 1 — ACLs that identify the traffic** (a `permit` means *"belongs in this class"*, not "allow"):

```
ip access-list extended COPP-ROUTING
 permit ospf any any
 permit tcp any any eq bgp            ! BGP sessions in either direction:
 permit tcp any eq bgp any            !   to port 179 and from port 179
ip access-list extended COPP-MGMT
 permit tcp 10.99.0.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 22
 permit udp 10.99.0.0 0.0.0.255 any eq snmp
 permit udp any eq ntp any eq ntp
ip access-list extended COPP-ICMP
 permit icmp any any echo
 permit icmp any any echo-reply
 permit icmp any any ttl-exceeded
 permit icmp any any unreachable
```

**Step 2 — classes:**

```
class-map match-any CM-COPP-ROUTING
 match access-group name COPP-ROUTING
class-map match-any CM-COPP-MGMT
 match access-group name COPP-MGMT
class-map match-any CM-COPP-ICMP
 match access-group name COPP-ICMP
```

**Step 3 — policy: a rate per class:**

```
policy-map PM-COPP
 class CM-COPP-ROUTING
  police cir 1000000 conform-action transmit exceed-action transmit  ! measure, never drop
 class CM-COPP-MGMT
  police cir 512000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop
 class CM-COPP-ICMP
  police cir 64000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop       ! pings get a trickle
 class class-default
  police cir 128000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop      ! everything unexpected
```

**The order of classes matters.** A policy-map is evaluated **top-down, and the first class that matches wins**. A packet that would match two classes is policed only by the first. So put the most specific classes first (routing, then management from known sources, then ICMP) and broader ones after them. `class-default` is always evaluated **last**, whatever position you type it in, and catches everything nothing else matched. *If a broad class like "all TCP" sat above the BGP class, BGP would be policed at the generic rate, and the routing class above would never see a packet.*

**Step 4 — attach it to the control plane:**

```
R1(config)# control-plane
R1(config-cp)# service-policy input PM-COPP
```

### The design reasoning behind each class

- **Routing gets generous treatment, often `exceed-action transmit`.** Dropping your own OSPF or BGP packets causes the very outage CoPP exists to prevent. Many designs police routing only to *measure* it at first, then tighten.
- **Management is restricted by source.** SSH from the management subnet is in `CM-COPP-MGMT`. SSH from anywhere else doesn't match that ACL, so it falls into `class-default` and gets the small rate.
- **ICMP gets a trickle.** You want ping and traceroute to work for troubleshooting, but a ping flood shouldn't eat the CPU.
- **`class-default` is the safety net**, and it must be policed, not left unlimited. Anything you didn't anticipate lands here. *An unpoliced class-default means CoPP protects you from everything except what you didn't think of, which is exactly what attackers use.*

**How a policer decides, step by step.** `police cir 64000` sets a **CIR** (Committed Information Rate) of 64,000 bits per second, and IOS picks a burst size (**Bc**, here 2,000 bytes) for it. Think of a bucket of tokens, each token worth one byte:

1. Tokens drip into the bucket at the CIR: 64,000 bps = 8,000 bytes' worth per second. The bucket holds at most Bc (2,000 bytes); extra tokens spill away.
2. A punted ICMP packet of 100 bytes arrives. If the bucket holds at least 100 tokens, the packet **conforms**: 100 tokens are removed and `conform-action transmit` sends it to the CPU.
3. If the bucket holds fewer than 100 tokens, the packet **exceeds**, and `exceed-action drop` throws it away. No tokens are taken.

So short bursts up to 2,000 bytes pass at once, and anything sustained above 64 kbps is trimmed down to 64 kbps.

**Worked example — a ping flood meets CoPP.** A compromised host sends R1 **500 pings per second** of 100 bytes each: 500 × 100 × 8 = **400,000 bps**. The ICMP class only allows 64,000 bps, so about 64,000 ÷ 400,000 = **16%** of the pings reach the CPU (about 80 per second) and the other ~84% are dropped before they ever reach the CPU. The CPU barely notices, OSPF hellos (in the routing class) are untouched, and `show policy-map control-plane` shows the `exceeded` counter on CM-COPP-ICMP climbing, which tells you exactly what's happening.

**Worked example — the same SSH, two outcomes:**

| Packet | First class it matches | Policed at |
|--------|------------------------|------------|
| TCP SYN to port 22 from 10.99.0.15 | CM-COPP-MGMT (source in 10.99.0.0/24) | 512 kbps |
| TCP SYN to port 22 from 198.51.100.7 | none of the ACLs → class-default | 128 kbps, shared with every other unexpected packet |

The outsider isn't blocked by CoPP (that's the job of `access-class` and the iACL); they're just squeezed into the small shared pipe, so a flood from them can't starve the management class.

**Why `permit` in a CoPP ACL never means "allow".** The ACL is only a classifier. `permit` puts a packet *into* the class, and the policer decides its fate. A `deny` line just means "not this class, try the next one." Nothing is ever dropped *by* the ACL. *Read CoPP ACLs as membership lists.*

### Verifying

```
R1# show policy-map control-plane
 Control Plane
  Service-policy input: PM-COPP
    Class-map: CM-COPP-ICMP (match-any)
      14520 packets, 1393920 bytes
      5 minute offered rate 61000 bps, drop rate 12000 bps
      Match: access-group name COPP-ICMP
      police:
          cir 64000 bps, bc 2000 bytes
        conformed 11201 packets, 1075296 bytes; actions:
          transmit
        exceeded 3319 packets, 318624 bytes; actions:
          drop
```

Read it as: *ICMP is arriving at ~61 kbps against a 64 kbps contract, and 3,319 packets have been dropped.* That's either an attack or a monitoring system pinging too aggressively, and now you know which class to investigate. A climbing `exceeded` count on the **routing** class is a design error: the rate is too low for your network.

> 🔬 **Platform note.** On Catalyst 9000 switches, CoPP is **on by default** as a system-defined policy (`system-cpp-policy`). You tune its per-queue rates (`show policy-map system-cpp-policy`) rather than attaching your own policy to `control-plane`. Routers (ISR/ASR/Catalyst 8000) use the user-defined MQC policy shown above. Both follow the same idea: classify punted traffic and rate-limit it per class.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 17.6**

**Q1.** During a ping flood aimed at R1's own loopback, transit traffic keeps flowing at full speed, but R1's OSPF neighbors go down. What explains this, and what prevents it?

- **A.** The flood saturates the data plane; QoS on the egress interfaces prevents it
- **B.** Traffic to the router is punted to the CPU, which drowns and misses OSPF hellos; CoPP rate-limits each class of punted traffic
- **C.** OSPF hellos are dropped by the interface ACL; permit protocol 89 to fix it
- **D.** The forwarding hardware stops during the flood; enable CEF to fix it

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** Transit traffic is forwarded in hardware, which doesn't notice the flood, but packets addressed to the router itself go to the slow CPU. When the CPU is overwhelmed, it can't answer OSPF hellos, so neighbors time out. CoPP polices each class of punted traffic so a ping flood gets only a trickle. **Why not the others:** A, the data plane is fine; that's the clue. C, nothing in the scenario changed the interface ACLs. D, the forwarding hardware is still working, which is why transit traffic is unaffected.
</details>

**Q2.** A CoPP policy-map lists `class CM-ALL-TCP` (matching all TCP) above `class CM-COPP-ROUTING` (matching OSPF and BGP). How is BGP traffic to the router policed?

- **A.** At CM-ALL-TCP's rate, because the first matching class wins and BGP is TCP
- **B.** At CM-COPP-ROUTING's rate, because it is the more specific match
- **C.** At both rates, one after the other
- **D.** At the class-default rate, because BGP matches two classes

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** A policy-map is evaluated top-down and stops at the first class that matches. BGP runs over TCP port 179, so it matches CM-ALL-TCP first and never reaches the routing class. OSPF (not TCP) still reaches CM-COPP-ROUTING. Put specific classes first. **Why not the others:** B, MQC doesn't choose the most specific class, only the first. C, a packet is policed by one class only. D, class-default is only for traffic that matches no class.
</details>

**Q3.** CoPP class CM-COPP-ICMP is policed at `cir 64000` with `exceed-action drop`. A host sends R1 1,000 pings per second, each 100 bytes. Roughly how many pings per second reach the CPU?

- **A.** About 640
- **B.** About 160
- **C.** About 800
- **D.** About 80

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** The flood is 1,000 × 100 bytes × 8 = 800,000 bps. The policer allows 64,000 bps, which is 8% of that: about 80 pings per second (80 × 800 bits = 64,000 bps). The other ~920 per second are dropped before they reach the CPU. **Why not the others:** A treats the 64,000 bps CIR as 64% of the flood. B doubles the right answer, as if the pings were 50 bytes. C is the flood measured in kilobits per second (800 kbps), not pings per second.
</details>

**Q4.** In an ACL used by a CoPP class-map, what does a `deny` line do to a packet that matches it?

- **A.** The packet is dropped before it reaches the CPU
- **B.** The packet is sent to the CPU without any policing
- **C.** The packet is not a member of that class, so the next class is evaluated
- **D.** The packet is placed in class-default immediately, skipping the remaining classes

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** In CoPP, ACLs only classify. `permit` means "this packet belongs in the class"; `deny` means "not this class, try the next one". Nothing is dropped by the ACL itself; the policers decide. **Why not the others:** A and B treat the ACL as a filter, which it isn't here. D, the remaining classes are still checked in order; class-default is only for packets that match none of them.
</details>

## 17.7 Putting It Together — A Hardening Checklist

| Layer | Control | Section |
|-------|---------|---------|
| Doors | SSH only, `access-class`, `exec-timeout`, AUX disabled, all VTY ranges covered | 17.1 |
| Identity | scrypt secrets, local fallback admin, `login block-for` | 17.1, 17.2 |
| Central policy | `aaa new-model`, TACACS+ group with loopback source, local fallback | 17.3 |
| Least privilege | exec + command authorization, command accounting | 17.4 |
| Transit filtering | iACLs at the edge, object-group based policy ACLs, IPv6 equivalents | 17.5 |
| CPU protection | CoPP with routing / management / ICMP / default classes | 17.6 |

*Each layer assumes the one before it might fail. That's the defense-in-depth idea Chapter 18 applies to the whole network.*
