<a name="chapter-28"></a>
# Chapter 28: BGP In Depth

> **Blueprint:** ENARSI 1.11 — Troubleshoot BGP (internal and external, unicast, and VRF-Lite): 1.11.a address families (IPv4, IPv6) · 1.11.b neighbor relationship and authentication (next-hop, multihop, 4-byte AS, private AS, route refresh, synchronization, operation, peer group, states and timers) · 1.11.c path preference (attributes and best-path) · 1.11.d route reflector (excluding multiple route reflectors, confederations, dynamic peer) · 1.11.e policies (inbound/outbound filtering, path manipulation)

Chapter 7 covered the BGP foundations: path-vector routing, eBGP between directly connected neighbors, the message types, and the best-path algorithm in outline. ENARSI adds **iBGP** and everything it brings with it: next-hop handling, loopback peering, route reflectors, address families, VRFs. It also adds the policy tools that make BGP useful, and the troubleshooting skill to see why a session isn't Established or why the "wrong" path won.

**The mindset:** BGP has no automatic discovery and almost no automatic behavior. Every neighbor is configured by hand, every policy is explicit, and the best-path algorithm is deterministic. So when BGP does something surprising, the reason is always visible in the output somewhere. Your job is to know where to look.

**Words you'll meet in this chapter:**

| Term | Plain meaning |
|------|---------------|
| **AS** | Autonomous System: one organization's network under one routing policy, identified by an AS number (ASN) |
| **eBGP / iBGP** | BGP between routers in **different** ASes / in the **same** AS |
| **IGP** | Interior Gateway Protocol: the routing protocol inside your AS (OSPF, EIGRP). BGP relies on it to reach next hops and peers' loopbacks |
| **Prefix / NLRI** | a route BGP advertises (Network Layer Reachability Information is the RFC's name for it) |
| **Path attribute** | a property attached to a route: AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, LOCAL_PREF, MED and so on. Best-path selection compares these |
| **Next hop** | the address BGP says to send traffic to for that prefix. It doesn't have to be directly connected; the router looks it up again in the routing table (a *recursive* lookup) |
| **RR** | Route Reflector: an iBGP router allowed to pass iBGP routes between other iBGP routers |
| **AF** | address family: IPv4 unicast, IPv6 unicast, VPNv4… each one activated separately per neighbor |

**Story Time 📖 — BGP in one picture:** BGP is less like a road map and more like a **list of recommendations with notes attached**. Each neighbor says "you can reach 8.8.8.0/24 through me; here's the list of companies it passes through (AS_PATH), here's where to hand it over (NEXT_HOP)". Your router reads all the recommendations for a prefix, applies your company's rules (LOCAL_PREF, WEIGHT), and picks one. Nothing is discovered automatically; every friend you take recommendations from is configured by name.

---

## 28.1 iBGP vs eBGP — Different Rules for Different Neighbors

**The problem:** your border routers learn the internet's routes from your ISPs over eBGP. Your *other* routers need those routes too, so the border routers must pass them on inside the AS, over iBGP. But iBGP follows different rules from eBGP, and almost every "the route is in BGP but nothing works" ticket comes from one of those differences.

| Behavior | eBGP (different AS) | iBGP (same AS) |
|----------|---------------------|----------------|
| Administrative distance | **20** | **200** |
| Default TTL of BGP packets | **1** — neighbor must be directly connected | 255 — can be many hops away |
| Next hop when advertising | changed to **self** | **unchanged** (28.2) |
| AS_PATH | own AS **prepended** | unchanged |
| Re-advertising learned routes | to all peers | **never to another iBGP peer** (iBGP split horizon) |
| LOCAL_PREF | not sent | sent |
| Typical peering address | directly connected interface | **loopback** |

**Why can't an iBGP router pass an iBGP-learned route to another iBGP peer?** Because inside one AS, BGP has **no loop detection**. eBGP spots loops by finding its own AS number in the AS_PATH, but iBGP doesn't add to the AS_PATH, so a route circling among iBGP peers would look the same every time around. The **iBGP split-horizon rule** removes the possibility: a route learned from an iBGP peer is never sent to another iBGP peer. The consequence is that every iBGP router must hear every route **directly** from the router that learned it. That means either a **full mesh** of iBGP sessions, n(n−1)/2 of them, or a **route reflector** (28.7) that's allowed to break the rule under controlled conditions.

**Story Time 📖:** an office rule about news. "If you hear news from **outside** the company, tell all your colleagues. If you hear it from a **colleague**, don't repeat it to other colleagues." The rule stops the same rumour circling the office forever. The cost is that whoever hears outside news must tell **every** colleague personally (the full mesh), unless the office appoints a team lead who is allowed to repeat it (the route reflector).

**Worked example — counting sessions.** An AS has 10 iBGP routers.

- Full mesh: 10 × 9 / 2 = **45** iBGP sessions, and adding an 11th router means touching all 10 existing routers.
- One route reflector with 9 clients: **9** sessions, and adding a router means configuring only the new router and the RR.

**Why peer iBGP on loopbacks?** Because the session should survive any single link failure. A loopback never goes down, and the IGP finds *some* path to it as long as one exists. Peering on a physical interface IP ties the session to that one cable. Two pieces of configuration make it work:

```
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 2.2.2.2 remote-as 65001
 neighbor 2.2.2.2 update-source Loopback0    ! source my packets from my loopback
```

**Why is `update-source` needed?** Because BGP runs over TCP, and TCP checks addresses. R2 is configured with `neighbor 1.1.1.1`, so it only accepts a connection *from* 1.1.1.1. Without `update-source`, R1 sources the TCP SYN from its outgoing physical interface. R2 sees an unknown address and refuses it, so **R1's** connection attempts fail. Strictly, the session can still come up if R2 has `update-source Loopback0`: R2 opens the TCP connection *from* 2.2.2.2 to 1.1.1.1, R1 recognises 2.2.2.2 as a configured neighbor and accepts it. The session only stays stuck in **Active** when **neither** side can open a connection the other will accept. *Configure `update-source` on both ends anyway, so either side can initiate and the behavior is predictable — and both ends need a route to the other's loopback.*

**eBGP between loopbacks** (often used to load-share across two parallel links) runs into the TTL-1 rule, because the loopback is one hop beyond the directly connected interface:

| Command | What it does | Use when |
|---------|--------------|----------|
| `neighbor X ebgp-multihop 2` | sends eBGP packets with TTL 2 (or any number up to 255) | the eBGP peer really is more than one hop away |
| `neighbor X disable-connected-check` | keeps TTL 1, but skips the "peer address must be on a connected subnet" check | loopback peering between **directly connected** routers |
| `neighbor X ttl-security hops 1` | sends with TTL **255**, accepts only TTL ≥ 254 (GTSM) | protecting eBGP from spoofed remote packets; **can't be combined with `ebgp-multihop`** |

**Why is TTL security stronger than TTL 1?** Because an attacker anywhere on the internet can craft a packet that **arrives** with TTL 1. They just set the starting TTL to the right number of hops. Nobody, though, can make a packet *arrive* with TTL 254 from more than one hop away, because every router along the way decrements it. Starting high and requiring a high value on arrival proves the packet came from a directly connected router.

**Worked example — TTL security in numbers.** R1 and its ISP peer are directly connected, both with `ttl-security hops 1`. The accepted minimum is 255 − 1 = **254**.

1. The ISP router sends its BGP packets with TTL **255**. They cross no other router, so they arrive with TTL **255**. 255 ≥ 254: accepted.
2. An attacker five routers away also sends with TTL 255. Each of the five routers decrements it, so it arrives with **250**. 250 < 254: dropped before BGP ever looks at it.
3. With plain eBGP (TTL 1 sent, no check on arrival), the attacker would simply send with TTL 6, so the packet arrives with TTL 1 and looks exactly like the real peer's.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 28.1**

**Q1.** AS 65001 has three routers. R1 peers with R2 over iBGP, and R2 peers with R3 over iBGP. There is no R1–R3 session and no route reflector. R1 learns 8.8.8.0/24 from its ISP over eBGP. R2 has the route, but R3 never receives it. Why?

- **A.** R2's next hop for the route is unreachable.
- **B.** R2 is following iBGP split horizon: a route learned from an iBGP peer is never sent to another iBGP peer.
- **C.** iBGP sessions have a TTL of 1, so R3 is too far from R1.
- **D.** R1's AS number appears in the AS_PATH, so R3 rejects it as a loop.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** iBGP has no loop detection of its own (the AS_PATH doesn't change inside the AS), so BGP forbids passing iBGP-learned routes to other iBGP peers. Every iBGP router must hear the route directly from R1 (a full mesh), or R2 must be a route reflector with R3 as a client. **Why not the others:** A would stop R2 using the route, but not stop it advertising it. C is wrong because iBGP uses TTL 255. D is wrong because the AS_PATH gains no entries inside the AS.
</details>

**Q2.** R1 and its ISP peer are directly connected, and both are configured with `neighbor … ttl-security hops 1`. Which received TTL is the lowest that R1 accepts for BGP packets from that peer?

- **A.** 1
- **B.** 255
- **C.** 253
- **D.** 254

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** With TTL security, packets are sent with TTL 255 and must arrive with at least 255 minus the configured hop count: 255 − 1 = 254. A packet from farther away arrives lower and is dropped. **Why not the others:** A is plain eBGP's sending TTL, which an attacker can fake by choosing the right starting value. B would allow no hops at all. C would allow a peer two hops away.
</details>

**Q3.** R1 and its eBGP neighbor peer between their loopbacks over one directly connected link. Each router has `update-source Loopback0` and a static route to the other's loopback, but the session never establishes. Which two commands each fix the problem on their own? (Choose two.)

- **A.** `neighbor 192.0.2.2 next-hop-self`
- **B.** `neighbor 192.0.2.2 ebgp-multihop 2`
- **C.** `neighbor 192.0.2.2 soft-reconfiguration inbound`
- **D.** `neighbor 192.0.2.2 disable-connected-check`
- **E.** `neighbor 192.0.2.2 remove-private-as`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B, D.** By default eBGP sends with TTL 1 and expects the peer address on a connected subnet; the loopback is neither. `ebgp-multihop 2` raises the TTL. `disable-connected-check` keeps TTL 1 but skips the connected-subnet check, which suits directly connected routers peering on loopbacks. **Why not the others:** A changes the next hop in advertised routes, not the session. C stores received routes for troubleshooting. E strips private AS numbers from outbound paths.
</details>


---

## 28.2 Next Hop and `next-hop-self`

![iBGP keeps the eBGP next hop unless the border router rewrites it](images/c28_next_hop.png)

**The problem:** BGP tells a router *where to hand traffic over*, the next hop, but it doesn't tell the router how to get there. The router has to find the next hop in its own routing table. If it can't, the BGP route is useless, however good it looks.

When R1 learns 8.8.8.0/24 from the ISP, the next hop is the ISP's address, 203.0.113.1. When R1 passes the route to iBGP peer R2, **the next hop doesn't change**. R2 needs a route to 203.0.113.1, and the IGP usually doesn't carry the ISP link's subnet.

```
R2# show ip bgp 8.8.8.0
BGP routing table entry for 8.8.8.0/24, version 0
Paths: (1 available, no best path)
  65100
    203.0.113.1 (inaccessible) from 1.1.1.1 (1.1.1.1)
      Origin IGP, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, internal
```

**`(inaccessible)` and `no best path`** are the symptom. The route is in the BGP table but can't be used, because step 0 of the best-path algorithm (28.6) is "**is the next hop reachable?**". The two fixes:

```
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 2.2.2.2 next-hop-self      ! on R1: rewrite next hop to my update-source (1.1.1.1)
! — or — advertise the ISP link into the IGP (passive) so 203.0.113.1 is reachable
```

**Why doesn't iBGP change the next hop by default?** Because the original next hop is often the **better** forwarding answer. In a shared-segment design, or when the exit router isn't the BGP speaker, the true exit is the eBGP peer, and rewriting it would detour traffic through R1. BGP keeps the most specific forwarding information it has and leaves the choice to you. *In a typical enterprise edge, `next-hop-self` on the border router toward its iBGP peers is the standard configuration.*

**Story Time 📖:** a parcel arrives at your company's reception with the note "deliver via Door 203.0.113.1". Reception (R1) knows where that door is, because it's right next to it. It forwards the parcel to the third floor (R2) with the note unchanged. The third floor has never heard of Door 203.0.113.1, so the parcel sits there. `next-hop-self` is reception crossing out the note and writing "bring it back to reception (1.1.1.1)", an address every floor knows how to reach.

**How R2 resolves the route, step by step, before and after the fix:**

1. R1 learns 8.8.8.0/24 from the ISP with next hop 203.0.113.1, and sends it to R2 over iBGP with the next hop **unchanged**.
2. R2 looks up 203.0.113.1 in its routing table. The ISP link's subnet isn't in the IGP, so there's no match. R2 marks the path **inaccessible**, and it can't be best.
3. Add `neighbor 2.2.2.2 next-hop-self` on R1, then `clear ip bgp 2.2.2.2 soft out` so R1 resends its routes.
4. R2 now receives the route with next hop **1.1.1.1**, R1's loopback. R2's OSPF already has 1.1.1.1/32, so the lookup succeeds and the path becomes best.
5. Traffic from R2 to 8.8.8.8 goes to 1.1.1.1 using OSPF, and R1 forwards it to the ISP.

R2's view after the fix:

```
R2# show ip bgp 8.8.8.0
BGP routing table entry for 8.8.8.0/24, version 15
Paths: (1 available, best #1, table default)
  65100
    1.1.1.1 (metric 2) from 1.1.1.1 (1.1.1.1)
      Origin IGP, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, internal, best
```

`(metric 2)` is R2's IGP cost to the next hop: the value best-path step 9 compares.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 28.2**

**Q1.** Refer to the exhibit. R1 is the border router (1.1.1.1) and learned 8.8.8.0/24 from the ISP at 203.0.113.1. R2 is its iBGP peer. What is the best fix?

```
R2# show ip bgp 8.8.8.0
BGP routing table entry for 8.8.8.0/24, version 0
Paths: (1 available, no best path)
  65100
    203.0.113.1 (inaccessible) from 1.1.1.1 (1.1.1.1)
      Origin IGP, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, internal
```

- **A.** Configure `neighbor 1.1.1.1 next-hop-self` on R2.
- **B.** Configure `neighbor 1.1.1.1 ebgp-multihop 2` on R2.
- **C.** Configure `neighbor 2.2.2.2 next-hop-self` on R1.
- **D.** Raise LOCAL_PREF for the route on R1.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** iBGP keeps the eBGP next hop, 203.0.113.1, and R2 has no route to it, so the path fails step 0 ("is the next hop reachable?"). `next-hop-self` on R1 toward R2 rewrites the next hop to 1.1.1.1, which R2 reaches through the IGP. The other fix is to advertise the ISP link into the IGP. **Why not the others:** A is on the wrong router: next-hop-self changes the next hop of routes R2 *sends*, not routes it receives. B is an eBGP session setting and R1–R2 is iBGP. D can't help, because an inaccessible path is rejected before LOCAL_PREF is compared.
</details>

**Q2.** Refer to the exhibit. What does `(metric 2)` mean?

```
R2# show ip bgp 8.8.8.0
  65100
    1.1.1.1 (metric 2) from 1.1.1.1 (1.1.1.1)
      Origin IGP, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, internal, best
```

- **A.** The MED the ISP attached to the route
- **B.** The number of AS hops to the destination
- **C.** R2's IGP cost to reach the next hop, 1.1.1.1
- **D.** The route's LOCAL_PREF divided by 50

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** The value in brackets after the next hop is the IGP metric to that next hop, which best-path step 9 compares. **Why not the others:** A is the `metric 0` on the second line. B is wrong because the AS_PATH (`65100`) shows the AS hops. D isn't a BGP value; LOCAL_PREF appears as `localpref 100`.
</details>

**Q3.** Why does iBGP leave the next hop unchanged by default?

- **A.** Because the original eBGP next hop is often the better forwarding answer, and rewriting it could detour traffic through the advertising router.
- **B.** Because iBGP routers can't change any path attributes.
- **C.** Because iBGP peers always share the eBGP peer's subnet.
- **D.** Because the next hop is used for iBGP loop detection.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** BGP keeps the most specific forwarding information it has. Where other routers can reach the eBGP peer directly, sending traffic to it is better than sending it through R1. You choose `next-hop-self` when they can't. **Why not the others:** B is wrong because iBGP routers can set attributes such as LOCAL_PREF. C is wrong; usually they don't share it, which is why `next-hop-self` is so common. D is wrong because iBGP loop prevention is split horizon (and ORIGINATOR_ID/CLUSTER_LIST with route reflectors).
</details>

## 28.3 Sessions: States, Timers and Why They Get Stuck

**The problem:** a BGP session that isn't Established exchanges no routes at all. Unlike OSPF and EIGRP, BGP runs over **TCP port 179**, so a session can fail for TCP reasons (reachability, source address, TTL, ACLs, MD5) or for BGP reasons (wrong AS, wrong router ID). The state it's stuck in tells you which.

**Story Time 📖:** setting up a business phone call. **Idle**: you haven't picked up the phone. **Connect**: it's ringing. **Active**: the call didn't connect, so you're waiting for them to call you, and you'll redial shortly. **OpenSent**: they answered and you've introduced yourself ("I'm AS 65001, router 1.1.1.1"). **OpenConfirm**: they've introduced themselves and you're waiting for "OK, let's talk". **Established**: business begins. A call that never connects is a phone problem (TCP). A call that connects and then gets hung up straight after introductions is a "wrong person" problem (the OPEN parameters).

**How a session comes up, step by step** (R1 1.1.1.1 AS 65001, R2 2.2.2.2 AS 65001, loopback peering):

1. **Idle → Connect.** R1 has a route to 2.2.2.2, so it starts a TCP connection: SYN from 1.1.1.1 (thanks to `update-source Loopback0`) to 2.2.2.2 port 179.
2. **Connect → OpenSent.** R2 recognises 1.1.1.1 as a configured neighbor and completes the TCP handshake. R1 sends its **OPEN** message: version 4, my AS 65001, my hold time 180, my BGP ID 1.1.1.1, my capabilities (route refresh, 4-byte AS, address families).
3. **OpenSent → OpenConfirm.** R1 receives R2's OPEN and checks it: is the AS what my `remote-as` says? Is the hold time acceptable? Is the BGP ID valid (an iBGP peer using my own router ID is rejected)? If all is well, R1 sends a **KEEPALIVE** to accept it.
4. **OpenConfirm → Established.** R1 receives R2's KEEPALIVE. Both sides now send **UPDATE** messages with their routes, then KEEPALIVEs every 60 s.
5. If TCP fails at step 1 or 2, R1 goes to **Active**, keeps listening for R2 to connect to it, and retries later. If a check fails at step 3, R1 sends a **NOTIFICATION** naming the error and closes the session.

BGP's finite-state machine:

| State | Meaning | Stuck here usually means |
|-------|---------|--------------------------|
| **Idle** | not trying (or waiting before retrying) | no route to the neighbor; `neighbor shutdown` → `Idle (Admin)`; max-prefix exceeded → `Idle (PfxCt)` |
| **Connect** | TCP three-way handshake in progress | — (brief) |
| **Active** | the TCP attempt **failed**; retrying and listening | wrong neighbor IP, missing `update-source`, missing `ebgp-multihop`, ACL blocking **TCP 179**, peer not configured |
| **OpenSent** | TCP up, OPEN sent, waiting for theirs | — |
| **OpenConfirm** | OPENs exchanged, waiting for KEEPALIVE | — |
| **Established** | exchanging UPDATEs | healthy |

**The trap in the name:** "Active" sounds healthy, but it means **failure**. The router is actively *trying* to connect and not succeeding. A session that **flips between Idle and Active** is a TCP problem. A session that reaches OpenSent and then drops back is a **parameter mismatch** detected in the OPEN message, and the router logs a NOTIFICATION that names it:

```
%BGP-3-NOTIFICATION: sent to neighbor 10.1.12.2 passive 2/2 (peer in wrong AS) 2 bytes FDE9
%BGP-5-ADJCHANGE: neighbor 10.1.12.2 Down BGP Notification sent
```

`2/2` is the OPEN error **bad peer AS**. The `FDE9` is the AS the peer actually sent (0xFDE9 = 65001).

**Timers:** keepalive **60 s**, hold **180 s** by default. They're **negotiated**: each side proposes a hold time in its OPEN, and both use the **lower** value. Set them per neighbor with `neighbor X timers 10 30` or globally with `timers bgp 10 30`. *The timers don't have to match, unlike OSPF's.* For sub-second failure detection, use **BFD** (`neighbor X fall-over bfd`, Chapter 25), not aggressive timers.

**Worked example — negotiated hold time.** R1 is configured with `neighbor 10.1.12.2 timers 10 30` (keepalive 10, hold 30). R2 keeps the defaults (60/180). In the OPEN messages R1 proposes hold 30 and R2 proposes 180. Both routers use the lower, **30 seconds**. `show ip bgp neighbors 10.1.12.1 | include hold` on R2 (10.1.12.1 being R1's address) shows the negotiated value, which is not the one R2 was configured with. If R1 had proposed a hold time of 0, both sides would agree to send no keepalives and never time the session out, which is why you'll rarely see 0 outside a lab.

**Authentication** uses a TCP MD5 signature on every segment (RFC 2385):

```
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 10.1.12.2 password BGPs3cr3t
```

A mismatched or missing password means the TCP session never establishes. The session sits in **Active/Idle**, and the log names the cause directly:

```
%TCP-6-BADAUTH: Invalid MD5 digest from 10.1.12.2(179) to 10.1.12.1(34521)
%TCP-6-BADAUTH: No MD5 digest from 10.1.12.2(179) to 10.1.12.1(34521)
```

"Invalid" means the passwords differ. "No digest" means the other side has none configured.

**The summary command** shows everything at a glance:

```
R1# show bgp ipv4 unicast summary
BGP router identifier 1.1.1.1, local AS number 65001
Neighbor     V    AS  MsgRcvd MsgSent  TblVer InQ OutQ Up/Down  State/PfxRcd
2.2.2.2      4 65001     1204    1199      88   0    0 18:22:41       14
10.1.12.2    4 65100       31      29      88   0    0 00:27:10      812
10.1.13.3    4 65200        0       0       1   0    0 never    Active
```

A **number** in State/PfxRcd means Established, and the number is how many prefixes were received. A **word** (Idle, Active) means the session is down.

**Worked ticket — the loopback session stuck in Active.** R1 (1.1.1.1) and R3 (3.3.3.3) are in AS 65001 and should peer between loopbacks. `show bgp ipv4 unicast summary` on R1 shows `3.3.3.3 ... never  Active`.

1. **Is it a routing problem?** `ping 3.3.3.3 source Loopback0` from R1 succeeds, so each router can reach the other's loopback. That rules out the Idle-type causes.
2. **Active means TCP keeps failing.** Look at how each side connects:

```
R1# show run | section router bgp
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 3.3.3.3 remote-as 65001
R3# show run | section router bgp
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 1.1.1.1 remote-as 65001
```

3. **Reason it through.** Neither side has `update-source`. R1 opens its TCP connection from its outgoing interface, 10.1.13.1. R3 only accepts connections from a configured neighbor, 1.1.1.1, so it rejects it. R3 does the same thing in reverse, from 10.1.13.3, and R1 rejects that. Neither direction can ever succeed.
4. **Fix:** `neighbor 3.3.3.3 update-source Loopback0` on R1 and `neighbor 1.1.1.1 update-source Loopback0` on R3. Within seconds the summary shows a prefix count instead of `Active`.
5. **If it's still Active** after that, the next suspect is an ACL on the path. BGP needs TCP port 179 in **both** directions: to port 179 from the side that opens the connection, and from port 179 for the replies. The safest entries are `permit tcp host 1.1.1.1 host 3.3.3.3 eq bgp` and `permit tcp host 1.1.1.1 eq bgp host 3.3.3.3` (plus the mirror pair on the other router's inbound ACL).

**📝 Exam-style questions — 28.3**

**Q1.** Refer to the exhibit. What is the state of the session with 10.1.13.3?

```
R1# show bgp ipv4 unicast summary
Neighbor     V    AS  MsgRcvd MsgSent  TblVer InQ OutQ Up/Down  State/PfxRcd
2.2.2.2      4 65001     1204    1199      88   0    0 18:22:41       14
10.1.13.3    4 65200        0       0       1   0    0 never    Active
```

- **A.** Established, and actively exchanging routes
- **B.** Established, but no prefixes have been received yet
- **C.** Waiting for the peer's KEEPALIVE after the OPEN messages
- **D.** Down: R1's TCP connection attempts to the peer are failing

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** A word in State/PfxRcd means the session is down. "Active" sounds healthy, but it means the TCP attempt failed and R1 is retrying and listening. Typical causes are a wrong neighbor address, a missing `update-source` or `ebgp-multihop`, or an ACL blocking TCP 179. **Why not the others:** A and B would show a number (the prefix count) instead of a word. C is the OpenConfirm state.
</details>

**Q2.** Refer to the exhibit. What is wrong?

```
%BGP-3-NOTIFICATION: sent to neighbor 10.1.12.2 passive 2/2 (peer in wrong AS) 2 bytes FDE9
%BGP-5-ADJCHANGE: neighbor 10.1.12.2 Down BGP Notification sent
```

- **A.** The `remote-as` configured for 10.1.12.2 doesn't match the AS it sent, which is 65001.
- **B.** The MD5 password doesn't match.
- **C.** The hold timers don't match.
- **D.** 10.1.12.2 isn't reachable.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** The session got far enough to exchange OPEN messages, and the OPEN check failed with error 2/2, bad peer AS. FDE9 is the AS the peer sent, in hex: 0xFDE9 = 65001. **Why not the others:** B fails at the TCP level with `%TCP-6-BADAUTH`, before any OPEN. C is wrong because hold timers are negotiated (the lower is used), so they never cause a mismatch. D would leave the session in Idle or Active, with no OPEN exchanged.
</details>

**Q3.** R1's BGP session to 10.1.12.2 is stuck in Active, and R1 logs `%TCP-6-BADAUTH: No MD5 digest from 10.1.12.2(179) to 10.1.12.1(34521)`. What is the cause?

- **A.** The two routers have different MD5 passwords.
- **B.** R1 has an MD5 password configured for the neighbor, but 10.1.12.2 has none.
- **C.** An ACL is dropping TCP port 179.
- **D.** 10.1.12.2 has a password configured, but R1 has none.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** R1 expects a digest and received a segment with none, so the other side has no password configured. **Why not the others:** A logs "Invalid MD5 digest". C produces no BADAUTH message, because no segments arrive. D is the reverse situation: R1 would then be receiving digests it doesn't expect, not missing ones.
</details>

**Q4.** R1 is configured with `neighbor 10.1.12.2 timers 10 30`. R2 uses the default timers. Which hold time do both routers use for the session?

- **A.** 180 seconds
- **B.** 90 seconds
- **C.** 30 seconds
- **D.** Each router uses its own configured hold time

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Each side proposes a hold time in its OPEN message, and both use the lower value: 30 versus 180, so 30. **Why not the others:** A is R2's configured value, which loses. B isn't a value either router proposed. D describes EIGRP; BGP negotiates.
</details>


---

## 28.4 Address Families, MP-BGP and IPv6

**The problem:** the original BGP could only carry IPv4 prefixes. Networks now need IPv6 routes, VPN routes and more, and running a separate protocol for each would be a mess. Multiprotocol extensions let one BGP process (and even one session) carry many kinds of routes, each kept in its own table.

Multiprotocol BGP (MP-BGP) carries any **address family** (IPv4 unicast, IPv6 unicast, VPNv4, …) over any session. One TCP session can carry several families, and each neighbor must be **activated** per family.

```
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 1.1.1.1
 no bgp default ipv4-unicast                  ! don't auto-activate IPv4 for every neighbor
 neighbor 10.1.12.2 remote-as 65100           ! IPv4 transport session
 neighbor 2001:DB8:12::2 remote-as 65100      ! IPv6 transport session
 !
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  neighbor 10.1.12.2 activate
  network 198.51.100.0 mask 255.255.255.0
 exit-address-family
 !
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  neighbor 2001:DB8:12::2 activate
  network 2001:DB8:100::/48
 exit-address-family
```

**Why use `no bgp default ipv4-unicast`?** By default, IOS activates **every** neighbor for IPv4 unicast, including IPv6-transport neighbors. You end up with IPv4 routes being exchanged over sessions you meant for IPv6 only. Turning the default off makes activation explicit: a neighbor carries exactly the families you `activate`. *It's what you want in any dual-stack design, and if you forget an `activate`, the session comes up but no prefixes are exchanged for that family.*

**Carrying IPv6 prefixes over an IPv4 session works, with one catch.** The next hop has to be an IPv6 address, so IOS builds an **IPv4-mapped** one (`::FFFF:10.1.12.2`). It isn't routable, so the routes show as inaccessible. Either run a native IPv6 session for the IPv6 family (as above, the clean design), or set a real next hop with an outbound route map (`set ipv6 next-hop 2001:DB8:12::1`).

Verify per family: `show bgp ipv6 unicast summary`, `show bgp ipv6 unicast`, and `show bgp all summary`.

**4-byte AS numbers.** ASNs were 16-bit (to 65535) and are now 32-bit. There are two notations for the same number:

| asplain | asdot | Calculation |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 65546 | 1.10 | 1 × 65536 + 10 |
| 131072 | 2.0 | 2 × 65536 |

`router bgp 65546` and `router bgp 1.10` are the same AS. To convert asplain to asdot, divide by 65,536: the whole number goes before the dot and the remainder after it. For example, the first 4-byte private ASN, 4,200,000,000, is 64,086 × 65,536 + 59,904, so in asdot it's **64086.59904**. `bgp asnotation dot` changes only how IOS **displays** it. Older speakers that only understand 2-byte ASNs see **AS 23456** (AS_TRANS) standing in for any 4-byte AS. *If you see 23456 in a path, an old router is somewhere upstream.*

**Private ASNs:** **64512–65534** (2-byte) and **4200000000–4294967294** (4-byte). They're fine inside an organization or between a customer and its ISP, but they must never reach the internet. The ISP (or your edge) strips them:

```
neighbor 203.0.113.1 remove-private-as              ! strip if the path is ALL private ASNs
neighbor 203.0.113.1 remove-private-as all          ! strip private ASNs wherever they appear
neighbor 203.0.113.1 remove-private-as all replace-as   ! replace them with my own AS
```

**📝 Exam-style questions — 28.4**

**Q1.** Refer to the exhibit. The IPv6 session to 2001:DB8:12::2 is Established, but no IPv6 prefixes are exchanged. What is missing?

```
router bgp 65001
 no bgp default ipv4-unicast
 neighbor 2001:DB8:12::2 remote-as 65100
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  network 2001:DB8:100::/48
 exit-address-family
```

- **A.** `neighbor 2001:DB8:12::2 activate` under `address-family ipv6 unicast`
- **B.** `bgp default ipv4-unicast`, so the neighbor is activated automatically
- **C.** `neighbor 2001:DB8:12::2 update-source Loopback0`
- **D.** A route map that sets an IPv6 next hop

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** With `no bgp default ipv4-unicast`, every neighbor must be explicitly activated in each address family. Without `activate` the session can come up, but nothing is exchanged for that family. **Why not the others:** B only auto-activates IPv4 unicast, which wouldn't help IPv6. C is a session-source setting, and the session is already up. D is needed only when IPv6 prefixes ride an IPv4 session.
</details>

**Q2.** What is the 4-byte AS number 131080 in asdot notation?

- **A.** 1.65544
- **B.** 13.1080
- **C.** 2.8
- **D.** 0.131080

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Divide by 65,536: 131,080 = 2 × 65,536 + 8, so the asdot form is 2.8. **Why not the others:** A would mean 1 × 65,536 + 65,544, but the part after the dot must be below 65,536. B just splits the digits. D isn't how asdot works for numbers above 65,535.
</details>

**Q3.** An engineer sees AS 23456 in the AS_PATH of several routes. What does this indicate?

- **A.** The route passed through a private AS.
- **B.** A router that understands only 2-byte AS numbers is in the path, and 23456 is standing in for a 4-byte AS.
- **C.** The route was aggregated with `as-set`.
- **D.** The route was prepended by a confederation.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** AS 23456 is AS_TRANS. Older 2-byte-only speakers see it in place of any 4-byte AS number, so its appearance means an old router is upstream. **Why not the others:** A is wrong because 23456 isn't in the private ranges (64512–65534 and 4200000000–4294967294). C would show an AS set in braces. D isn't what 23456 means.
</details>


---

## 28.5 Operations: Refreshing Policy, Synchronization, Peer Groups

**The problem:** BGP sessions can carry hundreds of thousands of routes and stay up for months. Dropping one just to apply a new route map would be a self-inflicted outage. You also need ways to keep dozens of neighbor configurations consistent. This section is the day-to-day operational toolkit.

**Applying a policy change.** BGP doesn't re-evaluate routes it already holds when you change a route map. You have to make it reprocess them:

| Method | How | Cost |
|--------|-----|------|
| Hard reset | `clear ip bgp 10.1.12.2` | drops the session — **avoid in production** |
| **Route refresh** (default, negotiated capability) | `clear ip bgp 10.1.12.2 soft in` | asks the peer to resend its routes; no session drop, no extra memory |
| Soft reconfiguration inbound | `neighbor X soft-reconfiguration inbound`, then `clear … soft in` | stores an **unfiltered copy** of everything received — memory-heavy |
| Outbound | `clear ip bgp 10.1.12.2 soft out` | re-sends my routes through the new outbound policy |

**Why does `soft-reconfiguration inbound` still exist when route refresh works?** For **troubleshooting**. With it, `show ip bgp neighbors X received-routes` shows exactly what the peer sent **before** your inbound policy filtered it, next to `routes` (what survived the policy). Comparing the two tells you immediately whether a route is missing because the peer never sent it or because your filter dropped it. Without it, `received-routes` isn't available. (`advertised-routes` always works for the outbound direction.)

**Story Time 📖:** route refresh is phoning a colleague and saying "please resend me that list, I've changed how I file things". Soft reconfiguration inbound is keeping a **photocopy** of every list you've ever received, before you filed it. The photocopy costs drawer space (memory), but it lets you prove exactly what you were sent.

**Worked example — "the ISP says they sent it".** The ISP insists they advertise 812 prefixes, including 198.18.0.0/15, but R1 doesn't have that route. R1 has `soft-reconfiguration inbound` toward the ISP.

```
R1# show ip bgp neighbors 10.1.12.2 received-routes | include 198.18
*  198.18.0.0/15    10.1.12.2                0             0 65100 i
R1# show ip bgp neighbors 10.1.12.2 routes | include 198.18
R1#
```

The prefix **was received** (it's in `received-routes`) but **didn't survive the inbound policy** (it's missing from `routes`). So the ISP is right, and the cause is on R1: an inbound prefix list or route map denies it. (198.18.0.0/15 is a reserved benchmarking range, so a bogon filter is probably doing its job.) Had it been missing from `received-routes` too, the problem would have been on the ISP's side.

**Synchronization** was an old rule: *don't use or advertise an iBGP-learned route unless the same prefix is also in the IGP.* It existed for transit ASes whose internal routers didn't all run BGP. It made sure traffic sent across the AS wouldn't reach a non-BGP router that would drop it. Modern designs run BGP on every transit router (or use MPLS), so synchronization is **disabled by default** (since IOS 12.2(8)T) and is deprecated — many current IOS XE releases no longer accept the `synchronization` command at all. *Know what it was and why it's off. Turning it on would also mean redistributing the full BGP table into the IGP.*

**Peer groups and templates** keep large neighbor lists consistent:

```
! Peer group — neighbors share one outbound policy (and one update calculation)
router bgp 65001
 neighbor IBGP peer-group
 neighbor IBGP remote-as 65001
 neighbor IBGP update-source Loopback0
 neighbor IBGP next-hop-self
 neighbor 2.2.2.2 peer-group IBGP
 neighbor 3.3.3.3 peer-group IBGP
```

```
! Peer templates — session and policy separated, inheritable, more flexible
router bgp 65001
 template peer-session IBGP-SESSION
  remote-as 65001
  update-source Loopback0
 exit-peer-session
 template peer-policy IBGP-POLICY
  next-hop-self
  send-community both
 exit-peer-policy
 neighbor 2.2.2.2 inherit peer-session IBGP-SESSION
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  neighbor 2.2.2.2 inherit peer-policy IBGP-POLICY
```

**Why were peer groups originally about CPU, not convenience?** Because a peer group's members are guaranteed to share the **same outbound policy**, so BGP computes the update **once** and copies it to every member. On a route reflector with hundreds of clients, that saves a lot of CPU. Modern IOS builds **update groups** automatically from any neighbors with identical outbound policy, so the CPU benefit no longer depends on peer groups. Templates add flexibility: a neighbor can inherit a session template *and* a policy template, and templates can inherit from each other.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 28.5**

**Q1.** Refer to the exhibit. R1 has `soft-reconfiguration inbound` toward the ISP. What explains the output?

```
R1# show ip bgp neighbors 10.1.12.2 received-routes | include 198.18
*  198.18.0.0/15    10.1.12.2                0             0 65100 i
R1# show ip bgp neighbors 10.1.12.2 routes | include 198.18
R1#
```

- **A.** The ISP never advertised 198.18.0.0/15.
- **B.** The route is a RIB failure on R1.
- **C.** R1 has not refreshed the session since the ISP sent it.
- **D.** The ISP sent the prefix, but R1's inbound policy filtered it.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** `received-routes` shows what the peer sent before inbound policy; `routes` shows what survived the policy. The prefix is in the first and missing from the second, so an inbound prefix list, filter list or route map on R1 dropped it. **Why not the others:** A is disproved by `received-routes`. B would still list the route under `routes`, flagged `r`. C is wrong because received routes are processed as they arrive; a refresh only matters after a policy change.
</details>

**Q2.** An engineer changes the inbound route map on a production eBGP neighbor, but the BGP table doesn't change. What is the right way to apply the new policy?

- **A.** `clear ip bgp 10.1.12.2`
- **B.** `clear ip bgp 10.1.12.2 soft out`
- **C.** Remove and re-add the `neighbor` statement
- **D.** `clear ip bgp 10.1.12.2 soft in`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: D.** BGP doesn't re-evaluate routes it already holds. A soft inbound clear asks the peer to resend its routes using route refresh, so the new inbound policy is applied without dropping the session. **Why not the others:** A is a hard reset that drops the session. B re-sends *your* routes through your outbound policy, which doesn't apply an inbound change. C also tears the session down.
</details>

**Q3.** Route refresh lets BGP re-apply inbound policy without storing anything. Why would an engineer still configure `soft-reconfiguration inbound`?

- **A.** To make `received-routes` available, showing what the peer sent before inbound policy, for troubleshooting.
- **B.** Because route refresh drops the session.
- **C.** To reduce the memory BGP uses.
- **D.** Because it is required for outbound policy changes.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** It keeps an unfiltered copy of everything received, so you can compare `received-routes` with `routes` and prove whether the peer sent a route. **Why not the others:** B is wrong because route refresh is non-disruptive. C is the opposite: the stored copy costs memory. D is wrong because `soft out` and `advertised-routes` work without it.
</details>

## 28.6 Path Preference — the Best-Path Algorithm in Full

**The problem:** for most internet prefixes, a multi-homed router hears several paths. It must pick exactly one to use and to advertise onward, it must pick the same way every time, and you must be able to steer the choice with business policy. The best-path algorithm is that deterministic recipe.

BGP picks **one** best path per prefix (unless multipath is on), comparing candidates **one attribute at a time** in a fixed order. The first difference decides:

| Step | Prefer | Scope / default | How you manipulate it |
|------|--------|-----------------|-----------------------|
| 0 | Next hop **reachable** | — | `next-hop-self`, IGP (28.2) |
| 1 | Highest **WEIGHT** | Cisco-only, **this router only**; default 0 (32768 if locally originated) | `neighbor X weight 200` or `set weight` (inbound) |
| 2 | Highest **LOCAL_PREF** | whole AS (iBGP); default **100** | `set local-preference 200` (inbound), `bgp default local-preference` |
| 3 | **Locally originated** | `network`, `aggregate-address`, `redistribute` | originate it yourself |
| 4 | Highest **AIGP** | rarely used; ignored unless configured | — |
| 5 | Shortest **AS_PATH** | `AS_SET` counts as 1 | `set as-path prepend 65001 65001` (outbound); `bgp bestpath as-path ignore` skips this step |
| 6 | Lowest **ORIGIN** | IGP (`i`) < EGP (`e`) < incomplete (`?`) | `set origin igp` |
| 7 | Lowest **MED** | compared only between paths from the **same neighbor AS**; default 0 | `set metric 50` (outbound) |
| 8 | **eBGP over iBGP** | — | — |
| 9 | Lowest **IGP metric to the next hop** | — | IGP costs |
| 10 | (multipath check if `maximum-paths` configured) | — | `maximum-paths 2` (28.11) |
| 11 | **Oldest** eBGP path | stability | — |
| 12 | Lowest **BGP router ID** of the advertiser | (originator ID if reflected) | `bgp router-id` |
| 13 | Shortest **CLUSTER_LIST** | reflected paths | — |
| 14 | Lowest **neighbor address** | — | — |

The numbering and mnemonic are the same as Chapter 7's (7.7): **"N WLLA OMNI"** — **N**ext hop reachable, **W**eight, **L**ocal pref, **L**ocally originated, **A**S path (with AIGP folded in), **O**rigin, **M**ED, **N**eighbor type (eBGP over iBGP), **I**GP metric. After those, the tie-breakers run oldest → router ID → cluster list → neighbor address.

**The direction rule, and the logic that ties it together.** Every attribute either influences **your own outbound traffic** or **asks your neighbors** to send traffic to you a certain way:

| Goal | Tool | Applied |
|------|------|---------|
| Choose which exit **my** traffic uses — this router only | WEIGHT | **inbound** on routes from the preferred peer |
| Choose which exit **my whole AS** uses | LOCAL_PREF | **inbound** at the preferred border router |
| Influence how **other ASes** send traffic **to me** | AS_PATH prepend, MED | **outbound** toward the less-preferred link |

**Why does LOCAL_PREF beat AS_PATH length?** Because BGP is **policy first, distance second**. LOCAL_PREF is *your* decision about your own traffic: "we pay less on ISP-A, so leave through ISP-A". AS_PATH length is only a rough measure of distance, the number of networks the route crosses. An AS's own business policy has to override that, or BGP couldn't express commercial reality. *That's also why weight and LOCAL_PREF come first: they're the attributes you control. Everything after them is information you received.*

**Story Time 📖:** choosing a flight. Your company's travel policy (LOCAL_PREF: "use Airline A, we have a contract") comes first, whatever the itinerary. Only if the policy doesn't decide do you prefer fewer stopovers (AS_PATH length). Only after that do you look at smaller details: which one the airline itself recommends (MED), whether it's a direct booking (eBGP over iBGP), how far the departure gate is from your desk (IGP metric to the next hop). And if it's still a tie, you keep the booking you already have (oldest path).

**Worked example — walking the steps.** R1 (AS 65001) has three paths to 172.20.0.0/16:

| Path | Learned from | Weight | LOCAL_PREF | AS_PATH | Origin | MED | Type | IGP metric to NH |
|------|-------------|--------|------------|---------|--------|-----|------|------------------|
| A | 203.0.113.1 (AS 65100) | 0 | 100 | 65100 65300 | i | 0 | eBGP | 0 |
| B | 2.2.2.2 (iBGP, R2 learned it from AS 65200) | 0 | 100 | 65200 65300 | i | 0 | iBGP | 20 |
| C | 198.51.100.1 (AS 65200) | 0 | 100 | 65200 65400 65300 | i | 0 | eBGP | 0 |

1. **Next hop reachable? (step 0)** All three: yes. Continue.
2. **Weight (step 1):** all 0. Tie.
3. **LOCAL_PREF (step 2):** all 100. Tie.
4. **Locally originated? (step 3)** None. (AIGP, step 4, isn't in use.) Tie.
5. **AS_PATH length (step 5):** A = 2, B = 2, C = 3. **C is eliminated**; A and B continue.
6. **Origin (step 6):** both `i`. Tie.
7. **MED (step 7):** A came from AS 65100, B from AS 65200: different neighbor ASes, so MED isn't compared. Tie.
8. **eBGP over iBGP (step 8):** A is eBGP, B is iBGP. **A wins.**

**Now change the policy.** On R2, add an inbound route map from AS 65200 with `set local-preference 150`. R2 sends path B to R1 with LOCAL_PREF 150. Walk again: weight (step 1) ties, and at LOCAL_PREF (step 2) B (150) beats A and C (100). **B wins** at step 2, and the AS_PATH and eBGP steps are never reached. *That's "first difference decides" in action: a later step can never overturn an earlier one.*

**Why is MED compared only between paths from the same neighbor AS?** Because MED values are **set by the neighbor AS to suit its own network**. AS 65100's MED 10 and AS 65200's MED 50 come from different scales with different meanings, so comparing them is meaningless. `bgp always-compare-med` overrides this when you know both neighbors use a consistent scheme (for example, two ISPs that both use IGP cost). Configure it **on every router in the AS**, or the routers will make inconsistent decisions. Related: a path with no MED counts as **0** (the best value), unless `bgp bestpath med missing-as-worst` is set.

### Worked policy: dual-homed to two ISPs

Requirement: all outbound traffic uses ISP-A; inbound traffic should arrive via ISP-A too.

```
route-map FROM-ISPA permit 10
 set local-preference 200             ! my whole AS prefers ISP-A's routes
!
route-map TO-ISPB permit 10
 set as-path prepend 65001 65001 65001  ! make my prefixes look 3 hops farther via ISP-B
!
router bgp 65001
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  neighbor 203.0.113.1 route-map FROM-ISPA in
  neighbor 198.51.100.1 route-map TO-ISPB out
```

Then `clear ip bgp * soft`. Verify outbound with `show ip bgp` (look for `200` in the LocPrf column on ISP-A's paths). For inbound, check from outside, for example on a looking glass, that your prefix shows the prepended path via ISP-B.

```
R1# show ip bgp 8.8.8.0
Paths: (2 available, best #1, table default)
  65100
    203.0.113.1 from 203.0.113.1 (203.0.113.1)
      Origin IGP, metric 0, localpref 200, valid, external, best
  65200 65100
    198.51.100.1 from 198.51.100.1 (198.51.100.1)
      Origin IGP, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, external
```

*To explain why a path won, compare the two entries in the table's order and stop at the first difference. Here it's localpref 200 vs 100, at step 2.*

**📝 Exam-style questions — 28.6**

**Q1.** R1 has three paths to 172.30.0.0/16. All have weight 0 and LOCAL_PREF 100, none is locally originated, and AIGP isn't used. Which path wins, and at which step?

| Path | Type | AS_PATH | Origin | MED |
|------|------|---------|--------|-----|
| A | eBGP | 65100 65300 | i | 0 |
| B | iBGP | 65200 | ? | 0 |
| C | eBGP | 65400 | i | 0 |

- **A.** Path A, at the eBGP-over-iBGP step
- **B.** Path B, at the AS_PATH step
- **C.** Path C, at the origin step
- **D.** Path C, at the eBGP-over-iBGP step

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Weight, LOCAL_PREF and "locally originated" tie. AS_PATH (step 5): A has 2 ASes, B and C have 1, so A is out. Origin (step 6): B is incomplete (`?`) and C is IGP (`i`). IGP is preferred, so **C wins at step 6** and the eBGP-over-iBGP step is never reached. **Why not the others:** A was eliminated at AS_PATH length. B ties C on AS_PATH length and loses on origin. D names the right path but the wrong step: the first difference decides, and that is origin.
</details>

**Q2.** Path X has weight 200 and LOCAL_PREF 100. Path Y has weight 0 and LOCAL_PREF 300. Both are valid with reachable next hops. Which path does the router choose?

- **A.** Path Y, because LOCAL_PREF applies to the whole AS
- **B.** Path X, because weight is compared before LOCAL_PREF
- **C.** Path Y, because 300 is higher than 200
- **D.** Neither; the router compares AS_PATH length to break the conflict

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** Weight is step 1 and LOCAL_PREF is step 2. The first difference decides, so weight 200 wins before LOCAL_PREF is looked at. **Why not the others:** A and C describe LOCAL_PREF correctly but ignore that weight comes first. C also compares two different attributes as if they were one number. D is wrong because the decision is already made at step 1.
</details>

**Q3.** A company is dual-homed to ISP-A and ISP-B. It wants traffic from the internet to its prefixes to arrive through ISP-A. What should it configure?

- **A.** A higher LOCAL_PREF on routes received from ISP-A
- **B.** A higher weight on routes received from ISP-A
- **C.** `set as-path prepend` on its own prefixes, outbound toward ISP-B
- **D.** A lower MED on routes received from ISP-B

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** Inbound traffic is decided by *other* ASes, so you influence them with what you advertise. Prepending makes your prefixes look farther away through ISP-B, so other networks prefer the path through ISP-A. **Why not the others:** A and B choose the exit for *your own* outbound traffic. D is set on routes you receive, so it only influences your own outbound choice (and would favor ISP-B).
</details>

**Q4.** R1 has two paths to the same prefix. Path P came from AS 65100 with MED 10. Path Q came from AS 65200 with MED 50. All earlier attributes tie, `bgp always-compare-med` is not configured, and Q wins. Why?

- **A.** MED is compared only between paths from the same neighbor AS, so it was skipped and a later step chose Q.
- **B.** A higher MED is preferred.
- **C.** MED is compared before AS_PATH length.
- **D.** Q has a lower router ID, which is checked before MED.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Each neighbor AS sets MED on its own scale, so BGP compares MED only between paths from the same neighbor AS. Here the ASes differ, so the decision fell to a later step (for example eBGP over iBGP, or IGP metric). **Why not the others:** B is wrong because the lowest MED is preferred. C is wrong because MED is step 7, after AS_PATH. D is wrong because router ID is one of the last tie-breakers.
</details>

## 28.7 Route Reflectors

**The problem:** iBGP split horizon (28.1) means every iBGP router must peer with every other one. At 10 routers that's 45 sessions; at 50 it's 1,225. Every new router means reconfiguring all the old ones. Route reflection cuts this down to one or two sessions per router.

A **route reflector (RR)** is the scalable alternative to an iBGP full mesh. Its **clients** peer only with the RR, and the RR is allowed to re-advertise iBGP routes, under rules that preserve loop-freedom.

![Route reflector reflection rules for clients and non-clients](images/c28_route_reflector.png)

```
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 2.2.2.2 remote-as 65001
 neighbor 2.2.2.2 update-source Loopback0
 neighbor 2.2.2.2 route-reflector-client     ! the ONLY extra line — configured on the RR
```

Clients need no special configuration. They peer with the RR as an ordinary iBGP neighbor.

| Route received from | RR reflects it to |
|---------------------|-------------------|
| an **eBGP** peer | all clients and non-clients (normal behavior) |
| a **client** | all **other clients** and all **non-clients** |
| a **non-client** | **clients only** (non-clients must still be fully meshed with each other) |

**Loop prevention: two new attributes.** Reflection removes the iBGP split-horizon protection, so the RR adds two attributes:

- **ORIGINATOR_ID**: the router ID of the router that first put the route into the AS. A router that receives a route carrying its **own** RID as originator drops it.
- **CLUSTER_LIST**: each RR **prepends its cluster ID** (by default its router ID; set with `bgp cluster-id`) as it reflects. An RR that sees its own cluster ID in the list drops the route. It's the iBGP equivalent of AS_PATH loop detection.

**Why does a route from a non-client only go to clients?** Because non-clients are, by definition, still in a full mesh with each other. The non-client that originated the route has already sent it to every other non-client directly, so reflecting it again would only create duplicates. Clients rely entirely on the RR, so they must receive it.

**Story Time 📖:** back to the office news rule from 28.1. The route reflector is the team lead who's officially **allowed to pass on colleagues' news**. To stop the same news going round in circles, the team lead stamps each item with **who first reported it** (ORIGINATOR_ID) and **which team leads have already relayed it** (CLUSTER_LIST). Anyone who gets an item they reported themselves, or a team lead who sees their own stamp, bins it.

**How reflection works, step by step.** R2 (RID 2.2.2.2) is the RR. R1 (1.1.1.1) and R3 (3.3.3.3) are its clients. R1 is the border router and learns 8.8.8.0/24 from the ISP.

1. R1 sends 8.8.8.0/24 to R2 over iBGP, with `next-hop-self`, so the next hop is 1.1.1.1.
2. R2 received it from a **client**, so it may reflect it to all other clients and to non-clients. It adds **ORIGINATOR_ID 1.1.1.1** (R1 put the route into the AS) and prepends its cluster ID to the **CLUSTER_LIST**: `2.2.2.2`.
3. R2 sends it to R3. Nothing else changes: the next hop is still 1.1.1.1, LOCAL_PREF and AS_PATH are untouched.
4. R3 installs it, recursing to 1.1.1.1 through the IGP:

```
R3# show ip bgp 8.8.8.0
BGP routing table entry for 8.8.8.0/24, version 22
Paths: (1 available, best #1, table default)
  Not advertised to any peer
  65100
    1.1.1.1 (metric 3) from 2.2.2.2 (2.2.2.2)
      Origin IGP, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, internal, best
      Originator: 1.1.1.1, Cluster list: 2.2.2.2
```

Reading it: `from 2.2.2.2` says who **sent** the route (the RR); `1.1.1.1` before it is the **next hop**; `Originator: 1.1.1.1` says who **originated** it inside the AS. Three different routers, three different roles. `Not advertised to any peer` is iBGP split horizon in action: R3, a client, doesn't pass the iBGP route on.

**The loop check in action:** if the route were ever reflected back to R1 (for example by a second RR), R1 would see its own RID as the originator and discard it. A second RR in the same cluster would see its cluster ID already in the CLUSTER_LIST and discard it too.

**Exam traps:**

- An RR **doesn't change the next hop** or any other attribute when it reflects. Clients still need a route to the original next hop, so `next-hop-self` belongs on the **border** router.
- An RR only reflects its **best** path. Clients therefore see fewer alternatives than a full mesh would give them, which can make their path choice suboptimal.
- Reflected paths show `Originator: … Cluster list: …` in `show ip bgp <prefix>`. Use that to confirm a route came through the RR.

**📝 Exam-style questions — 28.7**

**Q1.** A route reflector receives a route from a **non-client** iBGP peer. To which peers does it reflect the route?

- **A.** To clients only
- **B.** To all clients and all non-clients
- **C.** To non-clients only
- **D.** To no one; routes from non-clients are never reflected

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: A.** Non-clients are still fully meshed with each other, so the originating non-client has already told them. Clients depend on the RR, so they must receive it. **Why not the others:** B is the rule for routes from a *client* (or from eBGP). C reverses the rule. D is wrong because clients would then never learn the route.
</details>

**Q2.** Refer to the exhibit, taken on R3, a route-reflector client. Which statement is correct?

```
R3# show ip bgp 8.8.8.0
  65100
    1.1.1.1 (metric 3) from 2.2.2.2 (2.2.2.2)
      Origin IGP, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, internal, best
      Originator: 1.1.1.1, Cluster list: 2.2.2.2
```

- **A.** 2.2.2.2 is the next hop, and 1.1.1.1 is the route reflector.
- **B.** 1.1.1.1 originated the route and is the next hop; 2.2.2.2 is the route reflector that sent it.
- **C.** 1.1.1.1 is the route reflector, and 2.2.2.2 originated the route.
- **D.** 2.2.2.2 changed the next hop to 1.1.1.1 when it reflected the route.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: B.** The address before `(metric 3)` is the next hop, `from 2.2.2.2` is the router that sent the route (the RR, whose ID is also in the cluster list), and `Originator: 1.1.1.1` is the router that put the route into the AS. **Why not the others:** A and C swap the roles. D is wrong because an RR never changes the next hop; R1 set it to 1.1.1.1 with `next-hop-self`.
</details>

**Q3.** An engineer is converting a full mesh to a route-reflector design. What must be configured on each **client**?

- **A.** `neighbor <RR> route-reflector-client`
- **B.** `bgp cluster-id` matching the RR's
- **C.** Nothing special; the client peers with the RR as an ordinary iBGP neighbor.
- **D.** `neighbor <RR> next-hop-self`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer: C.** The only extra line is on the RR: `neighbor <client> route-reflector-client`. **Why not the others:** A goes on the RR, pointing at each client. B is an RR setting (by default the cluster ID is the RR's router ID). D is unrelated to reflection; `next-hop-self` belongs on the border router.
</details>
